Chapter 1 — The National Agencies Market

Front-matter glossary.

  • SIGINT (signals intelligence) — intelligence derived from intercepting and analysing signals, of which communications intelligence (COMINT) is the network-carried sub-discipline; this front’s strategic variant is standing, mass-scale, network-side collection at national-backbone scale, the opposite of a deployed field team’s portable collection.

  • DPI (deep packet inspection) — technology that classifies network traffic by application and protocol “up to layer 7 and beyond” and extracts metadata and, where decryptable, content, at line rate; a technology used in both this front (mass/strategic) and the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers (warrant-scoped), not a front in itself.1

  • CDR / IPDR (call-detail record / IP-detail record) — structured metadata records of communications events — who contacted whom, when, for how long, over which application or endpoint — the durable, encryption-resilient yield of backbone collection, as distinct from intercepted content.

  • Mass profiling — population-scale construction of behavioural and relational profiles over collected network data; named in this chapter as public vendor positioning, never asserted as a verified capability.

  • Relation analytics — analytics that map relationships across collected communications data to “expose networks, surface relevant entities and generate investigative leads,” turning a population of records into a graph.2

  • Crypto de-anonymization — resolution of identities, or de-anonymization of traffic, at population scale; named in this chapter strictly as public vendor positioning where it appears, never asserted, and read against the structural encryption headwind that cuts against it.

  • National-backbone collection — collection performed by a standing, passive probe wired into a carrier core, an international gateway, or an Internet Exchange Point, sized for terabit throughput and petabyte retention — this front’s defining property of volume plus standing infrastructure.

  • Encrypted-traffic intelligence (ETI) — the vendor category for machine-learning classification of encrypted flows by behaviour and statistical fingerprint, marketed as restoring visibility that TLS 1.3, ECH, and QUIC remove from classic cleartext inspection.13

1.1 The Playing Ground

National-agency SIGINT is the top of the collection stack. It is the front where an agency collects and analyses communications at the scale of a country’s network backbone, standing, continuously, and remotely. Every front below this one collects against a narrower aperture. In the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers front, a law-enforcement unit serves a warrant on a Monitoring Center for a named target. In Tactical Intelligence, a deployed team stands up an RF sensor near a present target in the field. This front is different in one defining way: the sensor is wired into the infrastructure itself. The buyer is not a police unit but a National Security, National Intelligence, or Military Intelligence agency. It needs to see, profile, and relation-map a population of communications as infrastructure — plumbed into the carrier core or the international gateway, sized in terabits per second and petabytes of retention, running without pause. The vendors name the property themselves. Vehere markets its national-scale offering as “a passive, packet-based interception system that empowers defense and intelligence agencies to detect and disrupt terror and criminal activities,” one that “silently captures and analyzes network packets without altering or interfering with communication channels ensuring non-intrusive data collection,” delivering “Terabit-speed packet capture with petabyte-scale storage and retrieval in seconds,” deployable “at international gateways, Internet Exchange Points (IXPs), or within state-level and national networks.”4 “Terabit-speed,” “petabyte-scale,” “national networks” — the vendor’s own lexicon names the single property that fixes the chapter: volume plus standing infrastructure. Tactical collection is portable and present-tense; strategic collection is fixed and continuous.

The category is also anchored from the agency-build side. NSA publicly describes developing and employing state-of-the-art SIGINT tools and systems, while PCLOB describes XKEYSCORE as an NSA data-analysis tool rather than a data-collection system.5 This public record supports an in-house analytical-capability example; it does not establish a collection topology. So the boundary that keeps this chapter coherent remains volume plus standing infrastructure on the commercial side, with the sovereign-build ceiling stated separately as the author’s market-structure inference:

National Agencies is strategic, standing, mass-scale passive collection and analytics over network and signals data at national-backbone scale — defined by volume plus standing infrastructure, not by any single technology it touches. The bright line against the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers is the legal trigger plus the scale, not the technology: DPI lives in both fronts. DPI is a technology, not a front.

That sentence does the central grading work of the chapter, so it is worth unpacking what it includes and excludes.

What this front IS. Strategic, standing, mass-scale passive collection plus analytics over network and signals data, sized to a national backbone. The recurring capabilities across the public vendor pages and the public agency record are:

  • bulk metadata collection (CDR / IPDR);
  • deep-packet inspection at carrier scale to classify protocols and applications and extract metadata and, where decryptable, content;
  • mass profiling and relation analytics over the collected population;
  • application and protocol resolution at layer 7;
  • and — as publicly positioned by some vendors, never asserted here as fact — de-anonymization and identity resolution at scale.

The form factor is the tell: a passive probe wired into a carrier core, an international gateway, or an IXP, sized for terabit throughput and petabyte retention, running continuously. That is the opposite of Tactical Intelligence’s backpack.

What this front is NOT. Three boundaries matter, and the first is the one this chapter is built around.

First, it is not warrant-scoped, per-target lawful interception delivered to a LEA Monitoring Center — that is the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers front. This is the boundary this front is built around, and it has to be stated precisely, because the technology overlaps and the front does not. A Law-Enforcement Monitoring Center receives intercept product through the carrier, under a warrant, for a named target, mediated by the lawful-interception standards (ETSI TS 102 232; 3GPP TS 33.107 / 33.108; CALEA). This front collects without a per-target warrant trigger, at population scale, standing. The bright line versus the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers is the legal trigger plus the scale — not the technology. Deep-packet inspection lives in both fronts: a DPI probe can serve a warrant-scoped Law-Enforcement-Monitoring-Center interception or a mass-strategic National-Agencies collection. DPI is a technology, not a front. The same vendor — Vehere, ClearTrail, and others — can sell into both, and several explicitly do. The grade follows the deployment posture (mass and standing versus warrant-scoped and targeted), not the silicon. I read this legal-trigger-plus-scale line as the only defensible boundary between this front and the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers, precisely because any technology test would split the same product across two fronts and double-count it. The front is defined by how, and under what authority, the box is deployed, which is observable in the vendors’ own positioning — “national intelligence,” “strategic,” “mass” versus “lawful interception,” “warrant,” “handover.”

Second, it is not field or proximity collection — that is Tactical Intelligence. A tactical IMSI catcher or direction-finding kit collects locally, against a present target, portably. This front collects remotely, at the backbone, standing. The catcher may feed identifiers into a National-Agencies analytics platform, but the catcher is Tactical Intelligence and the standing backbone platform is this front.

Third, it is not the source-agnostic fusion and analytics layer sold standalone — that is Fusion / Decision Intelligence. A mass-collection platform with a built-in profiling and relation-analytics dashboard is graded here, because its analytics are inseparable from its own collection at the carrier core. A source-agnostic fusion platform that ingests this front’s output but performs no collection of its own is Fusion / Decision Intelligence. Where a vendor sells both, the National-Agencies grade rests only on the collection-and-analytics-at-scale product, and the standalone analytics platform is referenced to Fusion / Decision Intelligence.

There is one more occupant of this front that no vendor list captures, and it sits above the commercial market rather than inside it.

Author’s inference: NSA’s public in-house-development posture, with XKEYSCORE as a documented analysis-tool example, suggests that capable buyers can build material capability and buy selectively, creating a Tier-0 ceiling that may narrow the commercially addressable top tier; public procurement shares are not established.

Three buyer misconceptions

“Mass collection means reading everyone’s content.” Increasingly, no — and this is the front’s central technical story. The reliable, durable yield of backbone collection is metadata and traffic classification, not plaintext content, because transport encryption now protects most content on the wire between TLS endpoints. Plaintext exists at those endpoints. Application end-to-end encryption is a different architecture in which an intermediary service need not hold the keys required to read the content. The report therefore treats backbone visibility and provider-held content as separate questions.6 The DPI vendors have visibly repositioned around this. ipoque (a Rohde & Schwarz company) markets its R&S PACE 2 engine to “identify and classify thousands of applications and protocols and extract metadata in real time, even if traffic is encrypted or obfuscated,” via “encrypted traffic intelligence” that “combines machine learning, deep learning and high dimensional data analysis with advanced caching methods to identify and classify underlying traffic flows.”1 I read the industry-wide pivot from “inspect content” to “classify-and-fingerprint encrypted flows” as the single most important technical fact in this front. The value proposition is migrating from content toward metadata, classification, and behavioural inference, because content is going dark — the same structural force that compresses Tactical Intelligence’s over-the-air interception, expressed at the network’s scale. The buyer who thinks a backbone tap is a national wiretap is buying yesterday’s network.

“DPI tells you who everyone is talking to.” Less and less, at the front edge of the protocol stack. QUIC carries TLS handshake bytes in CRYPTO frames over UDP and protects them according to the encryption level. Initial packet protection is publicly derivable and provides no confidentiality against a passive observer, while later Handshake and 1-RTT keys are secret. Without ECH, that observer can derive QUIC Initial keys and inspect ClientHello; with ECH, the true SNI is protected inside ClientHelloInner while ClientHelloOuter remains observable.3 Per public technical analysis, ECH “wraps the standard Server Name Indication (SNI) within an encrypted key exchange,” so “SNI filtering… breaks when ECH is in play.”78 I read the loss of classic passive content-and-true-SNI visibility as the structural headwind - and the reason vendors market ML-based encrypted-traffic intelligence instead.

Browser support is a capability ceiling, not an on-the-wire deployment share. ECH is used only when the client obtains a usable ECH configuration and the server accepts it; RFC 9849 points deployments to SVCB/HTTPS DNS publication and says effective privacy also requires encrypted DNS. A browser-version statement therefore cannot be used as a measured share of observed network connections.6

“Crypto de-anonymization at national scale is a solved, off-the-shelf capability.” It is vendor positioning where it appears at all, and is treated as such throughout this chapter. Some vendors market identity-resolution and de-anonymization at scale; this report quotes such claims only as that vendor’s public positioning, attributed, and never asserts that any vendor “can” de-anonymize at national scale. The capability is, by its nature, not externally verifiable. The strongest crypto headwind cuts directly against it: transport encryption with Perfect Forward Secrecy, plus 5G’s encryption of the permanent subscriber identifier (SUPI is concealed and the encrypted SUCI transmitted). I read crypto-de-anon-at-scale as the National-Agencies claim with the widest gap between marketing and outside-verifiability, and the one most exposed to the encryption headwind. The honest public posture is that it is an aspiration vendors position around, not a verified national capability. A named independent benchmark or reference win is the only thing that would move it from claim to evidence, none of which is publicly available.

The data and technology stack

This front’s stack is best read as four layers the national buyer assembles, unified by the fact that the sensor is wired into the backbone, standing, and sized for volume.

The first and workhorse layer is bulk access and capture at the carrier core, gateway, or IXP — terabit-speed, petabyte-scale. The workhorse is a passive probe at a high-volume aggregation point. Vehere markets “High speed and real-time passive interception platforms for lossless data extractions with next-gen DPI probe” and “Terabit-speed packet capture with petabyte-scale storage and retrieval in seconds,” deployable “at international gateways, Internet Exchange Points (IXPs), or within state-level and national networks.”4 I read “passive, at the gateway or IXP” as the commercial architectural signature of this front. Passivity plus a backbone aggregation point delivers volume plus standing, and that proposition is observable in Vehere’s first-party deployment-location language. XKEYSCORE is not used as evidence of collection topology.

The second layer is DPI and metadata extraction — classify, then extract. DPI is the engine that turns raw backbone packets into structured intelligence. It classifies which application or protocol a flow is, and extracts metadata and, where available, content. ipoque markets R&S PACE 2 as “an advanced protocol and application classification engine based on next-gen deep packet inspection (DPI) technology” delivering “real-time IP network traffic visibility up to layer 7 and beyond.”1 Allot markets its network-intelligence line as the ability to “Generate actionable intelligence through analysis of every packet of network, user, application, and security data,” delivering “carrier grade solutions that meet government security requirements” with “the capacity to manage up to 1Tbps of traffic.”9 I read DPI as the genuinely hard, capital-intensive table-stakes of this front, because sustaining “every packet” classification at carrier line rate (the 1Tbps figure) is an engineering moat. The public proxy for it is throughput claims plus classified-application count, both of which vendors publish, rather than de-anonymization, which they do not substantiate. (Allot’s scale figures are vendor self-reported and directional, not independently verified.)

The third layer is encrypted-traffic intelligence — the machine-learning pivot as cleartext disappears. Because transport encryption is removing the cleartext fields DPI traditionally read, the front has pivoted to ML classification of encrypted flows. ipoque markets R&S PACE 2 as “Future-proof: classifies encrypted (TLS 1.3, DoH, ESNI etc.) and obfuscated traffic,” via ETI that “combines machine learning, deep learning and high dimensional data analysis… to identify and classify underlying traffic flows.”1 The historical record on the same modality runs through PacketLogic, which AppLogic Networks (formerly Sandvine) built on “a proprietary library of over 3,500 application signatures updated weekly,” and the broader public technical literature describes “Encrypted Traffic Analytics… analyzing unique patterns in just the TLS Client Hello packet to derive actionable intelligence without requiring full decryption.”108 I read encrypted-traffic intelligence as the defining technical contest of this front in 2026: the winners are the engines that hold classification accuracy as the cleartext labels (SNI, handshake) vanish. “Classifies encrypted traffic” is therefore a positioning claim about ML fingerprinting accuracy, not a verifiable statement that content is being read. The credible public proxy is the published detection-rate claim plus the named protocol set (TLS 1.3 / QUIC / DoH), not any content-interception assertion. What survives is an inference surface, not plaintext: destination IP and ASN; resolver identity or plaintext DNS observations where the sensor sees them; observer-visible ClientHelloOuter and outer hello material available for JA3/JA4-style fingerprinting; packet and encrypted-record size; inter-arrival timing; and flow direction, duration, volume, and 5-tuple properties. ECH protects ClientHelloInner and the true SNI; outer/provider and network metadata plus correlation can still expose or narrow the destination. These techniques neither recover the protected SNI nor decrypt application content.6

The fourth layer is mass profiling and relation analytics over the collected population. Once collected, the population of metadata and classified flows is profiled and relation-mapped. ClearTrail markets solutions that “enable law enforcement agencies (LEAs) to perform MASS, TARGETED & TACTICAL Monitoring and Analysis across a variety of communication networks,” transforming “communication data into actionable intelligence” via “data integration and advanced data analytics by leveraging artificial intelligence models on big data.”11 I read the analytics layer as the point where this front most blurs into Fusion / Decision Intelligence, because mass profiling over collected data is analytics. The grading discipline resolves it: where the analytics are inseparable from the vendor’s own backbone collection, they are National-Agencies; where the vendor sells the analytics layer standalone to bring-your-own-source buyers, that product is Fusion / Decision Intelligence. The same vendor can land in both fronts, on two different products. (ClearTrail’s positioning explicitly spans the mass and the targeted, so its National-Agencies grade must rest on the mass-and-strategic pillar; the same line is the warrant-scoped business that belongs to the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers.)

The axes buyers discriminate on

Six dimensions separate the serious national-scale vendors, each mapping to a real, publicly observable cost-and-capability structure — with the crypto-de-anon and mass-profiling dimensions treated strictly as positioning.

  1. DPI depth and protocol coverage. How many applications and protocols a system classifies, and how deep — layer 7 “and beyond.” The public proxy is the published classified-application count and the signature-update cadence: ipoque’s “thousands of applications and protocols,” “highest traffic detection rate on the market,” weekly updates; the historical PacketLogic “over 3,500 application signatures updated weekly.”110 Every serious vendor now claims thousands of signatures plus weekly updates. I read raw signature count as necessary table-stakes, not the discriminator. The real, harder-to-verify differentiator has moved to accuracy on encrypted and obfuscated traffic, where the cleartext signature is gone. If, through H2 2026, a DPI vendor publishes an independent benchmark of classification accuracy on TLS 1.3 plus QUIC plus ECH traffic — not a self-asserted one — the “signature count is table-stakes, encrypted-accuracy is the real axis” read hardens, while with no independent benchmarks all “classifies encrypted traffic” claims stay vendor positioning.

  2. Throughput and mass-scale — the axis that is the front. Sustained classification and capture at carrier line rate. This is the cleanest public discriminator in this front, because vendors publish it: Vehere’s “terabit-speed… petabyte-scale,” Allot’s “up to 1Tbps of traffic” and “analysis of every packet.”49 I read throughput as this front’s analog of Tactical Intelligence’s form factor — the visible, hard-to-fake discriminator — because sustaining “every packet” at terabit rates is a capital and engineering reality, not a slide. If vendors continue to lead with throughput and retention figures (Tbps, PB) in their public national-grade positioning through H2 2026, the “throughput is the public discriminator” read holds. It weakens only if the front’s public marketing pivots wholly to AI and analytics and drops the scale numbers — which would itself signal the content-value erosion the next axis names.

  3. Encrypted-traffic erosion (TLS 1.3 / ECH / QUIC) — the structural headwind. The defining macro-force on this front, exactly parallel to Tactical Intelligence’s encryption compressing classic passive interception, and it works through three compounding effects. First, TLS 1.3 removed static RSA and Diffie-Hellman cipher suites; its public-key exchanges provide forward secrecy, so a server’s long-term certificate key alone no longer enables passive after-the-fact decryption.83 TLS 1.3 also permits the PSK-only psk_ke mode, which RFC 8446 says is not forward-secret. Separately, ETSI TS 103 523-3 V1.3.1 defines an explicitly enabled enterprise profile that replaces the server’s ephemeral Diffie-Hellman share with a static key and permits authorized key consumers to decrypt operator-controlled sessions. ETSI scopes that profile to enterprise and edge-termination architectures and explicitly trades away per-session forward secrecy; it does not restore arbitrary backbone decryption of third-party services.6 Second, ECH protects the true SNI inside ClientHelloInner while leaving ClientHelloOuter visible to a passive observer.73 Third, QUIC carries TLS handshake bytes in CRYPTO frames over UDP and protects them according to encryption level: Initial protection is publicly derivable and provides no passive confidentiality, while later Handshake and 1-RTT keys are secret.3 The classic passive content-and-SNI inspection value proposition is structurally shrinking as encryption hardens. I read this as the force pushing the entire front from content toward metadata, ML-based flow fingerprinting, and behavioural inference — which is why every DPI vendor now markets “encrypted traffic intelligence” rather than “content interception.” If, through H2 2026 and into 2027, vendor roadmaps and named-outlet coverage keep foregrounding ML encrypted-traffic classification over classic content interception, the compression read holds. It weakens if a vendor publicly demonstrates durable, independently verified content visibility into TLS 1.3 plus ECH plus QUIC at backbone scale.

  4. Mass-profiling capability — positioning, not asserted capability. How well a system builds population-scale profiles and relation graphs over collected data. This is framed as how a vendor markets itself, not as a fact. The public proxy is explicit profiling and relation-analytics positioning (ClearTrail’s “MASS… Monitoring and Analysis”).11 I read mass-profiling claims as the analytics-layer positioning that most needs the grading discipline applied. A “mass profiling” claim inseparable from the vendor’s own backbone collection is National-Agencies positioning; the same capability sold standalone is Fusion / Decision Intelligence. The accuracy and scale are not outside-verifiable, so it is reported as positioning with the named-reference proxy as the only escalation path.

  5. Crypto de-anonymization at scale — positioning only, handled with maximum strictness. Whether a system can resolve identities or de-anonymize traffic at population scale. This chapter makes no assertion that any vendor can do this. Such a claim enters only if a vendor states it publicly, quoted and attributed as that vendor’s positioning. The strongest structural countercurrent is documented: 5G encrypts the permanent subscriber identifier and transmits the encrypted SUCI, and for a TLS 1.3 session established using a forward-secret public-key exchange, possession of the server’s long-term certificate key alone does not enable after-the-fact decryption of a recorded session3 — both cut against de-anon at scale. I read crypto-de-anon-at-scale as the single National-Agencies claim with the widest marketing-to-verifiability gap. The honest public posture is that it is an aspiration vendors position around, citing the encryption headwind as the structural reason for skepticism, without naming any vendor as capable.

  6. Deployment resilience. Whether a system sustains collection through network change — new protocols, encryption shifts, the 2G/3G sunset, carrier-topology change — without re-engineering. The public proxy is “future-proof” positioning, signature-update cadence, and ML-adaptation claims (ipoque’s “Future-proof… classifies encrypted (TLS 1.3, DoH, ESNI),” weekly updates).1 I read resilience as a roadmap-velocity axis — the front’s macro-headwind means the durable winner is whoever adapts classification fastest as encryption and protocols move, which is why “future-proof, weekly-updated, ML-based” is the recurring public claim. The verifiable proxy is update cadence and the named-protocol set the vendor commits to publicly, not the unfalsifiable “future-proof” label itself.

The public barriers

This front’s defining barrier is not technology — it is export control, which is also the legitimacy frame for the entire national-surveillance discussion. And naming the right control line matters, because this front’s modality — IP-network surveillance — sits under a different control category from the mobile-implant and intrusion-software class that Tactical Intelligence carves out, and conflating them blurs the boundary.

Export-control regimes — the defining public barrier. National-scale network-surveillance equipment is dual-use, and three overlapping regimes gate who may sell it across borders. The Wassenaar Arrangement controls “Internet Protocol (IP) network communications surveillance systems or equipment, and test, inspection, production equipment, specially designed components therefor, and development and production software and technology therefor.”1213 The relevant control for this front is the IP-network-surveillance line under Category 5 Part 1 (Telecommunications) — distinct from the intrusion-software line under Category 4 (Computers) that governs the mobile-implant class carved out of Tactical Intelligence.12 I read the Category 5 Part 1 placement as the cleanest official articulation of this front’s boundary itself. This front’s mass-network-surveillance equipment is a Telecommunications-category control, where Tactical Intelligence’s carved-out implant class is a Computers-category intrusion-software control. The cross-front boundary is encoded in the export-control taxonomy, not asserted by this report.

The US controls track the same line and are unusually precise about what makes a system a National-Agencies-grade national-surveillance box. EAR ECCN 5A001.j captures “IP network communications surveillance systems or equipment, and ‘specially designed’ components therefor” meeting a list of specifications “on a carrier class IP network (e.g., national grade IP backbone)” — including “[a]nalysis at the application layer,” extraction of “selected metadata and application content (e.g., voice, video, messages, attachments),” “indexing of extracted data,” execution of “searches on the basis of ‘hard selectors,’” and mapping “the relational network of an individual or of a group of people.”1415 The 5A001.j definition is, in effect, a regulator’s specification of a National-Agencies system: “carrier class… national grade IP backbone,” application-layer analysis, metadata-plus-content extraction, hard-selector search, relational-network mapping. I read this as the single best public table-stakes description of the front. The capability list this chapter opened with (DPI, mass profiling, relation analytics, application resolution) is the same list the US export regime uses to define the controlled item. So the front’s existence and shape are anchorable to a primary legal instrument, not to internal knowledge.

The EU layer adds a human-rights end-use test. Under Dual-Use Regulation 2021/821, Article 5 imposes an authorization requirement on the export of non-listed cyber-surveillance items where “the exporter has been informed by the relevant authority that the items in question are or may be intended for use in connection with internal repression and/or the commission of serious violations of human rights and international humanitarian law.” It defines cyber-surveillance items as dual-use items “specially designed to enable the covert surveillance of natural persons by monitoring, extracting, collecting or analysing data from information and telecommunication systems.” The Commission issued implementing guidelines on 15 October 2024.1617 I read the Article 5 catch-all as the regime most directly aimed at this front’s reputational reality. It reaches IP-network and metadata-analysis surveillance items even when no specific listing applies, and imports a human-rights end-use test. So an EU-headquartered National-Agencies vendor carries a due-diligence burden that is itself a competitive and reputational variable. Throughout, one discipline binds: any control-classification claim about a named vendor cites the regime text or the vendor’s own statement, never an analyst assertion — a wrong classification on a named company is a credibility and a defamation hit.

The enforcement edge is real and named — the Sandvine case. The most concrete public proof that this barrier has teeth is the Sandvine / AppLogic episode, and it is also the front’s cautionary public record. In February 2024 the US Department of Commerce added Sandvine Incorporated to the Entity List. Per the US Department of State, the action followed findings that Sandvine supplied deep-packet-inspection technology used by the Government of Egypt “in mass web-monitoring and censorship to block news as well as target political actors and human rights activists.”1819 Separately, Citizen Lab’s named research documented PacketLogic middleboxes being used for network injection — “Sandvine’s PacketLogic Devices Used to Deploy Government Spyware” and, in the Eltantawy case, “a Sandvine PacketLogic middlebox” on “a link between Telecom Egypt and Vodafone Egypt” used to inject Predator spyware against a former Egyptian MP after he announced a presidential bid.2021 Commerce removed Sandvine from the Entity List in October 2024 “following significant corporate reforms,” and the company rebranded as AppLogic Networks in March 2025.2223 (Every negative in this paragraph is attributed to a named outlet, an official record, or the company’s own statement; this report asserts no negative about any named vendor on its own authority. Predator / Intellexa appears only as the named-outlet-documented injected payload, never as a graded contender.) I read the Sandvine episode as the front’s defining public legitimacy fact. The same DPI-at-backbone capability that defines this front is the capability regulators and researchers scrutinize for human-rights misuse. That is why export-control posture, end-use due diligence, and “we exited non-democratic markets / sell software only” positioning have become competitive and reputational variables in this front, not just compliance overhead.

Clearance and FOCI for US programs. For classified US national-security programs, the vendor and its personnel must clear, and foreign ownership is a structural barrier independent of product quality. That barrier is treated in depth in the Fusion / Decision Intelligence chapter (FOCI mitigation via the SF 328 process administered by DCSA) and applies to this front’s vendors identically. For this front specifically, FOCI compounds the in-house-build ceiling: the top-tier US buyer may build its own, and where it buys, the foreign-headquartered vendor faces a FOCI gate an excellent product cannot route around without a mitigation structure.

The export-control regime stack (Wassenaar Cat 5 Part 1, EU 2021/821 Art. 5, US EAR 5A001.j, FOCI/clearance) with the accountability/sanctions overlay that concentrates legitimate supply. Control-classification claims cite regime text, never analyst-asserted. Conceptual, not data-derived. Not investment advice.

1.2 The Terrain

Market size: four named markets, walled, never averaged — and one honest non-claim

There is no clean public dollar figure for this front’s national mass-collection software slice. The honest way to size this front is to set the public estimates of the adjacent markets side by side and let the spread between definitions speak. The defining problem is structural. National mass-collection budgets are opaque or classified, much of the equipment is sold under export control, and the specialist vendors are mostly private. So no research publisher isolates this front’s mass-collection slice. What exists publicly are several adjacent markets — lawful interception, deep-packet inspection / network intelligence, signals intelligence, and telecom / network analytics. Each is scoped differently. Each is blended across National Agencies (mass strategic collection) and the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers (warrant-scoped lawful interception), or across the commercial technology layer. And each disagrees with the others by multiples. They are walled below and deliberately not summed — summing would multiply-count the vendors that appear in more than one definition. The spread between definitions, and the opacity within the National-Agencies slice, is the finding. All figures are research-publisher numbers and are directional; none should be quoted as authoritative.

The first market is lawful interception, the broadest published figure that touches this terrain. But as published it blends warrant-scoped, carrier-mediated interception (the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers’ domain) with the network-collection plumbing that also serves strategic collection (National Agencies). The publishers disagree wildly, on the level and on the trajectory alike. It is carried only as the outer interception envelope, with the explicit caveat that the National-Agencies mass-collection slice is a small, opaque sub-fraction of it.

I read the tight CAGR cluster as evidence the interception category overall is genuinely fast-growing. But the dollar level is a blended figure spanning this front and the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers dominated by carrier-mediated lawful interception — the warrant-scoped business that belongs to the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers. The binding caveat: this is the outer interception envelope, and strategic mass collection is an un-isolated sliver of it; it is not the National-Agencies market.

The second market is deep-packet inspection / network intelligence, the closest technology proxy to this front’s mass-collection core — bulk inspection of network traffic at the backbone. But the published DPI market is dominated by commercial telecom and enterprise use cases (traffic management, quality-of-experience, cybersecurity), not government mass collection. And the publishers disagree by an order of magnitude on the 2025 base.

The DPI 2025 base ranges from roughly USD 5.7B (Market Research Future) to roughly USD 33.7B–38.3B (Precedence, Fortune) — a roughly six-to-seven-fold spread for ostensibly the same technology category. It turns entirely on whether “DPI” is scoped as a standalone inspection-software market or as the whole network-traffic-analysis stack it sits inside. I read the spread itself as the result: DPI is a horizontal technology, not a National-Agencies market. The government mass-collection use of DPI is a thin, opaque slice of a market whose mass is commercial telecom and enterprise security. The CAGRs cluster high (19%–24.5%), consistent with AI and ML being bolted onto DPI for encrypted-traffic handling. If a methodology-disclosed publisher ever isolates “government / national-security DPI collection,” it lands far below any of these horizontal DPI figures.

The third market is signals intelligence (SIGINT) / communications intelligence (COMINT), the most conceptually aligned public anchor to this front — strategic, national, mass-scale. But as published it is dominated by airborne, naval, and space SIGINT platforms and the defense primes’ hardware, far broader than the network-collection software this front’s commercial vendors sell. It is carried as the strategic ceiling on the addressable pool.

The COMINT sub-segment is stated to be ~59% of SIGINT in 2025 (GM Insights) — the slice most aligned to this front’s network and communications focus. I read SIGINT as the strategic and military ceiling on the addressable pool, not a mass-network-collection software size; this front’s commercial-vendor slice is an un-isolated sub-fraction dominated by the primes’ platform revenue.

The National Agencies mass-collection slice: a labeled non-claim, not a segment size

No clean public dollar figure isolates this front’s national mass-collection software slice. National-collection budgets are opaque or classified, much of the equipment is sold under export control, and the specialist vendors are mostly private. Given that, the thin-material result is expected and honest, not a gap to be filled by invention. The four definitions above bracket adjacent markets that overlap heavily and must not be summed. Set them side by side. Lawful interception (roughly USD 5.5B–8.2B, 2025/26) is the blended interception outer envelope spanning this front and the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers, dominated by the Monitoring Centers’ warrant-scoped business. Deep-packet inspection / network intelligence (roughly USD 5.7B–38B, 2025) is the technology layer this front rides on, but with six-to-seven-fold publisher disagreement and overwhelmingly commercial. SIGINT (roughly USD 17.7B–18.5B, 2025), with COMINT ~59% of it, is the prime-and-platform-dominated strategic ceiling. And telecom / network analytics (roughly USD 4.1B–9.3B, 2025) is the commercial analytics envelope. The DPI makers appear in both the DPI and lawful-interception figures, the SIGINT primes appear in SIGINT, and the analytics players span telecom analytics and network intelligence. So summing would multiply-count the same companies and the same revenue. The hardest public currency for National Agencies sizing is not any market derivative at all. It is the two public issuers whose disclosures touch this front directly.

The first is Allot Ltd. (NASDAQ / TASE: ALLT), the single near-pure-play public issuer in the DPI / network-intelligence layer this front rides on. Its disclosed revenue is therefore the cleanest filing-grade evidence that commercial demand for DPI and network intelligence is real and the technology base is healthy. The figure is carried strictly at the disclosed level, the most recent reported quarter, never as a National-Agencies government-collection size and never extrapolated. For the quarter ended 31 March 2026 (Q1 2026), Allot reported total revenue of USD 26.4M, up 14% year-over-year — a third consecutive quarter of double-digit growth. Security-as-a-Service revenue was USD 8.7M (up 71%), March 2026 SECaaS ARR was USD 33.7M (up 59%), and recurring revenue was 67% of total. The company returned to GAAP operating income of USD 1.5M (5.8% margin), versus a USD 0.7M operating loss a year earlier, at a GAAP gross margin of 70.9%. Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was reaffirmed at USD 113–117M.38 Allot describes itself as “a leading global provider of innovative Security-as-a-Service (SECaaS) and network intelligence solutions for communications service providers and enterprises.”38 I read Allot as evidence that the commercial DPI and network-intelligence base is healthy and pivoting toward recurring security services. Allot is a near-pure-play DPI / network-intelligence vendor running roughly USD 105M annualized revenue, returned to GAAP operating profit, with SECaaS the growth engine. I do not read it as evidence on the National-Agencies government mass-collection market: Allot’s disclosed business is service-provider and enterprise, not national mass collection. The datapoint anchors the technology layer’s health; it does not size the National-Agencies slice. If Allot’s revenue growth falls back below roughly 5% across two consecutive 2026 quarters, the “DPI / network-intelligence technology base is healthy and growing” read weakens. (Allot trades as NASDAQ / TASE: ALLT and the trading-position statement in the front-matter applies; the figure should be re-verified against the next 6-K at authoring rather than carried out of date.)

The second is BAE Systems (LSE: BA.L), the relevant public anchor for the strategic national-security end of this front, carried strictly at the disclosed Cyber & Intelligence segment level, never as total BAE revenue. BAE Systems Digital Intelligence (formerly Detica, then BAE Systems Applied Intelligence) is the unit closest to this front, operating in “cyber security, data and digital solutions, space systems and battlespace integration,” with products spanning cybersecurity, surveillance, and data analysis.39 For the year ended 31 December 2025 (FY2025), BAE reported Cyber & Intelligence segment sales of £2.4B, within group sales of £30.7B and a record order backlog of £83.6B.40 I read the £2.4B Cyber & Intelligence segment as confirming that a prime-scale national-security cyber and intelligence business is real and material. But the National-Agencies mass-collection software slice inside it is opaque, because the segment also carries cybersecurity, digital solutions, space, and battlespace, and the National-Agencies-specific slice is not separately disclosed. Trading-position statement applies (BA.L is a named public security). If BAE discloses a material decline in Cyber & Intelligence segment sales through FY2026, the “prime national-intelligence demand is durable” read weakens. (Re-verify against the next BAE results at authoring.)

Demand drivers

Four forcing functions carry the analytical weight the opaque market numbers cannot.

The encryption arms race compressing classic passive inspection — the structural ground. TLS 1.3, ECH, QUIC / HTTP-3, and encrypted DNS are eroding classic passive network inspection. ipoque states that modern encryption increasingly restricts exposed data and positions encrypted-traffic intelligence as behavioural, statistical, heuristic, and ML-based classification.41 Its separate characterization of QUIC as hiding the full ClientHello and hostname is vendor wording and is overbroad: QUIC Initial protection is publicly derivable and provides no passive confidentiality, so without ECH a passive observer can inspect ClientHello; ECH protects ClientHelloInner and the true SNI while ClientHelloOuter, provider identity, destination IP/ASN, DNS observations, and correlation signals remain observable.413 The published encryption-analysis literature independently documents the challenge for older traffic-analysis methods.42 I read this arms race as compressing classic passive payload inspection while expanding demand for metadata-, behavioural-, and ML-based profiling. (Vendor positioning plus primary protocol boundaries; true collection architecture is not externally verifiable.)

National cyber-sovereignty and data-localization mandates forcing in-country infrastructure. A measurable, dated forcing function is the wave of data-sovereignty and localization mandates that require interception and network infrastructure to sit on national territory — directly expanding national agencies’ standing-collection footprint. The count is rising: “In 2017, 35 countries had localization or cross-border control requirements. By 2023, that figure had grown to 62.”43 The interception-specific instance is concrete: in November 2025, the Netherlands, granting Starlink a license, “required that all lawful interception infrastructure sit on Dutch territory — explicitly to avoid data flowing through ‘American servers beyond Dutch oversight,’” and India “now requires satellite operators to route data through domestic ground infrastructure and localize at least 20 percent of ground stations within five years.”44 I read cyber-sovereignty as a demand multiplier specific to this front — every localization mandate that forces interception or collection infrastructure in-country is a standing-infrastructure procurement, the exact volume-plus-standing-infrastructure property that defines this front. If the count of localization and in-country-interception mandates plateaus or reverses through 2026–2027, this read weakens.

The 5G standalone core build-out forcing a collection-architecture refresh. The migration to standalone 5G cores is a named, standards-driven refresh function. The lawful-interception architecture for 5G is fixed by ETSI / 3GPP standards: ETSI TS 133.127 (LI architecture) and TS 133.128 (LI delivery). These standards define new interception interfaces (X1 task management, X2 intercept-related information, X3 communication content) that operators migrating to 5G standalone must expose.45 Each generational transition (2G → 3G → 4G → 5G-SA) obsoletes a portion of the installed collection base and forces a standards-aligned refresh. I read the 5G-SA transition as a structural, standards-driven demand pulse that favours vendors who can track 3GPP releases. If 5G-SA-aligned collection and interception solutions fail to out-grow the legacy base through 2026–2027, the refresh-cycle read weakens. (Framed strictly on the public ETSI / 3GPP standards — no vendor-specific 5G-readiness claim is asserted, which would be a defamation and credibility surface.)

Author’s inference: NSA’s public in-house-development posture, with XKEYSCORE as a documented analysis-tool example, suggests that capable buyers can build material capability and buy selectively, creating a Tier-0 ceiling that may narrow the commercially addressable top tier; public procurement shares are not established.46 Public reporting of a top-tier agency materially shifting between in-house build and commercial procurement through 2026–2027 would move this fault line.

The tech trend: from payload to inference, with AI on collected data

The single clearest 2025–2026 public tech signal in this front is the shift of the collection center-of-gravity from reading payload off the wire to inferring from metadata and behaviour, with AI and ML applied to the collected corpus. This is framed strictly as what the public record shows, not as verified architecture. As classic passive payload inspection is compressed by encryption, the public product motion is toward metadata and behavioural analysis (ML-based application and behaviour fingerprinting) and toward AI applied to whatever is collected. The vendor framing is explicit and quotable: ETI “combines improved DPI with artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques to restore visibility into encrypted network traffic” and uses “behavioural, statistical and heuristic analyses” to “identify protocols, applications and services across encrypted traffic, in real time.”41 You cannot verify the true collection architecture from outside. The observable proxies are public product-page repositioning toward ETI / AI / behavioural framing, the academic record confirming TLS-1.3 and QUIC analysis difficulty, and the health of the public DPI / network-intelligence issuer (Allot). I read the center of gravity as migrating from reading content off the wire to inferring from metadata and behaviour — which is why the DPI vendors’ public messaging now centers on ETI and AI rather than payload inspection. If vendor positioning reverts to payload-decryption framing through 2026–2027, this demotes to a watchlist item rather than a load-bearing trend.

The procurement structure

This front’s procurement is the most opaque in the report at the buy side and the most export-control-and-sanctions-gated at the sell side: national mass-collection budgets are largely classified, so the procurement is rarely visible on public portals. The supply side, meanwhile, is gated by dual-use export licensing and increasingly reshaped by sanctions and accountability actions. The gates are public-anchorable even where the deals are not.

Export licensing as the gate. For national-scale network-surveillance equipment, export control is the single richest public table-stakes barrier — and doubles as the legitimacy frame for the surveillance-vendor discussion. The Wassenaar Arrangement controls IP-network surveillance systems under Category 5 Part 1 (Telecommunications) and intrusion software under Category 4 (Computers) — the multilateral basis the national regimes implement. EU Dual-Use Regulation 2021/821 implements the Wassenaar controls into the EU’s binding dual-use list and adds the Article 5 catch-all for cyber-surveillance items not on the list where there is awareness of potential misuse. EU guidance defines controlled cyber-surveillance items to include “equipment for covertly extracting communication content and metadata that is transmitted over the air via wireless communication, and radiofrequency monitoring equipment,” and the EU updated its dual-use control list on 8 September 2025.4748 The US implemented complementary EAR controls on cybersecurity items in March 2022, reaching IP-network communications surveillance (ECCN 5A001.j) and intrusion software (4D004).47 I read export licensing as the real barrier to entry in this front’s network-collection segment: a regime-gated, licence-by-destination gate that constrains who can sell to whom independent of product quality. It is also the public lever through which accountability pressure reshapes the supply side. (Specific ECCN classifications are not asserted per vendor here; that is a defamation and credibility surface, and the regime, not a vendor-specific classification, is what is cited.)

The accountability and sanctions overhang reshaping who can sell — the Sandvine precedent. The most concrete, named, dated public signal that accountability pressure is reshaping the National-Agencies supply side is the Sandvine case — a DPI / network-intelligence vendor sanctioned, materially impaired, and forced to restructure. On 27 February 2024 the US Bureau of Industry and Security added Sandvine to the Entity List, on information that Sandvine “supplies deep packet inspection technology to the Government of Egypt, where it is used in mass web-monitoring and censorship to block news as well as target political actors and human rights activists,” with a license requirement for all EAR items and a “presumption of denial.”49 The commercial impact was material and public: Sandvine announced in September 2024 it would withdraw from 56 “non-democratic” countries, which “represent approximately 45% of Sandvine’s 2023 revenue.”50 On 21 October 2024, BIS removed Sandvine from the Entity List “following significant corporate reforms to protect human rights,” and the company subsequently completed a debt restructuring and emerged rebranded as AppLogic Networks.51 I read the Sandvine episode as the clearest public evidence that the sanctions and accountability overhang is now a first-order force on this front’s supply side. A single Entity-List designation cost a DPI vendor roughly 45% of its revenue base (its own disclosed figure) and forced a restructuring and rebrand. The mechanism is public, named, and dated; it concentrates the addressable supply toward vendors who can clear export licensing and survive scrutiny. A further named Entity-List or sanctions action materially constraining a National-Agencies network-surveillance vendor through 2026 — named-outlet-attributed — would strengthen the read; such a claim is named-outlet-attributed or dropped. (All Sandvine claims here are stated facts of the public regulatory and press record — designation, stated rationale, the company’s own disclosed revenue-exposure figure, removal, restructuring — not internal-knowledge characterizations.)

Sovereign procurement opacity. At the national mass-collection end, procurement is opaque sovereign buying, frequently classified, NDA-bound, or routed through defense-procurement channels that do not surface on public portals. A tender enters this report only via a public procurement portal or a named-outlet citation, dated — never from internal knowledge. Specific national-collection deal values are not publicly isolable and are carried as channel structure only, never as a sized figure. Layered on top of this opacity is a slow structural shift in the collection base itself. As of December 2025, “more than 300 2G and 3G switch-offs have been completed, planned, or are underway across 88 countries,”52 retiring the legacy networks that historically offered downgrade and legacy-collection paths. That is a quiet erosion of the collection surface that compounds the encryption headwind over time.

1.3 The Contenders

The National Agencies front is the deepest collection front in the report on the demand side. It covers strategic, standing, mass-scale passive collection over network and signals data, at national-backbone scale, for national-security, foreign-intelligence, and military-intelligence buyers. It is also one of the most opaque on the supply side. Classified-program opacity limits public visibility. NSA publicly states that it develops and employs SIGINT tools and systems. I use that statement as evidence that one capable operator builds material capability, not as proof that it buys nothing or that peer agencies behave the same way.

Grading therefore turns on a single boundary test, applied without exception. A vendor grades in National Agencies only if its own dated public pages market mass-scale, standing, national-backbone collection or network intelligence: bulk passive interception, deep-packet inspection at carrier or national scale, mass profiling, relation analytics over network metadata. A vendor whose public surface markets the analytical layer on top of collected data — entity resolution, fusion, decision intelligence — is graded in Fusion / Decision Intelligence and only referenced here. A vendor whose public surface markets field-deployable proximity collection is graded in Tactical Intelligence. DPI is a technology, not a front — it lives in National Agencies, the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers, and Tactical Intelligence alike — so the line is scale plus standing infrastructure, never the underlying technique.

Eight vendors are graded, against the front’s cap of eight, plus a non-vendor Tier-0 market force. The front fills its cap, and one discipline shapes the cut. The most-recognized name adjacent to this market — the rebranded Sandvine, now AppLogic Networks — has publicly and deliberately repositioned out of the intelligence framing. As a result, its current self-positioning no longer supports a mass-collection grade. It is carried as the front’s defining play and in the cut line, not force-graded on an outdated pillar.

Palantir, the other name a casual reader expects here, fails the boundary test on its public surface (analytics and decision intelligence, not standalone backbone collection). It is documented in the cut line rather than force-graded from what an insider might know. Cognyte — the name most likely to provoke “but you know more than the public page” — is graded here, but strictly on its own dated public material. Its current network-intelligence glossary describes gathering communications and SIGINT data across whole network types, which on the public record is a National-Agencies network-collection surface distinct from the decision-intelligence platform graded in Fusion / Decision Intelligence.

The eight graded names are placed across three tiers. Three are Gravity: the names a buyer cannot map the mass-collection and network-intelligence market without naming, each with a rich dated public pillar. Four are Attention: specialists whose 2026 public posture is shaping the encrypted-traffic and mass-monitoring demand. One is a Wildcard: a network-intelligence vendor graded at the edge of the rubric and held there with explicit caution because its self-positioning straddles QoE and intelligence. The analysis also carries a non-vendor Tier-0 structural force: an author-defined in-house-build ceiling. Its evidence is narrower than the label: NSA publicly states it develops and employs SIGINT tools and systems. Extending that example to a wider sovereign-program class is the author’s inference, not an established cross-agency fact.

The eight graded contenders plus the in-house Tier-0 sovereign build (the structural ceiling), across stack position (DPI-engine layer ◄──► full mass-intelligence platform) and mission orientation. Palantir and Sandvine/AppLogic are referenced, not graded (see the cut line). Conceptual, not data-derived. Not investment advice.

The cut line at the end of this section documents every candidate that did not grade and why. That lets the boundary be defended against the obvious objection — where is Palantir?, and the harder one, how is Cognyte graded here at all? — with public material, not assertion.

Gravity tier

BAE Systems — the prime-scale communications-intelligence anchor

⚠️ BAE Systems (LSE: BA.) is a public issuer; the front-matter trading-position disclosure applies. This grade is built solely from public material and is sized at the disclosed business-line level only — BAE’s digital-intelligence line is a small slice of a defence prime, never sized at total revenue.

“The BAE Systems IntelligenceReveal portfolio of solutions for Communications Intelligence and Multi-Source Analysis assists agencies in lawfully obtaining digitally sourced intelligence from the data generated by people, events and systems … The investigation of criminal or terrorist activities requires information to be gathered from the digital transactions and communications data of users.” — BAE Systems, IntelligenceReveal Communications Intelligence and Multi-Source Analysis product page, published 13 February 2025, accessed 2026-06-14 53

BAE Systems Digital Intelligence — the former Detica / BAE Systems Applied Intelligence line — is the prime-scale communications-intelligence anchor of this front. It is the one Western defence-prime name a buyer cannot map the national-agency market without naming, and the clearest public exemplar of a vendor marketing mass-scale, multi-source intelligence collection-and-analysis to nation-state agencies under a lawful frame. Its IntelligenceReveal portfolio is marketed for “Communications Intelligence and Multi-Source Analysis,” explicitly to “assist agencies in maximizing digitally sourced intelligence” across the full intelligence cycle.53 The stated wedge is national-scale multi-source ingestion. The public page describes searching “across a wide variety of data stored in different databases in different formats (including structured, semi-structured and unstructured data such as communications metadata — CDR, communications content, geolocation data, flight information, ANPR data, open-source data, etc.).”53 CDR-and-content at agency scale, across federated databases, is the mass-collection-and-analysis posture this front grades on.

The target buyer, per the public pages, is national-security, intelligence, defence, and law-enforcement agencies, served “according to the stringent regulations and laws that exist in the different countries of the customers we serve.”53 On pricing, BAE Digital Intelligence is a business line inside a public defence prime, so economics are disclosed only at the segment level in group reporting, never per program, and there is no clean per-seat public figure. Architecturally, IntelligenceReveal markets a portfolio mapped to the intelligence cycle — acquisition through dissemination — with a federated Search & Analysis module across multiple databases.53 I read this as positioning, not verified capability; true collection reach against any named network cannot be read from outside. Sourcing here is among the richest in the front, combining vendor self-positioning on a dated page with group-level filer disclosure. The disclosed-segment discipline is nonetheless strict: BAE’s digital-intelligence revenue is a slice of a much larger defence business and is never sized at total-company revenue.

Vehere — the explicit mass-network-intelligence specialist

“AI-powered Network Intelligence for National and Enterprise Security … Built for Combat. Engineered for Scale. On-Premises by Design … 100% Lossless packet capture … Petabyte-scale, Terabit-speed Performance … Mass Interception System For Security Agencies and LEAs.” — Vehere, homepage and AI Crime & Counter-Terrorism positioning, accessed 2026-06-14 54

Vehere is the clearest public exemplar in the front of a specialist that names the mass-collection mission in its own words — the vendor whose dated public pages state the National-Agencies boundary almost verbatim. It markets “AI-powered Network Intelligence for National and Enterprise Security,” built “for Scale” and “On-Premises by Design,” around “100% Lossless packet capture and forensic investigation” at “Petabyte-scale, Terabit-speed Performance.”54 Its national-security line is marketed explicitly as a “Mass Interception System For Security Agencies and LEAs,” and its external-intelligence page describes “mass collection at international gateways,” supporting “mass, wide, and targeted intelligence collection with terabit-speed packet capture and petabyte-scale storage,” capturing “raw network traffic across subsea cables and satellite communications … at national scale” from “subsea cable landing stations, terrestrial network nodes, satellite ground stations, and telecom exchange points.”55 Mass collection at international gateways, at national scale — volume plus standing infrastructure — is the defining property of this front, stated by the vendor itself.

The target buyer, per the public pages, is national-security and intelligence agencies, CERTs/CSIRTs/national SOCs, and telecom operators (for the warrant-scoped lawful-interception line, which sits adjacent in the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers).5455 On pricing, Vehere is private; economics are undisclosed and not asserted. Architecturally, Vehere markets a full-packet-capture-and-NDR core with petabyte storage and terabit-line-rate processing, layered with AI analytics for crime and counter-terrorism.54 The “process massive traffic volumes at full line rate” and “see everything, everywhere” claims are read as positioning, not externally verified throughput. Sourcing rests on the vendor’s own pages: the homepage and the external-intelligence page were re-fetched 2026-06-14 carrying the pillars verbatim. No public 2026 financial disclosure exists, so the war-chest read for Vehere is “private, undisclosed.”

ClearTrail Technologies — the mass-monitoring COMINT specialist

“ClearTrail solutions enable the LEAs to perform MASS, TARGETED & TACTICAL Monitoring and Analysis across a variety of communication networks.” — ClearTrail Technologies, corporate positioning, accessed 2026-06-14 56

ClearTrail Technologies is the third Gravity name — an India-headquartered communication-intelligence specialist whose public positioning names the mass-collection mission directly and whose flagship platform is marketed for nationwide IP-and-voice monitoring. The corporate framing markets solutions that “enable the LEAs to perform MASS, TARGETED & TACTICAL Monitoring and Analysis across a variety of communication networks,”56 and ClearTrail describes more than two decades “creating powerful intelligence and investigation technologies for federal and state level security agencies across the globe.”56 Its ComTrail platform is publicly described as “an integrated product suite for centralized interception and monitoring of voice and data networks,” a “next generation monitoring center” that “undertakes mass monitoring of IP and Voice networks and retains data upon request,” paired with a CARBN.AI product for “extracting intelligence from IP transactions.”5657 Mass monitoring of IP and voice networks, with retention, is the standing-collection posture this front grades on, distinct from the warrant-scoped, single-target Monitoring Center that anchors the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers front.

The target buyer, per the public pages, is national and state-level security and intelligence agencies and law enforcement, with a footprint the company describes publicly across multiple countries.56 On pricing, ClearTrail is private; economics are undisclosed and not asserted. Architecturally, ClearTrail markets a centralized interception-and-monitoring core (ComTrail) with DPI, COMINT, and analytics layers, plus an AI module (CARBN.AI) for IP-transaction intelligence and an Intelligence Fusion Platform.5657 The mass-monitoring and AI-analytics claims are read as positioning, not externally verified capability. Sourcing rests on the vendor’s own current corporate and product pages (re-confirmed 2026-06-14) for the current self-positioning, and on named third-party documentation for the older mass-monitoring detail. That historical detail — the description of an “Internet Monitoring Suite” referencing “mass monitoring, deep packet inspection, COMINT, SIGINT, tactical Internet monitoring, network recording and lawful interception” — is carried via named third-party surveillance-industry documentation (the WikiLeaks Spy Files 3 / CIS-India catalogue), dated and explicitly attributed as third-party characterization, not as ClearTrail’s current self-positioning.57 No public 2026 financial disclosure exists (private).

Attention tier

Cognyte — the network-intelligence/SIGINT surface, graded on its own glossary

Banner: Cognyte is graded here on dated public material only, with no internal knowledge used. The author served as VP Product at Cognyte; this grade is independent ProductBeacon research built from Cognyte’s own current product/glossary pages, registered trademark, and SEC filing, and reflects the author’s personal analysis, not Cognyte’s position. The gap between Cognyte’s soft public headline and its own deeper public/legal record is shown as a sourced contrast, never as an asserted intent.

“Network Intelligence refers to intelligence which is obtained from fixed, mobile, IP, cable and satellite communications networks … the gathering and analysis of signals intelligence (SIGINT) data sources using machine learning and AI.” — Cognyte, Network Intelligence glossary, cognyte.com/glossary/network-intelligence/ (accessed 2026-06-16) 58

Cognyte sits in the Attention tier. As with its placements elsewhere in this report, the grade rests on one dated public pillar: here the network-intelligence/SIGINT glossary. That pillar is deliberately not the NEXYTE decision-intelligence platform that anchors Fusion / Decision Intelligence, nor the border-protection page that anchors Tactical Intelligence.

The pillar is Cognyte’s own glossary. It defines Network Intelligence as intelligence “obtained from fixed, mobile, IP, cable and satellite communications networks,” and as “the gathering and analysis of signals intelligence (SIGINT) data sources using machine learning and AI.”58 In Cognyte’s own words, that is a description of gathering communications and SIGINT data across whole network types. It is the network-collection surface this front grades, separate from the analytics layer above it.

What makes the grade defensible is keeping Cognyte’s two public surfaces apart. One is a soft “decision intelligence” national-security platform page (NEXYTE), graded in Fusion / Decision Intelligence as the analytics layer. The other is this network-intelligence/SIGINT-gathering glossary, describing collection across network types, which is the National-Agencies surface graded here. The contrast is itself the publishable observation: the same vendor publishes both a soft platform headline and a harder collection-and-SIGINT glossary, and each is graded where its own public page puts it.

Here is the analytically interesting read, and I label it as mine. I read “Network Intelligence,” as Cognyte’s own glossary defines it — the gathering of communications data from fixed, mobile, IP, cable and satellite networks plus SIGINT sources — as a description of mass-scale collection. It is the softer label for what Cognyte’s own registered VANTAGE trademark calls “the integrated interception, collection, monitoring, analyzing, searching, tracking and reporting of data and voice communications.”59

Put as a falsifiable frame: is there another way to read “gathering and analysis of communications data obtained from fixed, mobile, IP, cable and satellite communications networks” than as collection at network scale? I do not see one, but the read is stated as a read, grounded in Cognyte’s own two sources, the glossary and the trademark. A Cognyte public page that defined Network Intelligence as something narrower than network-scale gathering would weaken it.

The word “mass” here is drawn from Cognyte’s own current sources. Those are the glossary’s framing of network-wide gathering across fixed, mobile, IP, cable and satellite networks plus SIGINT data, and Cognyte’s own registered VANTAGE goods-description (“integrated interception, collection, monitoring”). It is not drawn from the Verint-era “nationwide mass interception” collateral, which is carried only as inherited lineage and is corroboration of that lineage, never the semantic source of the word “mass.”

The read also does not depend on its corroborators. It holds on the current glossary alone — Cognyte’s own definition of network-wide gathering of communications and SIGINT data across fixed, mobile, IP, cable and satellite networks. So even setting aside the VANTAGE goods-description and the 20-F sentence entirely, the opinion-labeled read still rests on the directly-fetched glossary.

Both corroborators are now confirmed. The 20-F origin sentence is verbatim-confirmed against Cognyte’s filed SEC Form 20-F. The VANTAGE goods-description is confirmed against the USPTO record. The glossary-only robustness point is retained regardless.

This is an opinion about terminology, drawn from Cognyte’s own dated material. It asserts no specific Cognyte mass-deployment as fact, and it attributes no intent. The contrast between the soft glossary label and the hard trademark wording is shown, not narrated as motive.

The grade construction is explicit about what carries it and what does not. Cognyte is placed in Attention, not Gravity. The Gravity tier here is the names with a rich dated public collection-platform pillar — BAE’s IntelligenceReveal, Vehere’s mass-interception system, ClearTrail’s ComTrail. Cognyte’s public National-Agencies footprint is a glossary plus filing-and-trademark lineage, not a standalone national-backbone collection product page.

The corroboration runs through Cognyte’s own filings and lineage. Cognyte’s SEC Form 20-F describes the company’s origin as an “initial focus on products for lawful communications interception.”60 The VANTAGE mark — “telecommunication surveillance software for the integrated interception, collection, monitoring, analyzing, searching, tracking and reporting of data and voice communications” — is now a registered mark of Cognyte Software Ltd. (USPTO Serial 78417244), the bridge that makes the interception lineage Cognyte-attributable today even though the richest product collateral predates the spinout.59

That collateral is Verint-era and is framed strictly as inherited lineage, not as a current Cognyte product. Cognyte spun out of Verint Systems in February 2021, and Verint’s own VANTAGE marketing was quoted by a named outlet — Slate (Gallagher, 2013-01-30) — as a monitoring centre that “enables ‘nationwide mass interception’” of “billions of communications,”61 which I carry only as the documented Verint-era lineage Cognyte inherited at the spinout, attributed to the outlet and to Verint’s own words, never as a present Cognyte capability.

The target buyer, on the glossary’s own framing, is the national-security and intelligence agency. On pricing, Cognyte’s network-intelligence line is not separately disclosed; its public financials are group-level, and the Convergence chapter carries those.

The current glossary was directly fetched and quoted verbatim. The 20-F business-description sentence is now verbatim-confirmed against Cognyte’s filed SEC Form 20-F (FY2026, filed 2026-03-25; the origin clause recurs across FY2021–FY2026). The VANTAGE goods-description is confirmed against the USPTO record. Both corroborate the central scale read above.

A separate Cognyte-era named-outlet item — Reuters (2023), reporting, based on documents provided by Justice For Myanmar, that Cognyte won a tender to supply intercept technology to a Myanmar state-backed telecom — is carried as a litigation-sensitive footnote only, attributed, never headlined, and not as an asserted fact in this report’s voice.62

Consistent with the front-wide discipline, none of Cognyte’s lineage artifacts is asserted here as a present collection capability; they are dated records of positioning, registration, and origin, quoted and attributed. The only scale characterization in this grade is the explicitly opinion-labeled read above.

Cognyte is a cross-front vendor. It is also graded in the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers (the NEXYTE lawful-interception “data source” framing), Tactical Intelligence (the border-protection “SIGINT, OSINT and VISINT” line), Fusion / Decision Intelligence (the NEXYTE decision-intelligence platform), and Open-Source Intelligence (LUMINAR WEBINT). The National-Agencies pillar graded here — the network-intelligence/SIGINT glossary — is distinct from each of those and is logged for the cross-front reconciliation.

Trovicor — the monitoring-and-intelligence incumbent (National Agencies surface)

“Trovicor’s Intelligence Platform fuses and enriches data with both structured and unstructured data from existing 3rd-party systems or national databases and performs real-time analysis.” — Trovicor, Intelligence Platform / Monitoring Center positioning, accessed 2026-06-14 63

Trovicor is the long-standing monitoring-and-intelligence incumbent, a Munich-rooted vendor (with a present-day FZ-LLC structure) that is a cross-front name. Trovicor is graded in National Agencies here on its mass-data Intelligence Platform surface and is a primary Monitoring-Center name in the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers on a different pillar. Founded in 1993, Trovicor publicly describes itself as a provider of “end-to-end monitoring and intelligence solutions” to governments worldwide.63 For the National-Agencies mass-intelligence surface, the graded pillar is its Intelligence Platform, which Trovicor markets to “fuse and enrich data with both structured and unstructured data from existing 3rd-party systems or national databases” and “perform real-time analysis,”63 sitting above a Monitoring Center publicly described as capturing, monitoring, evaluating, and sorting “vast amounts of communication, interaction and transaction data from fixed and mobile telephone networks and internet in one single platform.”63 Vast amounts of communication data from fixed, mobile, and internet networks, against national databases is the mass-scale property graded here. The warrant-scoped Monitoring Center pillar is reserved for the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers, and the cross-front ledger keeps the two pillars distinct.

The target buyer, per the public pages, is government security and intelligence agencies.63 On pricing, Trovicor is private; economics are undisclosed and not asserted, and no internal or CI-derived sizing is used. Architecturally, Trovicor markets a modular Monitoring-Center-plus-Intelligence-Platform stack spanning collection, mediation, enrichment against national databases, and real-time analysis.63 This is read as positioning. Sourcing rests on the vendor’s own current pages (re-confirmed 2026-06-14). No public 2026 financial disclosure exists (private); funding and ownership color circulating via aggregators is not carried as fact.

Kommlabs Dezign — the passive mass-interception specialist

“Passive Mass Communication Interception Solution … Mass Interception solution for Intelligence Agencies using passive probes for traditional circuit switched networks and packet switched networks.” — Kommlabs Dezign, VerbaPROBE product positioning, accessed 2026-06-14 64

Kommlabs Dezign is the passive-mass-interception specialist — an India-headquartered vendor whose product line names the standing-collection mission explicitly and separates it cleanly from the warrant-scoped lawful-interception product. The company publicly cites “27 Years Experience,” “100+ Installations Worldwide,” and a “3 Continents” deployment footprint, and states that it serves “Counter Terrorism, Intelligence and Law Enforcement Agencies.”64

Architecturally, it markets a passive-probe mass-collection product (VerbaPROBE) alongside a standards-compliant lawful-interception product (VerbaCENTRE), a real-time location product (VerbaTRACK), and an analysis layer (ReveaLINX).64 All read as positioning. The installation and experience counts are carried as the company’s own publicly-stated claims, attributed to its pages, not as independently verified figures.
