Chapter 3 — The Tactical Intelligence Market

Front-matter glossary.

  • IMSI / IMEI catcher (cell-site simulator) — a field device that, per the Electronic Frontier Foundation, “masquerade[s] as legitimate cell-phone towers, tricking phones within a certain radius into connecting to the device.” Its purpose is to collect cellular identifiers (IMSI = the subscriber identity, IMEI = the device/equipment identity), detect a handset’s presence, and — on a downgraded link — intercept. Active variants transmit; passive variants only listen.207

  • Direction finding (DF) / geolocation — locating a transmitting device to a physical point using techniques such as Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA — “comparing the signal’s arrival time at three or more nodes”) and Angle of Arrival (AoA — “using two direction finding arrays”).208

  • Tactical vs strategic interception — tactical collection is field-deployable, proximity-bound, portable, and run against a present target in operational time (this front). Strategic collection is standing, mass-scale, network-side collection at national-backbone scale (the National Agencies front). The dividing line is proximity / portability / tempo versus volume / standing infrastructure.

  • Device forensics / extraction — recovery of digital evidence from a seized device “under forensically sound conditions.” It runs via logical (the tool communicates with the operating system through an API), full-file-system (privileged “root” access to copy the entire file system and its decryption keys), or physical (“a bit-by-bit copy of the physical memory (NAND flash)”) methods. This is the device-in-hand modality of this front.209

  • RF-proximity collection — collection performed by hardware operating on the radio link in the physical vicinity of the target (catchers, DF, Wi-Fi / Bluetooth collection). It is distinct from remote software-implant exploitation, which compromises the device over the network from inside its trust boundary and is carved out of this front entirely (see the Plays section).

3.1 The Playing Ground

Tactical intelligence is the front where collection comes off the network backbone and into the field. Every front above this one collects at a distance — a national agency tapping a carrier core, a law-enforcement unit serving a warrant on a Monitoring Center. This front is different in a single, defining way: the collector is physically present. The buyer is a deployed team — a surveillance unit, a counter-terror element, a border or prison authority, a military tactical cell. That team needs to identify, locate, or collect from a target device in the operator’s own vicinity, in operational time. The vendors name the property themselves. Rayzone Group markets its tactical line as “last-mile SIGINT capabilities, empowering tactical teams with real-time situational awareness and on-site threat mitigation,” delivered through “Tactical RF interception for 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G networks” and “Designed for stationary, portable, and airborne deployment.”210 “Last-mile,” “on-site,” “portable,” “airborne” — the vendor’s own lexicon names the line that fixes the chapter: physical proximity / portability plus operational tempo. That property, and nothing about the underlying radio technology, is what separates this front from the two collection fronts above it.

The category’s core sensor is anchored just as cleanly from the other side. The Electronic Frontier Foundation defines a cell-site simulator as a device that “masquerade[s] as legitimate cell-phone towers, tricking phones within a certain radius into connecting to the device rather than a tower.”207 The phrase within a certain radius is the boundary itself: this front’s sensors are range-limited and locally present, where the National Agencies’ collection is standing and remote. The boundary that keeps this chapter coherent has to be stated with unusual precision. The technology rhymes across fronts even as the operational shape does not:

Tactical Intelligence is field-deployable RF / proximity collection against a present target — defined by physical proximity, portability, and operational tempo, not by the radio technology it touches. Remote mobile-implant exploitation (the NSO / Candiru / Intellexa / Pegasus / Predator class) is a technically distinct modality that is carved out of this front and is never graded.

That sentence does the central grading work of the chapter, so it is worth unpacking what it includes and excludes.

What this front IS. Field-deployable RF / proximity collection against a present target. The recurring capabilities across the public vendor pages are: cellular-identity collection — IMSI / IMEI and related identifiers — via active or passive catchers; tactical cellular interception; Wi-Fi and Bluetooth identifier collection and exploitation; direction finding and geolocation of a handset to a physical point; and border or checkpoint cellular identification. The form factor is the tell — fixed, vehicular, body-worn, backpack, or airborne — because the system has to go where the target is. Septier, for one, markets a Guardian “Airborne” variant alongside its ground units.211 Sitting adjacent to the RF modalities is a second, increasingly inseparable one: device forensics at the edge. Where the target device itself is in hand — seized at a border, an arrest, a checkpoint — the tactical act is extraction, not interception, and Cellebrite, MSAB, and Magnet occupy that edge of the front.

What this front is NOT. Three boundaries matter, and the third is the one this chapter is built around. First, it is not network-side mass collection. A deep-packet-inspection appliance or a national-backbone passive-collection system sits standing at a carrier core and collects at scale and remotely; this front collects locally, against a present target. The technologies can touch the same cellular protocols, but the defining property is the line: proximity / portability / tempo versus volume / standing infrastructure. A mass-profiling SIGINT platform is strategic National-Agencies collection even if it ingests data a tactical catcher fed it. Second, it is not carrier-mediated lawful interception. A lawful-interception Monitoring Center receives intercept product through the carrier, under a warrant, mediated by the LI standards; a tactical system asks no carrier — it stands up its own transient cell or RF sensor in the field and collects directly. The legal trigger and the carrier’s involvement are the lawful-interception markers; their absence, plus proximity, is this front’s marker.

Third — and this is the line that costs the most to state and the most to get wrong — it is not remote mobile-implant exploitation. A mobile-implant product is a remote software implant: it compromises a target handset over the network, often with no proximity at all and frequently zero-click, and exfiltrates content from inside the device’s trust boundary. A tactical system is RF-proximity hardware: it manipulates or listens to the radio link near the target and collects identifiers, metadata, location, or — on a downgraded link — content, from outside the device. These are distinct modalities. They operate at different points in the kill chain and sell to overlapping but not identical buyers. And — decisively — they are governed by different export-control language: intrusion software under Wassenaar Category 4 (Computers) versus IP-network and RF surveillance under Category 5 Part 1 (Telecommunications), a split detailed in the barriers below. I read the carve-out as doing double duty, and I want to be plain that the two halves align by construction rather than by convenience. It is the technically honest boundary — an implant is not a catcher — and it happens to remove from grading exactly the cohort that is most litigation-sensitive. Because the boundary tracks three independent export-control regimes rather than an analyst’s preference, drawing it costs the analysis nothing and protects the report. The implant cohort therefore appears only as descriptive market-force commentary in the Plays section, never as a graded contender.

The graded modalities of this front (field RF/proximity collection + device-in-hand forensics) versus the carved-out remote locked never-graded set and the neighbouring fronts, anchored to the Wassenaar Category 4 / Category 5 Part 1 split. Author’s read of public material, June 2026. Conceptual, not data-derived. Not investment advice.

Three buyer misconceptions

“An IMSI catcher lets you listen to the calls.” On a modern network, mostly not. The catcher’s native, reliable yield is identity and presence — pulling identifiers, detecting and locating a device. Content interception over 4G or 5G requires defeating encryption, which is why the public record describes catchers resorting to a 2G downgrade. Per the EFF, “if the cell-site simulator is able to downgrade the cellular connection to a 2G/GSM connection then it can potentially perform much more intrusive acts such as intercepting call metadata… the content of unencrypted phone calls and text messages.”207 I read the downgrade dependency as the single most important technical fact in this front. As carriers sunset 2G and 3G, the downgrade target narrows, and the classic content-interception value proposition erodes structurally — a force the differentiation axes and the Terrain section both track. The buyer who thinks a catcher is a wiretap is buying yesterday’s network.

“Active and passive catchers are the same product with a label.” They are different risk-and-yield profiles. Passive devices, per the EFF, “do not transmit any signals — they work by plucking cellular transmissions out of the air,” while active simulators “broadcast signals that are either stronger than the legitimate cell sites around them, or are made to appear stronger” to force connections.207 Active catchers emit, which makes them detectable and increasingly detected: in March 2025 the EFF released “Rayhunter,” described as “a new open source tool… to detect cellular spying.”212 The detectability cuts directly into product positioning. Several tactical vendors now sell both the catcher and its counter, with Rayzone marketing “ArrowCell,” which “detects the presence of an IMSI catcher” and lets users “disrupt and locate their attacker.”210 I read passivity as moving from an engineering choice toward a feature buyers pay for.

“Forensics is a lab activity, separate from tactical collection.” In 2026 the public record shows that line dissolving. MSAB states that “the trend in 2026 is moving extraction to the field,” via kiosk, tablet, and express devices,209 and Cellebrite markets a “UFED Touch3 Ruggedized Tablet” that “enables comprehensive data extraction collection capabilities anywhere, whether in the lab, a remote location, or in the field.”213 I read field-forensics as the device-in-hand tactical modality converging with the device-on-the-air RF modality. The same deployed unit increasingly wants both, which is why this chapter grades edge-forensics as a part of this front rather than treating it as a separate market.

The data and technology stack

The stack is best read as four modalities the same buyer assembles, unified by the fact that the sensor is physically near the target and portable.

The first and workhorse modality is cellular-identity collection and tactical interception — the IMSI-catcher core. An active catcher impersonates a base station to pull devices into connecting; a passive unit listens to the radio environment without transmitting. The public yield is identifiers. Septier’s Guardian is publicly described as “capturing up to 11 different identifiers for each cellular device, including those using Bluetooth and Wi-Fi,” extracting “cellular identities, location, and other information from GSM, UMTS, LTE, and 5G devices in its coverage area.”214 Rayzone’s “Piranha” is described as “an SDR (Software Defined Radio) collector of mobile phone identifiers (IMSI & IMEI) in 2G, 3G, 4G and 5G environments.”215 I read the migration to software-defined radio as the quiet architectural shift inside this modality. SDR is what lets a single box claim “2G through 5G” and absorb new-protocol support in software rather than silicon. So “covers 2G–5G” is a positioning claim about software breadth, not a verifiable statement that live 5G-standalone content interception works.

The second modality is direction finding and geolocation — turning a signal into a point on the ground. A catcher tells you a target is present; DF tells you where. The public technical record describes the two dominant primitives: TDOA, which geolocates a signal “by comparing the signal’s arrival time at three or more nodes,” and AoA, “another geolocation technique using two direction finding arrays.”208 Tactical vendors fold DF into the cellular line. Septier markets a “Cellular Locator” as “a tactical location tracking solution that provides accurate location information for cellular devices, using advanced direction finders such as Septier Hunter.”214 Here a discipline matters that recurs across the front. DF accuracy under real field conditions — multipath, urban canyon, single-node versus networked — is the least externally verifiable axis in the chapter, because no vendor publishes meters-of-error under adversarial conditions. The credible public proxy is therefore form factor — man-portable versus vehicular array — which is observable. Accuracy is not.

The third modality is Wi-Fi / Bluetooth proximity collection. Modern handsets emit far more than cellular, and the same Septier identifier count explicitly spans “those using Bluetooth and Wi-Fi.”214 A distinct historical sub-modality targeted Wi-Fi directly: the Wintego “WINT” system was described by named outlets as “a tactical solution for extracting intelligence over WiFi networks, intercepting emails, social networks chats, and web browsing patterns through Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) interception… small enough to fit into a backpack.”216 (Wintego is named here only as descriptive context for the Wi-Fi-MitM modality; no current dated self-positioning page surfaces for it, and it is not graded.216) I read this modality as the one most directly squeezed by platform-level defenses. MAC-address randomization, on by default in modern iOS and Android, erodes the durable-identifier yield the same way the 2G sunset erodes the cellular-content yield.

The fourth modality is device forensics at the edge — the device-in-hand case. When the device is seized, the tactical act is extraction. The public record describes a clear technical ladder. Logical extraction has “the forensic tool communicates with the OS via API.” Full file system has investigators “elevate privileges to gain ‘Root’ access, allowing them to copy the entire file system and its decryption keys.” Physical is “a bit-by-bit copy of the physical memory (NAND flash), this is the gold standard of extraction.”209 The 2026 inflection is encryption. Per MSAB, “if a device is in a BFU (Before First Unlock) state, the data is heavily encrypted.”209 The public answer is compute — “MSAB’s latest innovation allows agencies to utilize high-power GPUs to accelerate the brute-force process; what used to take weeks can now be accomplished in hours.” Cellebrite frames its UFED as “The Industry Standard for Lawfully Accessing and Collecting Digital Data,” telling buyers “don’t let complicated locks, encryption barriers, deleted and unknown content prevent critical evidence from coming to light,” with “full file system (FFS) and physical extractions.”213 Magnet’s AXIOM is positioned to “gather all digital evidence associated with a case… whether the evidence lived on a smartphone, the cloud, a computer, a USB drive, other removable media, or even IoT-related devices.”217

I read this sub-front as the healthiest part of this front commercially, precisely because it sidesteps the air-interface encryption problem. When the device is in hand and the unlock can be brute-forced, the transport-layer crypto that defeats the over-the-air catcher is bypassed entirely.

The axes buyers discriminate on

Five dimensions separate the serious tactical vendors, each mapping to a real, publicly observable cost-and-capability structure.

  1. RF / protocol coverage, 2G to 5G. How many cellular generations a system collects against — and the buried distinction beneath the spec sheet, whether “5G support” means 5G non-standalone (still anchored to a 4G core) or true 5G standalone (where the permanent identifier is encrypted). The public proxy is explicit generation enumeration: Rayzone’s “2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G,” Septier’s “GSM, UMTS, LTE, and 5G,” Piranha’s “2G, 3G, 4G and 5G.”210214215 Every serious vendor now lists 5G. I read uniform “supports 5G” listing as table-stakes positioning, not a capability discriminator. The real, undisclosed differentiator is performance against 5G standalone with SUCI encryption, which no vendor quantifies publicly. If, through H2 2026, a tactical vendor publishes a named government reference or an independent test asserting live identity collection against a 5G standalone network — not non-standalone — the “5G is just a checkbox” read weakens. Absent that, it holds, and market commentary already flags “5G SA-compatible interception” as the white space “where no vendor has yet established a clearly dominant globally deployed commercial solution.”218

  2. IMSI-less / passive identification. Whether a system can identify or track a target without actively transmitting. This matters because active catchers are detectable, now have an open-source detector in Rayhunter,212 and trip stricter legal treatment in some regimes for the act of transmitting. The public proxy is explicit “passive” positioning and hybrid active/passive designs. Market commentary notes that “hybrid IMSI catchers, which combine active and passive capabilities, are gaining traction and are expected to be the most lucrative design niche through 2030.”219 I read the hybrid push as a direct response to detectability and to legal-operational pressure against transmitting — the same force, surfacing as an architecture choice.

  3. DF accuracy and form factor. How precisely, and from what platform, a system localizes a handset. As the stack section noted, accuracy itself is not outside-verifiable; the credible public proxy is form factor — fixed, vehicular, body-worn, or airborne (Rayzone’s “stationary, portable, and airborne deployment,”210 Septier’s airborne Guardian variant211). I read airborne and drone DF as the fastest-moving form-factor story of 2025–2026, because it closes coverage blind spots and reaches denied areas. The accuracy claims attached to any form factor, though, stay positioning until tied to a named reference.

  4. Portability and form factor as the defining axis. This is the axis that is the front. A capability delivered in a fixed rack is a strategic or lawful-interception box; the same capability in a backpack, a vehicle, a body-worn kit, or a drone payload is tactical. The public vendor lexicon foregrounds it relentlessly — “last-mile,” “tactical teams,” “portable,” “airborne,” “fits into a backpack.”210211216 I read form factor as the cleanest public discriminator in the entire front. Unlike DF accuracy or true 5G-standalone performance, it is visible in the marketing imagery and the spec sheets and cannot be faked.

  5. Encryption compressing classic passive interception — the structural headwind. This is the defining macro-force on the front, and it works through two compounding effects. First, transport encryption on 4G and 5G makes over-the-air content interception unreliable without a 2G downgrade,207 and 2G/3G sunset is steadily removing the downgrade target. Second, 5G SUPI/SUCI encryption — the standard “attempts to fix IMSI-catching issues by encrypting the permanent identifier (now SUPI) and transmitting the SUCI,” though “risks… remain through downgrade attacks and implementation flaws”220 — erodes even the identity yield over time. The classic passive content-interception value proposition is structurally shrinking as encryption hardens and legacy networks retire. I read this as the force pushing the whole front in three directions at once. It pushes toward active and hybrid catchers that manufacture a downgrade; toward device forensics, where brute-forcing the unlock sidesteps transport crypto entirely; and toward DF, metadata, and identity value over content value. If, through H2 2026 and into 2027, vendors’ public roadmaps and named-outlet coverage keep foregrounding forensics, DF, identity, and 5G-standalone research over classic passive-content interception, the compression read holds. If a vendor publicly demonstrates durable 5G-standalone content interception at scale, it weakens.

The public barriers

This front’s defining barrier is not technology — it is export control, which is also the legitimacy frame for the entire surveillance-vendor discussion. Two structural barriers sit on top of that, and naming the regimes precisely is itself a discriminator. The intrusion-software line is exactly where the carved-out mobile-implant class lives, and conflating it with RF surveillance would blur the front’s boundary.

Export-control regimes — the defining public barrier. Tactical surveillance hardware is dual-use, and three overlapping regimes gate who may sell it across borders. The Wassenaar Arrangement controls the two relevant modalities under different categories, and the split maps exactly onto the carve-out. Per a NIST summary, “the Intrusion Software and IP Network Surveillance controls represent two distinct types of definitions under different sections of the Control List, with the former under Category 4 (Computers) and the latter under Category 5 Part 1 (Telecommunications).”221 Intrusion software — the mobile-implant / Category 4 class carved out of grading — “is defined as software designed to covertly gain access to a computer or other networked device and, once inside, to extract or modify data or modify the execution path.”221 IP-network and RF surveillance — closer to this front’s graded modalities — sit under Category 5 Part 1. The December 2024 Plenary “adopted updated controls on intrusion software and IP-network surveillance systems.”221 I read the Category 4 / Category 5 Part 1 split as the cleanest official articulation of the front’s boundary itself: an implant is a Computers-category intrusion-software control; a catcher is a Telecommunications-category control.

The EU layer adds a human-rights end-use test on top of the list. Under Dual-Use Regulation 2021/821, Article 5 “mandates exporters to seek authorization if they know or suspect that their cyber-surveillance items could be used for human rights abuses, even if these items aren’t explicitly covered by existing export controls.”222 Cyber-surveillance items are defined to reach dual-use items “specially designed to enable the covert surveillance of natural persons by monitoring, extracting, collecting or analysing data from information and telecommunication systems.”223 I read the Article 5 catch-all as the regime most directly aimed at this front. It reaches RF and cellular surveillance items even where no specific control entry applies, which is why an EU-headquartered tactical vendor carries a due-diligence burden that is itself a competitive and reputational variable.

The US tracks the same split. EAR ECCN 5A001.j controls “IP network communications surveillance systems or equipment,” capturing “[a]nalysis at the application layer,” extraction of “selected metadata and application content,” and mapping “the relational network of an individual or of a group of people.”224 ECCN 4D004, by contrast, controls “‘software’ ‘specially designed’ or modified for the generation, command and control, or delivery of ‘intrusion software.’”224 The 5A001.j-versus-4D004 pairing mirrors the Wassenaar Category 5 Part 1 / Category 4 split — the same boundary, encoded in three independent regimes rather than asserted by this report. Throughout, one discipline binds: any control-classification claim about a named vendor cites the regime text or the vendor’s own statement, never an analyst assertion. A wrong classification on a named company is a credibility and a defamation hit.

Domestic-use law as a demand-shaping barrier. Export control governs cross-border sale; domestic interception law governs use, and it is a real demand gate — a buyer that cannot lawfully deploy will not buy. The US public record is the clearest. Department of Justice policy and proposed legislation treat catcher use as warrant-gated and pen-register-scoped. Cell-site simulators “must be configured as pen registers, and may not be used to collect the contents of any communication, in accordance with 18 U.S.C. § 3127(3),”225 and the bipartisan “Cell-Site Simulator Warrant Act” was reintroduced in November 2023 to “create clear warrant requirements for use of cell site simulators by any government agency.”226 I read the “configured as a pen register, no content” constraint as the legal codification of the technical reality this chapter opened with — the catcher’s reliable yield is identity and metadata, not content. The law and the physics point the same way, and together they narrow the legitimate use case toward identify and locate rather than intercept content. Outside the US, each EU member state runs its own interception-authorization regime, and comparable per-state public detail is not uniform. So this chapter asserts the US warrant frame and flags non-US domestic-use law as a thin-material area rather than manufacturing a universal rule.

3.2 The Terrain

Market size: four named markets, walled, never averaged

There is no clean public dollar figure for the tactical field-collection software slice. The honest way to size this front is to set the public estimates of the adjacent markets side by side and let the spread between definitions speak. The defining problem here is the sharpest in the report: no research publisher sells a methodology-disclosed “tactical SIGINT / field-collection software” figure. What exists publicly are four adjacent markets, each scoped differently, each bleeding into either carrier-mediated lawful interception, network-side mass collection, or general-purpose forensics. They are walled below and deliberately not summed — summing would multiply-count the vendors (Cellebrite, MSAB, the catcher makers) that appear in more than one definition. All figures are research-publisher numbers and are directional; none should be quoted as authoritative.

The first market is lawful interception, the broadest published figure that touches this terrain. It is dominated, though, by carrier-mediated, warrant-scoped interception, which is the Monitoring Centers’ domain, not field collection. It is carried only as the outer envelope, the largest published “interception” pool, with the explicit caveat that the tactical slice is a small, opaque sub-fraction of it.

MarketsandMarkets Lawful interception by network, component, type USD 8.20B (2026) → USD 24.60B (2032)228 20.1% (2026–2032)
Mordor Intelligence Lawful interception market USD 5.47B (2025) → USD 6.47B (2026) → USD 14.98B (2031)229 18.27% (2026–2031)

The three publishers bracket the 2025 lawful-interception market at roughly USD 5.5B–7.5B, with CAGRs clustering tightly in the high-teens to low-twenties. I read the tight CAGR cluster as evidence the interception category overall is genuinely fast-growing. The dollar level, though, is the Monitoring Centers’, not this front’s, because lawful interception as published is the warrant-scoped business of the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers front. The binding caveat: this is the outer interception envelope, and field / proximity collection is an un-isolated sliver of it. It is not this front’s market.

The second market is IMSI-catcher and cellular interception, the tightest public fit to this front’s field-collection core — RF-proximity collection against a present cellular target. It is also far smaller than lawful interception, consistent with the narrower field-hardware scope.

Publisher Definition used Figure (as stated) CAGR / period
MarketIntelo IMSI catcher market (devices mimicking cell towers for ID/location/interception) USD 400M (2024) → USD 950M (2033)230 9.8%
Mordor Intelligence Technologies/solutions to “intercept, monitor, and analyze cellular communications” for LEA/intelligence/government USD 695.49M (2025) → USD 735.69M (2026) → USD 921.57M (2031)231 4.61% (2026–2031)
Mordor Intelligence (IMSI-catcher variant) IMSI catcher market USD 182.57M (2025) → USD 207.68M (2026) → USD 306.47M (2031)232 8.08%

This is where the definitional incoherence is starkest, and the spread is the finding. The “cellular interception” framing brackets 2025 at roughly USD 695M; the narrower “IMSI catcher” framing brackets 2025 at roughly USD 183M; a third single-firm IMSI-catcher framing (MarketIntelo) puts the 2024 base at roughly USD 400M. That is a roughly four-fold spread (USD 183M to USD 695M) for ostensibly the same field-collection category, turning entirely on whether “cellular interception” pulls in software and services or only catcher hardware. I read the spread itself as the result. The field-collection software slice that this front’s contenders actually sell sits somewhere inside the USD 183M–695M envelope, but no publisher isolates it cleanly, and the publishers disagree by nearly four-fold on where the boundary even falls. Notably, the CAGRs here (4.6%–9.8%) run well below the lawful-interception category’s roughly 20% — consistent with the encryption-driven compression of classic passive cellular interception that the Playing Ground section named. If a methodology-disclosed publisher ever isolates “tactical cellular-collection software” and lands outside this USD 183M–695M envelope, the bracketing is weaker than I have assumed.

The third market is mobile and digital forensics, the device-in-hand modality — and the richest published material in the entire front, because three of the leading vendors are public or public-ish (Cellebrite, MSAB, Magnet under Thoma Bravo). This is the one definition of this front with filing-grade vendor anchors.

The mobile-forensics sub-definition brackets 2026 at roughly USD 5.7B; the broader digital-forensics parent brackets 2025 at roughly USD 13.5B–14.9B, with mobile forensics stated to be the dominant slice, and CAGRs cluster in the low-to-mid-teens. I read mobile forensics as the single best public proxy for this front’s device-extraction modality specifically — and it is the only definition adjacent to this front with a public-issuer anchor to validate it. The scope caveat: digital forensics also includes computer, cloud, and network forensics that are not field-tactical, so the mobile-forensics sub-figure (roughly USD 5.7B, 2026) is the tighter fit. One rare public concentration datapoint sits here as market structure. MSAB’s 2025 annual report states that “the top five vendors, OpenText, Cellebrite, Magnet Forensics, Exterro, and MSAB, accounted for about 38% of 2025 revenue” in digital forensics.235236

The fourth market is signals intelligence, the relevant anchor for the military-tactical end of the front. It is dominated, though, by strategic, airborne, and naval SIGINT systems (the National Agencies’ and the defense primes’ domain), far broader than tactical field-collection software. It is carried as a demand-envelope ceiling only.
