The SIGINT publishers bracket 2025 at roughly USD 17.7B–19.8B with low-to-mid-single-digit CAGRs (4.6%–5.4%) — a much slower growth profile than forensics or lawful interception, consistent with a mature, prime-dominated, hardware-platform market. I read SIGINT as the strategic / military ceiling on the addressable pool, not a tactical-collection-software size; tactical field SIGINT is an un-isolated sub-fraction. A pair of public budget figures fixes the demand envelope without being mistaken for a software market. The US Army allocated roughly USD 95.4M to tactical communications modernization, and US DHS allocated roughly USD 43.8B for surveillance in FY2026.231 I carry both strictly as demand-envelope proxies, far broader than the tactical-collection slice, never as a market size.

The tactical-collection slice: a labeled proxy, not a segment size

No clean public dollar figure isolates the tactical field-collection software slice. Given the deliberate opacity of this category, where much of the hardware is sold under classification or export control and the vendors are mostly private, that thin-material result is expected and honest, not a gap to be filled by invention. The four definitions above bracket adjacent markets that overlap heavily and must not be summed. Set side by side, they read as four walls. Lawful interception (roughly USD 5.5B–7.5B, 2025) is the carrier-mediated outer envelope, mostly the Monitoring Centers. IMSI-catcher / cellular interception (roughly USD 183M–695M, 2025) is the field-collection core proxy, where publishers disagree by nearly four-fold on the boundary. Mobile forensics (roughly USD 5.7B, 2026) and digital forensics (roughly USD 13.5B–14.9B, 2025) are the device-extraction modality and the front’s richest material. SIGINT (roughly USD 17.7B–19.8B, 2025) is the strategic / military ceiling, mostly the National Agencies and the primes.

Cellebrite and MSAB appear in the forensics figures, the catcher makers appear in the cellular-interception figures, and the military platforms appear in SIGINT. So summing would multiply-count the same companies and the same revenue. The hardest public currency for sizing this front is not any market derivative at all. It is the one near-pure-play public issuer in it.

That issuer is Cellebrite, the single near-pure-play public company touching this front. Its disclosed revenue and ARR are the cleanest filing-grade evidence that tactical and forensic demand is real — carried strictly at the disclosed level, the most recent reported quarter, never as a market size and never extrapolated.

For the three months ended 31 March 2026 (Q1 FY2026), Cellebrite reported total revenue of USD 128.3M, up 19% year-over-year, with subscription revenue of USD 117.9M (up 23%). It posted Annual Recurring Revenue of USD 493.0M, up 21% year-over-year, dollar-based net revenue retention of 115%, and GAAP gross margin of 82.5%.239

I read a single vendor running roughly USD 493M ARR, growing 21% year-over-year at 82.5% GAAP gross margin with 115% net retention, as the cleanest public evidence that the device-extraction end of tactical demand is real, recurring, and accelerating. That holds even though no publisher isolates the tactical-collection segment, and even as the catcher TAMs grow far more slowly. If Cellebrite’s ARR growth decelerates below roughly 12% across two consecutive quarters in 2026, the “accelerating device-extraction demand” read weakens. (Cellebrite trades as NASDAQ: CLBT and the trading-position disclaimer in the front-matter applies; the figure should be re-verified against the next 6-K at authoring rather than carried stale.)

The corroborating second pure-play is MSAB (Nasdaq Stockholm: MSAB B). Its full-year 2025 net sales reached SEK 461.8M, up 14.1% (currency-adjusted 19.7%), with operating profit of SEK 67.8M, in what the company called “the most successful year in the company’s history.”236 Magnet Forensics is the third name but is now private. Thoma Bravo agreed to acquire it for about C$1.8B (roughly USD 1.3B), announced 20 January 2023, combining it with Grayshift.240 No current revenue is public, and the take-private price is the last filing-grade figure.

Demand drivers

Five forcing functions carry the analytical weight the opaque market numbers cannot.

Encryption compressing passive interception — the structural ground. The root driver across the front is that the spread of end-to-end encryption has compressed the value of classic passive over-the-air interception: WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, and modern device-OS encryption mean that intercepting the wire increasingly yields ciphertext, not content. The practitioner framing is explicit: “the widespread use of end-to-end encryption by apps like WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram makes data extraction increasingly challenging.”241 The policy framing is institutional. The European Parliament’s 2025 briefing, “Access to data for law enforcement and digital forensics,” casts device-level forensic access as the law-enforcement response when communications interception is defeated by encryption.242 The market consequence is bimodal. Demand shifts toward the endpoint, where end-to-end encryption is defeated at the device rather than the wire — exactly the forensics-extraction demand the public-issuer anchors are capturing — and toward active RF collection that forces a target’s device to attach, over passive monitoring. I read the encryption shift as the single structural force reshaping this front. It simultaneously compresses the classic passive-interception sub-market and expands the device-extraction sub-market, which is why the forensics vendors are the front’s growth story and the catcher figures are flatter. If cellular-interception CAGRs re-accelerate above the forensics CAGRs through 2026–2027, that read weakens.

The device as the richest target — border and arrest extraction demand. The clearest quantified public signal of device-extraction demand is at the US border. Customs and Border Protection reported searching 47,000 electronic devices in 2024, up from roughly 8,500 in 2015 — a roughly five-and-a-half-fold increase over a decade,243 the kind of operational-volume growth that drives recurring extraction-tool spend. The procurement follows the volume. DHS/ICE and Homeland Security Investigations planned a five-year IDIQ with a USD 100M ceiling for Cellebrite mobile-device extraction. Between 2008 and April 2025, ICE awarded Cellebrite at least 213 contracts worth over USD 48.6M for UFED technology and related services.243244 I read the border and arrest context as the demand surface where this front’s modality is least encryption-defeated — physical possession plus compelled or exploited access — and most recurring, because every seized device is a unit of demand. If device-search volumes plateau or fall through 2026 — a policy reversal or a legal constraint — the recurring-extraction read weakens.

Border, migration, and event-security cellular ID. Beyond device-in-hand extraction, the field cellular-ID use case — identifying and locating devices at borders, migration chokepoints, and mass events — is a named driver in its own right. Publishers cite UAV-mounted interception payloads that “extend tactical flexibility and range, particularly for border surveillance,” and network densification (198,100 outdoor small cells in the US by mid-2025) concentrating traffic at fewer aggregation points.231 I read border and event security as the context that keeps the catcher sub-market alive even as encryption compresses passive content interception. Cellular identity (IMSI/IMEI presence and location) does not require breaking content encryption at all. If catcher procurement migrates wholly to content-interception framing rather than ID and location, this read is over-stated.

The 5G and VoLTE transition forcing a refresh cycle. Every generational network transition obsoletes part of the installed catcher and interception base and forces a refresh. Operators migrating to standalone 5G cores “must expose interception interfaces per ETSI TS 33.127 v18.11.0 standards,” and 181 carriers across 73 nations had invested in such upgrades by late 2025. The same source flags 5G NR interception solutions as the fastest-growing technology segment, at roughly 11.44% CAGR through 2031.231 I read this as a structural, standards-driven demand pulse that favors vendors who can keep pace with the protocol stack. If 5G-standalone interception solutions fail to out-grow the legacy cellular-interception base through 2026–2027, the refresh-cycle read weakens.

Accountability and oversight pressure reshaping who can buy and sell. The countervailing force is oversight and export control: EU dual-use controls explicitly capturing IMSI-catchers as cyber-surveillance items, US EAR cybersecurity-item controls, and sustained press and NGO scrutiny of border device searches. I read accountability pressure not as shrinking demand so much as reshaping the supply side. It concentrates sales toward vendors who can clear export licensing and survive public scrutiny, and pushes the most litigation-sensitive modality (remote mobile exploitation, the carve-out cohort handled in the Plays section) toward the regulatory and reputational margins. If a major vendor on this front is materially constrained by a named export-license denial or sanction through 2026, the “oversight reshapes supply” read strengthens — but any such claim is named-outlet-attributed or dropped.

The procurement structure

This front’s procurement is bimodal and uniquely export-control-gated. At the field-collection (catcher) end it tracks opaque sovereign and police buying constrained by dual-use export licensing. At the device-extraction (forensics) end it runs through the same accreditation-and-vehicle federal lane as the rest of government software, but with named, datable contract awards. Both modes are public-anchorable.

Export licensing as the gating barrier. For tactical RF-collection hardware, export control is the single richest public table-stakes barrier — and, as the Playing Ground section detailed, the legitimacy frame for the surveillance discussion. IMSI-catchers and cellular-interception equipment are explicitly captured as cyber-surveillance items under both the Wassenaar Arrangement and the EU framework. EU guidance states that controlled cyber-surveillance items include “equipment for covertly extracting communication content and metadata that is transmitted over the air via wireless communication, and radiofrequency monitoring equipment.”245 Annex I of EU Regulation 2021/821 implements the regime controls into the EU’s binding dual-use list, and Article 5 adds the catch-all for items not on the list where there is awareness of potential misuse.246 The US implemented complementary EAR controls on cybersecurity items in March 2022.245 I read export licensing as the real barrier to entry at this front’s field-collection end. It is a regime-gated, licence-by-destination gate that constrains who can sell to whom independent of product quality, and the public lever through which accountability pressure reshapes the supply side. A named export-license denial or sanction materially constraining a major vendor on this front through 2026 — named-outlet-attributed — would confirm the export-control-as-moat read. (Specific ECCN classifications are not asserted per vendor here; that is a defamation and credibility surface, and the regime, not a vendor-specific classification, is what is cited.)

Federal vehicles and named, datable device-extraction awards. At the device-extraction end, procurement runs through established federal vehicles and produces named, public awards — the cleanest procurement evidence in the front. The FBI and DOJ awarded Cellebrite a contract valued at USD 5,717,319 for unlock and extraction software, starting 30 September 2025 and completing 29 September 2030, through the NASA SEWP vehicle.247 DHS/ICE and HSI planned the five-year USD 100M-ceiling IDIQ for Cellebrite, and CBP had eight Cellebrite contracts set to end between July 2025 and April 2026.243 Vendors market availability through government-wide vehicles as a sales motion in its own right, and MSAB has publicly disclosed a US government-agency order.248 I read the device-extraction procurement lane as the transparent half of this front — recompeted, vehicle-routed, and datable on the public record — in sharp contrast to the opaque, export-gated, sovereign procurement of the catcher half. At that field-collection end, procurement is frequently under classification or NDA and surfaces only via named-outlet reporting or occasional procurement-portal notices. Specific catcher-vendor sovereign deal values are not publicly isolable and are carried as channel structure only, never as a sized figure.

3.3 The Contenders

Tactical intelligence is the front where the candidate list is shortest before you even start grading, and the reason is structural rather than accidental. The most-covered, most-named cohort in the popular surveillance discourse — the remote mobile-implant vendors — sits outside the boundary this front is built on. This front is field-deployable RF and proximity collection against a present target (IMSI/IMEI catchers, cellular interception, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth collection, direction-finding and geolocation) plus the adjacent device-in-hand modality of edge forensics, defined by physical proximity and operational tempo. A remote software implant delivered over the network is a different modality entirely, carved out of graded contention and treated only as market-force commentary in the Plays section. Remove that cohort and re-source what remains to dated public pages with verbatim positioning pillars, and the honest gradeable set is small.

Seven vendors are graded, not eight — and the boundary is still the finding. The cap for this report is eight contenders per front. This front comes in under the cap by design, and this is close to the inverse of the Fusion front. There, six graded under a deep candidate list because the boundary test (sell the analytical layer standalone) cut otherwise-rich vendors on architecture-fit. Here, seven grade because the gradeable universe is genuinely thin once two forces are applied. First, the never-graded mobile-implant carve-out removes the most-covered cohort from contention. Second, there is real public-material scarcity among the smaller RF specialists — Mer Group / Athena GS3, Wintego, and Cellxion at the margin lack the dated self-positioning that grading requires.

The count moved from six to seven on new public evidence, not a relaxed bar. Cognyte, previously held out of this front for want of a fitting public page, is graded here after its own dated border-protection page and a dated tactical-SIGINT deal surfaced as gradeable material for this front. The re-grade is captured in the report’s decision record superseding the original force-grade guard. Stating that the honest count is seven, on dated public pillars, is more useful than manufacturing the eighth grade by relaxing the sourcing bar. The seven are placed across three tiers. They are 3 Gravity (the device-forensics anchors a buyer cannot map the field-collection market without naming), 3 Attention (the tactical-SIGINT specialists shaping 2026 RF-collection demand), and 1 Wildcard (a marketing-thin cellular-interception vendor graded at the edge of the rubric, and held there with explicit caution). The candidates that did not make the cut, and why, are documented at the end of this section so the boundary can be defended.

The seven graded contenders across collection modality (air-interface RF intercept ◄──► device-in-hand forensics) and mission orientation. Vendor positions are conceptual, not data-derived. Remote mobile-implant exploitation (NSO/Candiru/Intellexa class) is a carved-out modality, not depicted; Cognyte is graded here in the Attention tier on its dated border-protection sensor-fusion page and a dated tactical-SIGINT deal. Not investment advice.

Gravity tier

Cellebrite — the primary

⚠️ Cellebrite (NASDAQ: CLBT) is a public issuer; the trading-position disclosure in the front-matter applies. This grade is built solely from public material.

“The Industry Standard for Lawfully Accessing and Collecting Digital Data … Access critical digital evidence lawfully from feature and smartphones, drones, SIM cards, SD cards, GPS devices, and more … Extract data from anywhere, whether in the lab, a remote location, or in the field.” — Cellebrite, UFED product page, accessed 2026-06-14 249

Cellebrite is the category-defining device-extraction standard. It is the de facto reference against which every other forensics vendor in this front is positioned, and the first name a buyer cannot map the field and edge-collection market without naming. Its UFED line is marketed as the lawful-collection standard, and the stated wedge is the broadest device and operating-system access coverage, extended past locks and encryption to the full file system. The public page tells buyers not to “let complicated locks, encryption barriers, deleted and unknown content prevent critical evidence from coming to light,” and markets “access to containerized and encrypted data to uncover every device’s Full File System (FFS) and protected data.”249 The 2026 R&D narrative runs on two axes — access coverage and field deployment. The Spring 2026 Release publicly claims it “expands device access capabilities across the widest range of iOS and Android devices and operating systems, including support for iPhone 17 and iOS 26,” and “strengthens AI-powered decoding.”250 On the field axis, the UFED variant is marketed to “extract data from anywhere, whether in the lab, a remote location, or in the field,”249 which is precisely the proximity-and-tempo modality this front is defined by.

The target buyer is law enforcement, defense, national security, and government investigators, with corporate and enterprise investigations as a secondary base. On pricing, the public record is a subscription/ARR model disclosed at the aggregate level as a public issuer; there is no clean per-seat public figure. Architecturally, Cellebrite markets a dedicated-collection hardware plus extraction-software stack across the logical, full-file-system, and physical extraction ladder, with AI-decoding positioned as the modernization layer. I carry that as positioning, not verified capability, because true internal access against any specific locked device cannot be read from outside. Sourcing here is the richest in the front — vendor self-positioning, heavy named-outlet coverage, and SEC-filer disclosure. Cellebrite reported Q1 2026 revenue of USD 128.3M (up 19% year-over-year), ARR of USD 493M (up 21%), and GAAP net income of USD 10.9M, with Q2 2026 ARR guidance of USD 510M–513M, per its quarterly release.251 It is the only contender on this front with fully disclosed, audited public financials, which makes it the front’s clearest war-chest anchor — a fact the War Chests section carries.

MSAB

“The trend in 2026 is moving extraction to the field … XRY Frontline (Kiosk, Tablet, Express) [deployed] at police stations and borders … MSAB’s latest innovation allows agencies to utilize high-power GPUs to accelerate the brute-force process. What used to take weeks can now be accomplished in hours.” — MSAB, “Mobile Forensics in 2026,” dated 28 April 2026, accessed 2026-06-14 252

MSAB is the field-first forensics anchor — the vendor whose 2026 public narrative maps most cleanly onto this front’s proximity-and-tempo boundary. It positions itself as a “Trusted Partner in Digital Forensics” built around the XRY extraction and XAMN analysis lines.253 Its 2026 guidance foregrounds the field shift directly: pushing the extraction act out of the central lab and to the point of seizure through “XRY Frontline (Kiosk, Tablet, Express)” form factors deployed “at police stations and borders.”252 Where Cellebrite leads on access-coverage breadth, MSAB’s stated wedge is decentralizing the extraction. Its public answer to the encryption headwind is compute, framed in its own words as using “high-power GPUs to accelerate the brute-force process” so that what “used to take weeks can now be accomplished in hours.”252 The target buyer is law enforcement, border and customs authorities, defense, and government, with a base oriented to operational field units rather than only central labs.

On pricing, MSAB is Stockholm-listed (Micro Systemation AB), so economics are disclosed at the financial-statement level; there is no clean per-seat public figure. Architecturally it markets the logical, full-file-system, and physical extraction ladder, with the Frontline field form factors and GPU brute-force as the 2026 modernization layers. A drone-forensics extension (XRY Drone) is added as a form-factor widening, carried via aggregator commentary.252254 On freshness, MSAB’s year-end 2025 report shows full-year net sales of SEK 462M (up 14.1%; up 19.7% currency-adjusted). Operating profit was SEK 68M at a 14.7% margin, with Q4 net sales of SEK 140.6M (up 19.6%).255 I read MSAB and Cellebrite together as the two device-forensics anchors converging on the field edge of this front from opposite starting points. Cellebrite annexes the field from access-coverage leadership; MSAB builds the field-first posture as its core identity. The Plays section tracks this as the front’s lab-to-field play.

Magnet Forensics

“Bring together evidence recovery, analysis, and insight … Recover, analyze and report on data from mobile, computer, cloud, and vehicle sources … Bring computer, mobile, cloud, vehicle, and acquired data into a single Axiom case.” — Magnet Forensics, Magnet Axiom product page, accessed 2026-06-14 256

Magnet Forensics is the analysis-led forensics anchor — the third device-forensics name a map of this front cannot omit, and the one whose ownership change is itself a market-structure datapoint. Its AXIOM platform is marketed as multi-source evidence consolidation: pulling mobile, computer, cloud, and vehicle data into one case file with “industry-leading artifact coverage,”256 positioned as the analyst-side complement to raw extraction. Where Cellebrite leads on getting into the device and MSAB on getting extraction to the field, Magnet’s stated wedge is unifying and analyzing the recovered evidence across sources, promising to “access the most data possible, see the full story, and reduce time to evidence.”256 The target buyer is law enforcement, government, defense, and enterprise investigators, supported by a large practitioner community (the Magnet User Summit).257

The ownership fact is central and frequently elided. Magnet was taken private by Thoma Bravo in a transaction valued at roughly USD 1.3–1.35B (announced January 2023; plan-of-arrangement closed April 2023) and brought together with Grayshift; Grayshift had announced a strategic growth investment from Thoma Bravo in June 2022 — into a single end-to-end digital-investigations entity.258 On pricing, that take-private removed the prior public disclosure: Magnet is now private, with no disclosed per-seat or aggregate ARR figure. Architecturally it markets a multi-source ingest, artifact-parsing, and analytics stack (AXIOM), now paired with Grayshift’s GrayKey mobile-access capability under the combined entity. I read the Grayshift combination as the inorganic route to an end-to-end “unlock then extract then analyze” workflow. It buys the access layer to pair with analysis-led incumbency, against Cellebrite’s organically-built breadth, and the Plays section tracks it as the front’s private-equity consolidation play. The combination also removed a public issuer from the front’s disclosure surface, leaving Cellebrite and MSAB as the only graded contenders with open financials.

Attention tier

Rayzone Group

“Full-scale, last-mile SIGINT capabilities … Tactical RF interception for 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G networks … Designed for stationary, portable, and airborne deployment … Tactical awareness. Real-time control … Real-Time Situational Awareness at the Tactical Edge.” — Rayzone Group, Proximity-Data Intelligence page, re-fetched 2026-06-14 259

Rayzone Group is the clearest public exemplar of the tactical “last-mile SIGINT” specialist — this front’s boundary stated almost word-for-word in the vendor’s own lexicon. Tel Aviv-headquartered and private, Rayzone markets its Proximity-Data Intelligence line as “full-scale, last-mile SIGINT capabilities” delivering “tactical RF interception for 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G networks,” explicitly “designed for stationary, portable, and airborne deployment.”259 Its public range spans the catcher, the counter-catcher, and geolocation. Publicly, the Piranha unit is described as a software-defined-radio IMSI-catcher collecting mobile-phone identifiers across 2G–5G environments, and it markets a counter-product, ArrowCell, for IMSI-catcher detection and elimination.260 The stated wedge is a one-vendor tactical RF stack — collection, counter-collection, and proximity intelligence — pitched to national agencies and tactical teams.

The target buyer is national agencies, internal-security services, and tactical units. Named-outlet profiles describe a client base concentrated in Asia, Central America, and Europe, which I carry as named-outlet-attributed color rather than asserted fact.261 On pricing, Rayzone is private and undisclosed; funding and ownership circulate via aggregator listings and are carried as undisclosed, not as facts.261 Architecturally it markets software-defined-radio collection across 2G–5G in modular, multi-form-factor configurations. Consistent with the caution that governs every RF specialist in this front, “covers 2G–5G” is a software-breadth positioning claim, not a verifiable statement of live 5G stand-alone content interception. Sourcing rests on the vendor’s own current pages for the product positioning — the live Proximity-Data Intelligence page was re-confirmed 2026-06-14 carrying the pillars verbatim259 — while the geographic-client and funding color is named-outlet-attributed; no public 2026 financial disclosure exists, as Rayzone is private.

Septier Communication

“Capturing up to 11 different identifiers for each cellular device, including those using Bluetooth and Wi-Fi … cellular identities, location, and other information from GSM, UMTS, LTE, and 5G devices in its coverage area … available in various configurations to meet a range of tactical requirements.” — Septier Communication, Septier Guardian product page, re-confirmed 2026-06-14 262

Septier Communication is the breadth-of-capture tactical specialist — the second Attention-tier IMSI-catcher vendor, Israel-headquartered and private, whose public wedge is the number of identifiers it captures and the range of form factors it ships. Its Guardian IMSI Catcher is marketed as “capturing up to 11 different identifiers for each cellular device, including those using Bluetooth and Wi-Fi,” extracting “cellular identities, location, and other information from GSM, UMTS, LTE, and 5G devices in its coverage area.”262 It is also marketed as “available in various configurations to meet a range of tactical requirements,” including a UAV-mounted airborne variant.263 Septier pairs the catcher with a direction-finding line, and its Cellular Locator is marketed as “a tactical location tracking solution that provides accurate location information for cellular devices, using advanced direction finders such as Septier Hunter.”262 Where Rayzone foregrounds the SDR catcher-and-counter-catcher stack, Septier’s stated differentiation is breadth of identifier capture plus an integrated catcher-locator-direction-finding platform — a full tactical cellular-intelligence platform rather than a single-function box.

The target buyer, named on Septier’s own audience pages, is intelligence agencies, police, and counter-terrorism units.263 On pricing, Septier is private and undisclosed. Architecturally it markets an active/passive cellular catcher across 2G–5G plus Wi-Fi and Bluetooth identifier capture and direction-finding (Hunter), in ground, portable, and airborne form factors. The same caution as Rayzone applies: the “11 identifiers” count and the 5G support are positioning sourced to the vendor’s own pages, not externally verified capability. Sourcing rests on the vendor’s own pages: the Guardian, Guardian Airborne, and Cellular Locator pages were re-confirmed live 2026-06-14, clearing the earlier sourcing flag on the exact identifier-count pillar.262263 No public 2026 financial disclosure exists (private).

Cognyte

Banner: Cognyte is graded here on dated public material only, with no internal knowledge used. The author served as VP Product at Cognyte; this grade is independent ProductBeacon research built from Cognyte’s own current product page and a dated public deal announcement, and reflects the author’s personal analysis, not Cognyte’s position. The gap between Cognyte’s soft public headline and its own deeper public record is shown as a sourced contrast, never as an asserted intent.

“Cognyte’s Border Protection solution takes a multi-layered approach by analyzing existing border sensors (cameras, radar, satellites and more) and fusing together with SIGINT, OSINT and VISINT sources.” — Cognyte, Border Protection / Maritime Intelligence page, cognyte.com/border-protection-maritime-intelligence-na/ (accessed 2026-06-16) 264

Cognyte is graded in the Attention tier, and like its placements elsewhere in this report the grade rests on a distinct dated public pillar — here the field-and-border collection page, not the network-intelligence glossary that anchors the National Agencies front or the NEXYTE “data source” framing that anchors the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers front. The primary pillar is Cognyte’s own border-protection page, which describes a solution that fuses “existing border sensors (cameras, radar, satellites and more)” together with “SIGINT, OSINT and VISINT sources.”264 That is the proximity-and-tempo shape of this front stated in Cognyte’s own words: sensor fusion against a present operational picture at the border and checkpoint, the field-collection edge rather than the carrier core. The corroboration is a dated deal: a Tier-1 military-intelligence agency contract of roughly USD 5M, publicly described as deploying “a tactical SIGINT solution for operational missions” (BusinessWire/StockTitan, 2025-11-19).265 The VANTAGE trademark — “telecommunication surveillance software for the integrated interception, collection, monitoring, analyzing, searching, tracking and reporting of data and voice communications,” a registered mark of Cognyte Software Ltd. — corroborates the interception lineage but is not this front’s pillar; it is weighted to the National Agencies front and carried as corroboration only.266

The grade construction is explicit about what carries it. Cognyte is placed in Attention, not Gravity, because the Gravity tier here is the device-in-hand forensics anchors a buyer cannot map the field-collection market without naming. Cognyte’s public footprint on this front is the field-and-border sensor-fusion line plus the dated tactical-SIGINT deal, not a standalone field-forensics product surface. An honesty note in the same register that governs the whole chapter: some tactical product names in this category are classified or non-public. So the tactical-SIGINT positioning and the dated deal are the gradeable public material, and the grade is built strictly from them — the classification of specific product names narrows what can be quoted rather than removing the grade.

The target buyer, on the border-protection page’s own framing, is the border, defense, and national-security operator. On pricing, Cognyte’s tactical line is not separately disclosed; its public financials are group-level (the Convergence chapter carries those). The current border-protection product positioning was directly fetched and quoted verbatim; the dated deal rests on a named-outlet release. The VANTAGE goods-description wording is confirmed verbatim against the USPTO record. Consistent with the front-wide discipline, none of Cognyte’s lineage artifacts is asserted here as a present tactical capability — they are dated records of positioning and a dated deal, quoted and attributed. Cognyte is a cross-front vendor. It is also graded in the National Agencies front (the network-intelligence glossary), the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers front (the NEXYTE lawful-interception “data source” framing), the Fusion / Decision Intelligence front (the NEXYTE decision-intelligence platform), and Open-Source Intelligence (LUMINAR WEBINT). The pillar graded here on this front — the border-protection “SIGINT, OSINT and VISINT” line — is distinct from each of those and is logged for the cross-front reconciliation.

Wildcard tier

Cellxion

Wildcard caution: Cellxion’s own current self-positioning page is thin. The pillar below is drawn from named-outlet and surveillance-industry-index descriptions, dated and explicitly attributed as third-party characterization rather than vendor self-positioning. The read stays descriptive throughout; this is a borderline grade that may be demoted to the Plays-section market-force discussion if a live dated vendor pillar cannot be captured.

Cellxion is publicly described — via the Surveillance Industry Index and named directory listings — as a UK-based supplier of cellular-interception and IMSI-catcher equipment (the GX/UGX cellular-intercept range), positioned for covert tactical cellular monitoring. — surveillance-industry-index / named-listing description, accessed 2026-06-14 267

Cellxion is the Wildcard, and its Wildcard status is precisely its thinness rather than its trajectory. It occupies the specialist cellular-interception niche — a smaller, lower-profile supplier in the same IMSI-catcher market as Rayzone and Septier. A real public footprint exists: it appears in surveillance-industry indices and directory listings as a cellular-interception vendor with the GX/UGX range.267 Yet it lacks the rich self-positioning of the Attention-tier specialists, so its continued presence in a niche being structurally compressed by encryption (per the headwind on classic passive content interception) is a descriptive market-force question, not an assertive read. I do not characterize its prospects in either direction.

The target buyer, per the index and listing descriptions, is law enforcement and security and intelligence agencies.267 On pricing, Cellxion is private and undisclosed. Architecturally, the classification is cellular-interception / IMSI-catcher hardware (the GX/UGX range, per the index listing), carried descriptively as named-outlet and index characterization; no capability claim is asserted as fact. Sourcing is the weakest of the graded set — named-outlet and surveillance-industry-index description, explicitly not vendor self-positioning — and the grade is held strictly to the report’s Wildcard caution: descriptive only, no pattern claim, no negative claim. No 2026 vendor disclosure surfaced. Cellxion is carried as a continuing niche presence on the strength of index listings, with the thinness stated as the finding.

The cut line — who is not graded here, and why

The front’s apparent depth in the popular discourse forces a defensible cut. On this front the cut is driven by three forces: the never-graded mobile-implant carve-out, genuine public-material scarcity among the smaller RF vendors, and the boundary that excludes diversified primes. Each candidate below is real; each is placed where the public record actually puts it.

  • Cognyte IS graded on this front — in the Attention tier above. An earlier pass concluded that no dated public cognyte.com page fit this front’s proximity-and-tempo boundary, and held Cognyte out of this front. On a fuller reading of Cognyte’s own dated public record, that conclusion was too narrow. Cognyte’s border-protection page describes a field-and-border collection solution fusing “existing border sensors (cameras, radar, satellites and more)” with “SIGINT, OSINT and VISINT sources,”264 and a dated public release describes a Tier-1 military-intelligence deal deploying “a tactical SIGINT solution for operational missions” (2025-11-19).265 Those carry the grade on this front, in the Attention tier (the re-grade supersedes the original force-grade guard, captured in the report’s decision record). The true residual remains stated, not papered over: some tactical product names in this category are classified or non-public. But the gradeable public material is the border-protection page and the dated deal, and the grade is built strictly from them, with no internal knowledge of any Cognyte tactical product line used anywhere in this chapter.

  • Mer Group / Athena GS3 — no current dated standalone tactical-collection self-positioning that fits this front’s boundary surfaces. Mer is a diversified communications and security group, and Athena GS3’s public footprint is thin and dated. Referenced in the Plays section as market color; the thinness is stated, not papered over.

  • Wintego — described historically by named outlets (the WINT Wi-Fi man-in-the-middle “backpack” system, 2016) but with no current dated self-positioning page that the grading test requires.268 Carried in the Plays section as descriptive modality context only; not graded, and no operating-status claim is made.

  • Rohde & Schwarz / L3Harris / PKI Electronic Intelligence — these appear in the IMSI-catcher market sizing as named majors,269 but they are diversified RF and defense primes whose tactical-collection products are a small slice of a much larger business. On this front, a prime’s business line is gradeable only where its own dated public product-line page supports proximity RF collection against a present target; any financial scale is kept to the relevant disclosed business line or segment and never inferred from total-parent revenue. These three remain market references because that front-local product-line and sizing record does not support a primary specialist grade here.

  • The locked never-graded set — NSO, Candiru, Intellexa, Ability, Voyager Labs — is never graded. Remote mobile-implant exploitation (the Pegasus / Predator class) is a technically distinct modality — a remote software implant delivered over the network, governed by different export-control language (intrusion-software controls) than the RF-proximity hardware this front grades. It is carved out of graded contention by construction and appears only as descriptive market-force commentary in the Plays section (the encryption-and-accountability play), where any sanctions or distress statement is attributed to a named outlet or official record. No grade, no pattern claim, no negative-intent framing attaches to any vendor in this cohort.

A closing note on what the boundary buys. One discipline holds the graded set at seven: re-source to a dated public page with a verbatim pillar, carve out the modality that does not fit, and grade a vendor only where its footprint is publicly readable. It is the same discipline that keeps every placement above honest, and it moved Cognyte into the graded set once its own dated public pages supported it. Grade the field-collection layer on public material. Reference the rest.

3.4 Their Plays

Three strategic moves are in motion across the Tactical Intelligence front in 2026. The front carries a deliberately small play count — three, not five — because its evidence floor is the strictest in the report: every play here is anchored to a dated public event, and a play without a public datable anchor is dropped, not softened. Each names its participants, signals its opinion explicitly, and carries a falsifiable read grounded on a publicly observable proxy. The shape of the three is the shape of the front itself. One is the modality migration that is annexing the field-collection edge to the device-forensics cohort. One is the private-equity consolidation reshaping who owns the forensics stack. One is the twin squeeze — encryption from below and export-control accountability from above — bearing down on the classic RF-catcher modality and the broader surveillance market it sits next to. The carved-out locked never-graded set (NSO/Candiru/Intellexa class) appears in the third play only as descriptive, named-outlet-attributed market-force commentary — never graded, never pattern-claimed, never assigned intent.

Play 1: The Lab-to-Field Shift — Extraction Moves to the Point of Seizure

  • Observation. The device-forensics anchors are publicly relocating the act of extraction out of the central lab and to where the device is seized. MSAB states it plainly: “The trend in 2026 is moving extraction to the field,” answered by “XRY Frontline (Kiosk, Tablet, Express)” deployed “at police stations and borders” (MSAB, dated 28 April 2026).270 Cellebrite markets UFED extraction to “Extract data from anywhere, whether in the lab, a remote location, or in the field,”271 and its Q1 FY2026 portfolio commentary reports a drone-forensics expansion (reported 2026-05-14).272 Both vendors field ruggedized and field-form-factor hardware, and the encryption answer is being reframed as compute — MSAB markets that agencies can “utilize high-power GPUs to accelerate the brute-force process,” so that “what used to take weeks can now be accomplished in hours.”270

  • Participants. MSAB, Cellebrite, Magnet, and the deployed government field units — border, customs, arrest, and checkpoint teams — that are the named deployment surface in the vendors’ own pages.

  • My read. I read this as the forensics cohort annexing the field-collection edge of this front, not merely modernizing the lab. Pushing the extraction act to the point of seizure maps directly onto this front’s defining property — physical proximity plus operational tempo. And the device-in-hand modality, where brute-forcing an unlock sidesteps the transport-layer encryption that compresses the over-the-air RF-catcher modality, is the structurally healthiest part of the front. The forensics anchors are walking into the tactical edge from a position of growth, while the classic catcher modality is walking out of it under encryption pressure (Play 3).

  • Falsifiable read. If through H2 2026 the named forensics vendors publish further field and edge form factors — kiosks, drones, ruggedized units — and name government field-deployment references, the lab-to-field thesis hardens into the front’s defining migration. If instead their 2026 roadmaps and named wins re-center on lab-based throughput and back away from field form factors, the convergence read weakens and edge-forensics stays a niche of the lab market rather than the new tactical center of gravity.

  • Evidence. MSAB “Mobile Forensics in 2026” guidance, 28 April 2026 270; Cellebrite UFED field-extraction positioning 271; Cellebrite Q1 FY2026 drone-forensics expansion, reported 2026-05-14 272.

Play 2: Consolidation in Device Forensics Under Private Equity

  • Observation. The category’s defining capital event is private-equity consolidation at the forensics layer. Thoma Bravo took Magnet Forensics private: the plan of arrangement closed 2023-04-06 at CA$44.25 per share, with aggregate cash consideration of approximately CA$1.044B plus rollover shares of approximately CA$0.628B. The transaction was reported at a headline value of roughly C$1.8B (US$~1.3B per-share equity). It then combined Magnet with Grayshift (after Grayshift’s June 2022 strategic growth-investment announcement) into a single end-to-end digital-investigations entity.273274 The combined entity operates privately as of 2026, with no public re-listing or fresh disclosed valuation in the window.273

  • Participants. Thoma Bravo, Magnet Forensics, Grayshift, and the law-enforcement and government forensics buyer base.

  • My read. I read this as the front’s consolidation mode: buy the missing layer and assemble the full workflow under one owner. The analysis-led forensics leader (Magnet/AXIOM) and a mobile-access and unlock specialist (Grayshift/GrayKey) were merged under PE ownership into a combined access-plus-analysis stack — the inorganic route to an end-to-end “unlock then extract then analyze” workflow, set against Cellebrite’s organically built breadth. The move also removed a public issuer from the market’s disclosure surface, taking Magnet’s financials dark and leaving the front with only two issuers reporting numbers.

  • Falsifiable read. If H2 2026 brings a second comparable acquisition of an access, extraction, or analysis specialist by a forensics consolidator, the buy-the-stack pattern is the front’s structural direction. If instead the combined Magnet/Grayshift entity shows only feature-level integration without named end-to-end government wins, organic breadth — Cellebrite’s route — is out-competing the assembled stack, and the consolidation is a financing story rather than a competitive realignment.

  • Evidence. Thoma Bravo closing of Magnet plan of arrangement, 2023-04-06 273; transaction value reported at C$1.8B 274; Grayshift merged into Magnet following the take-private 273.

Play 3: The Encryption Headwind and the Export-Control Overhang Compress the RF-Catcher Modality

  • Observation. Two compounding public forces squeeze the classic RF-catcher modality and the surveillance market it neighbors. First, encryption and legacy-network sunset structurally compress passive content-interception: the catcher’s reliable yield narrows toward identity, metadata, and location rather than content. Market commentary already flags 5G-SA-compatible interception as white space “where no vendor has yet established a clearly dominant globally deployed commercial solution.”275 Second, an accountability and export-control overhang reshapes the broader surveillance market’s structure. The US Commerce Department added NSO Group and Candiru to the Entity List on 4 November 2021 under a “presumption of denial,” on a determination they “developed and supplied spyware to foreign governments” used to “maliciously target government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics, and embassy workers.” It added Intellexa/Cytrox on 18 July 2023.276 The EU Dual-Use Regulation 2021/821 Article 5 cyber-surveillance catch-all — with European Commission guidelines issued 15 October 2024 — imports a human-rights end-use test reaching RF and cellular surveillance items.277

  • Participants. The RF-catcher specialists (Rayzone, Septier, Cellxion) on the encryption side; the carved-out locked never-graded set (NSO, Candiru, Intellexa) and the US and EU regulators on the accountability side. The mobile-implant vendors are named only as a carved-out market force — a remote-software-implant modality technically distinct from this front’s RF-proximity hardware — with no grade, no pattern claim, and no negative-intent framing. The sanctions facts are attributed to US official records and named outlets, dated.

  • My read. I read this as a front being squeezed from two directions at once. The classic over-the-air content-interception value proposition is eroding technically as encryption advances and 2G/3G networks sunset, pushing tactical RF vendors toward active and hybrid catchers, direction-finding and identity value, and the device-in-hand forensics route. At the same time, the broader surveillance market operates under a hardening export-control and legitimacy regime that raises the cost and reputational risk of cross-border sale. That is the same regime that, per the war-chest evidence, discourages public funding signaling among the private tactical specialists.

  • Falsifiable read. If through H2 2026 and into 2027 tactical vendors’ public pages and named-outlet coverage keep foregrounding forensics, direction-finding, identity, active and hybrid catchers, and 5G-SA research over classic passive-content interception — and export-control actions continue — the squeeze thesis holds. If instead a vendor publicly demonstrates durable 5G-SA content interception at scale, or the export-control regime visibly loosens, the read weakens.

  • Evidence. IMSI-catcher market commentary on 5G-SA white space 275; US Commerce/BIS Entity List additions — NSO and Candiru (4 November 2021), Intellexa/Cytrox (18 July 2023) 276; EU Dual-Use Reg. 2021/821 Article 5 and the 15 October 2024 guidelines 277.

Commentary on the capital pattern (≤150 words)

This front’s capital structure is a two-issuer head and a private long tail. Only Cellebrite (CLBT) and MSAB (MSAB B) disclose financials, and both are growing: Cellebrite at ARR $493M, +21% 278 dwarfs MSAB’s SEK 462M FY2025 net sales 281, but both report record momentum, not distress. Everything else is opaque by design. The category’s defining capital event is private-equity consolidation at the forensics layer: Thoma Bravo took Magnet private in 2023 (~C$1.8B headline) and folded Grayshift in 283285, removing the second-largest mobile-forensics name from public markets and ending visibility into its numbers. The Israeli tactical specialists (Rayzone, Septier) and the UK IMSI-catcher house (Cellxion) raise little disclosed venture capital and publish no priced valuations — consistent with a field-collection segment where customer secrecy and export-control exposure discourage public funding signaling 286288290. Capital here is either public-market-disclosed or invisible; there is no middle.

3.6 Winning & Losing

Three pattern claims carry this front. Each begins with a dated public observation, separates the observation from my read of it, and ends with a conditional that a publicly observable proxy can confirm or refute before the next refresh. The throughline they share is the one structural fact the whole chapter is built on. Air-interface encryption is compressing the classic over-the-air interception modality, and the demand it sheds is migrating to two places — the device in hand, and the accountable end of the supply side. The three claims trace that migration from three angles: where the growth went (device/edge forensics), where the boundary is dissolving (lab to field), and who gets to buy and sell at all (the surveillance-market reckoning).

Pattern Claim 1 — The Edge-Forensics Ascendancy

Observation. The growth on this front is not in the catcher; it is in the seized device. The classic passive over-the-air interception value proposition is structurally compressing. End-to-end encryption on WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram, plus modern device-OS encryption, mean intercepting the wire increasingly yields ciphertext, and 2G/3G sunset is steadily removing the downgrade target that catchers relied on for content.291292 The public market figures show the split directly. The cellular-interception / IMSI-catcher segment runs at a flat-to-modest CAGR — Mordor Intelligence brackets the IMSI-catcher market at USD 207.68M (2026) growing at an 8.08% CAGR, and the broader cellular-interception framing at a 4.61% CAGR through 2031. The mobile-forensics market that the device-in-hand modality belongs to runs materially faster, with MarketsandMarkets bracketing it at USD 5.72B (2026) at an 11.8% CAGR and Mordor placing the digital-forensics parent at a 16.5% CAGR.293294 The single hardest datapoint anchors the same conclusion. Cellebrite (NASDAQ: CLBT), the front’s one near-pure-play public issuer, reported Q1 FY2026 ARR of USD 493M, up 21% year-over-year, at 82.5% GAAP gross margin and 115% net revenue retention. MSAB (Nasdaq Stockholm: MSAB B) reported FY2025 net sales of SEK 462M, up 14.1%, which the company called “the most successful year in the company’s history.”295296

My read. I read this as the defining structural fact of the front. When the device is in hand and the unlock can be brute-forced, the operator sidesteps the transport-layer crypto that defeats the over-the-air catcher entirely. So the structurally healthy growth sits in device and edge forensics (Cellebrite, MSAB, Magnet), and the RF-catcher modality is the laggard, kept alive mainly by the identity-and-location use case that does not require breaking content encryption. The catcher is not dead; its yield is just narrowing from content to presence, while the dollars accrete on the forensics side. The two public issuers are the proof the demand is real, recurring, and accelerating — not a publisher’s TAM derivative but disclosed, audited ARR.

Conditional prediction. If, through H2 2026 and into 2027, the device-extraction issuers keep posting low-to-mid-teens or better disclosed growth while the cellular-interception/catcher market figures stay in the mid-single-to-high-single-digit CAGR band, the edge-forensics-ascendancy read holds. If instead Cellebrite’s ARR growth decelerates below roughly 12% across two consecutive quarters, or a methodology-disclosed publisher shows the cellular-interception CAGR re-accelerating above the forensics CAGR, the read weakens — the compression of the wire would be reversing, not deepening.

Sources. Encryption-compression framing: Oxygen Forensics 2025 + EPRS PE 775879 (2025).291292 Market CAGRs: Mordor Intelligence (IMSI-catcher; cellular interception), MarketsandMarkets (mobile forensics), Mordor (digital forensics).293294 Disclosed financials: Cellebrite Q1 FY2026 (reported 2026-05-14); MSAB FY2025 year-end report.295296

Author’s read of public material, June 2026. Conceptual, not data-derived. Not investment advice.

Pattern Claim 2 — The Lab-to-Field Collapse

Observation. Extraction is moving out of the central lab and into the field, collapsing the tactical/forensic boundary the market used to keep. MSAB states plainly in its 2026 guidance that “The trend in 2026 is moving extraction to the field,” answered by “XRY Frontline (Kiosk, Tablet, Express)” deployed “at police stations and borders,” and it unveiled XRY Drone in November 2025.297298 Cellebrite markets its UFED to “Extract data from anywhere, whether in the lab, a remote location, or in the field,” delivered on a “UFED Touch3 Ruggedized Tablet,” and expanded into drone forensics in its Q1 2026 portfolio.299295 The demand surface is the border and the arrest. U.S. Customs and Border Protection reported searching roughly 47,000 electronic devices in 2024, up from about 8,500 in 2015 — a ~5.5× rise over a decade. The procurement tracks the volume, with DHS/ICE planning a five-year IDIQ at a USD 100M ceiling and the FBI/DOJ awarding Cellebrite a USD 5.7M extraction contract through the NASA SEWP vehicle (start 2025-09-30).300301

My read. I read this as the device-forensics anchors annexing the field-collection edge of this front — not merely modernizing the lab. The same deployed unit that used to choose between a catcher (device on the air) and a lab extraction (device in hand) increasingly wants both at the point of seizure, in operational time. That is exactly the proximity-plus-tempo property that defines this front. The winner of that collapse is not whoever extracts fastest; it is whoever makes field-grade extraction defensible — chain-of-custody, forensic soundness, oversight — because a kiosk at a border crossing is a legal and reputational surface in a way a lab bench is not. Cellebrite’s “lawfully accessing” framing and MSAB’s forensic-soundness language are positioning for exactly that defensibility contest.

Conditional prediction. If, through H2 2026, the named forensics vendors publish further field/edge form factors (kiosks, ruggedized units, drone-forensics lines) and name government field-deployment references, the lab-to-field-collapse read hardens into the front’s structural direction. The read weakens on either of two signals: 2026 roadmaps and named wins re-centering on lab-based throughput and backing away from field form factors, or a named legal or policy constraint cutting the border device-search volumes that anchor the demand. On either, the convergence read weakens and edge extraction stays a niche of the lab market.

Sources. Field-shift positioning: MSAB 2026 guidance (dated 28 April 2026); XRY Drone (Nov 2025); Cellebrite UFED page + Q1 2026 portfolio.297298299295 Demand and procurement: CBP device-search counts and DHS/ICE IDIQ via FedScoop; FBI/DOJ NASA-SEWP award.300301

Author’s read of public material, June 2026. Conceptual, not data-derived. Not investment advice.

Pattern Claim 3 — The Surveillance-Market Reckoning

Observation. The structure of who may buy and who may sell in this market is being reshaped by sanctions and export-control accountability — and the cohort it presses hardest is the one this report never grades. The U.S. Commerce Department added NSO Group and Candiru to the Entity List in November 2021 under a “presumption of denial,” and added Intellexa/Cytrox in July 2023, each on determinations tied to spyware misuse.302 The EU Dual-Use Regulation 2021/821 added an Article 5 catch-all reaching “cyber-surveillance items” — including, per EU guidance, “equipment for covertly extracting communication content and metadata that is transmitted over the air via wireless communication, and radiofrequency monitoring equipment” — importing a human-rights end-use test, with guidelines issued 15 October 2024.303 The regime is not monotonic. In December 2025 the U.S. administration partially lifted sanctions on three Intellexa-linked executives, an action industry read as an easing for surveillance providers.304

My read. I read this as a market-structure reckoning rather than a verdict on any one vendor. The remote locked never-graded set — NSO, Candiru, Intellexa, and the rest of the Pegasus/Predator class — is a technically distinct modality from this front’s RF-proximity hardware. It is governed by different export-control language: intrusion software under Wassenaar Category 4 / U.S. EAR 4D004, versus IP-network and RF surveillance under Category 5 Part 1 / 5A001.j. It is carved out of grading entirely and named here only as a market force, descriptively and on the official and named-outlet record.303 What the accountability regime does, structurally, is reshape the supply side. It concentrates legitimate sale toward vendors who can clear export licensing and survive public scrutiny, and pushes the most litigation-sensitive modalities toward the regulatory and reputational margins. The December 2025 partial lift is the reminder that this is a contested, oscillating equilibrium, not a one-way ratchet — which is precisely why it is a market force to watch rather than a settled outcome.

Conditional prediction. If, through H2 2026, further Entity-List actions or sanctions land on surveillance-cohort entities, or export-licensing friction visibly reshapes who sells field-collection hardware across borders, the reckoning read strengthens and budget continues migrating toward the accountable, forensic end of the market. If instead the December 2025 partial lift is followed by broader sanctions relief and a loosening export-control posture, the read weakens — the legitimacy pressure that has favored the accountable vendors would be relaxing.

Sources. Entity-List actions: BIS / Federal Register (NSO + Candiru, Nov 2021; Intellexa/Cytrox, Jul 2023) via official records and named outlets.302 EU Article 5 cyber-surveillance catch-all and the “over the air… radiofrequency monitoring equipment” definition: Akin Gump / SIPRI on Regulation 2021/821 (guidelines 15 Oct 2024).303 December 2025 partial sanctions lift: Access Now / named-outlet reporting on the Intellexa consortium.304

Author’s read of public material, June 2026. Conceptual, not data-derived. Not investment advice.

Winners, Watch, Losers

Winners. Cellebrite and MSAB are the front’s momentum winners, and the label rests on disclosed financials rather than positioning. Cellebrite reported Q1 FY2026 ARR of USD 493M, up 21% year-over-year, with subscription revenue up 23%, 82.5% GAAP gross margin, 115% net revenue retention, and Q2 ARR guided to USD 510M–513M — the only fully audited, public-issuer scorecard in the front.295 MSAB reported FY2025 net sales of SEK 462M, up 14.1% (currency-adjusted 19.7%), at a 14.7% EBIT margin, a record year on its own statement.296 Both are riding the edge-forensics ascendancy of Pattern Claim 1, and both are pushing extraction to the field per Pattern Claim 2 — Cellebrite’s “lab, a remote location, or in the field” UFED and MSAB’s XRY Frontline at “police stations and borders.”299297 I read these two not as winning a share war against each other but as winning the modality war. The seized device is where this front’s money is, and they are its public anchors. (Cellebrite is a public issuer — the trading-position disclaimer applies.)

Watch. Rayzone, Septier, and Cellxion are on Watch — the tactical RF-collection specialists operating in the modality the encryption headwind is compressing. Rayzone markets “full-scale, last-mile SIGINT capabilities” with “Tactical RF interception for 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G networks” designed for “stationary, portable, and airborne deployment.”305 Septier markets a Guardian catcher “capturing up to 11 different identifiers for each cellular device, including those using Bluetooth and Wi-Fi” across “GSM, UMTS, LTE, and 5G,” plus a DF/geolocation line.306 Cellxion is the marketing-thin Wildcard, described via surveillance-industry-index listings as a UK cellular-interception supplier and held to descriptive treatment only.307

All three are private with no disclosed financials, so the Watch placement is structural and modality-driven, not a vendor-distress read. The RF-catcher modality’s classic passive-content yield is eroding toward identity/DF/metadata and active/hybrid catchers as transport encryption hardens. And — as the same outside-verifiability limit that governs every RF specialist in this front — no vendor’s “5G” listing is externally verifiable as live 5G-standalone content interception, the white space where, per market commentary, “no vendor has yet established a clearly dominant globally deployed commercial solution.”293 Watch signal: a named field-deployment reference, a demonstrated 5G-SA capability, or movement up-stack toward the forensic edge.

Also on Watch as a market-structure datapoint: Magnet Forensics, taken private by Thoma Bravo (~C$1.8B headline; closed April 2023) and combined with Grayshift into an access-plus-analysis stack — a winner on capability but dark on disclosure since the take-private, so it cannot be graded on numbers.308

Losers. No graded contender on this front earns a Losers label in this section. A vendor reaches this line only when a cited public event — a layoff specific to the tactical/forensic business, a missed quarter, a down-round, a named executive departure framed as distress, or a customer-churn disclosure — anchors a vendor-specific decline, per the casualty-evidence discipline. The public events on this front are momentum and consolidation, not failure. Cellebrite and MSAB are growing on disclosed financials; Magnet sits inside a private-equity portfolio with no public distress event; and the private RF specialists publish no figures that would support either a winner or a loser label. The structurally pressured force on this front is the never-graded remote-implant surveillance cohort (NSO, Candiru, Intellexa), which faces a tightening — and, as of December 2025, partly loosening — sanctions and export-control regime. That pressure is referenced as a market structure, named-outlet-attributed, and is deliberately not a Losers grade on any contender, because the cohort is carved out of grading and because no graded vendor’s balance sheet is implicated.302304 Quarterly refreshes will populate this line if a tactical-specific distress signal emerges on the public record.
