Chapter 4 — The Fusion / Decision Intelligence Market

Glossary.

  • Fusion (data fusion) — the analytical layer that ingests already-collected data from multiple sources and combines it into a single, resolved, relationship-mapped intelligence picture, without itself performing the collection.309
  • Decision intelligence (DI) — per Gartner, “a practical discipline that advances decision making by explicitly understanding and engineering how decisions are made, and how outcomes are evaluated, managed and improved via feedback”; a decision-intelligence platform composes “data, analytics, knowledge and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques” to support, automate, and augment decisions.310
  • Entity resolution — the process of determining that records across different sources refer to the same real-world entity (a person, organization, device, or account), consolidating them into a single, accurate view that feeds a knowledge graph.311
  • Link analysis — the mapping and traversal of relationships between resolved entities — people, organizations, events, transactions — to surface connections, networks, and the significant paths between them, built on an entity-link-property methodology.312

4.1 The Playing Ground

Fusion is the front where intelligence stops being about getting the data and starts being about making sense of it. Every other front in this report produces material: intercepted signals, field-collected geolocation, open-source web extractions. All of that material has to be correlated, de-duplicated, resolved into real-world people and organizations, mapped into relationships, placed in space and time, and turned into something an analyst can act on. That work is fusion. The product an investigative-analytics vendor sells is described, in its own terms, as letting analysts “map and analyze connections between entities such as people, organizations, and events,” built on an “entity-link-property (ELP) methodology” that “reveals relationships between data entities to discover patterns.”312 The market now names the top of this layer decision intelligence, which Gartner defines as “a practical discipline that advances decision making by explicitly understanding and engineering how decisions are made,” delivered through a platform that composes “data, analytics, knowledge and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques.”310 The buyer is a national-intelligence or national-security agency, a military-intelligence fusion cell, a law-enforcement major-investigations or intelligence unit, a financial-intelligence unit, or a cross-agency task force.

The defining property of this front — the line that keeps the chapter coherent — is that it is an analytical layer, not a collection silo. And because fusion by construction touches everything else in the report, the boundary here is the most fragile in the whole study and has to be stated with unusual precision:

Fusion is the analytical LAYER on top of collection, not a peer collection silo; a vendor is graded here ONLY if it sells fusion standalone to bring-your-own-source buyers; collection vendors with built-in dashboards are graded in their collection front and only referenced here.

That sentence does more grading work than any other in the report, so it is worth unpacking what it includes and excludes.

What this front IS. The standalone analytical layer that ingests already-collected data from many sources and turns it into resolved entities, mapped relationships, geospatial and temporal context, and managed investigations. The work spans entity resolution, link and graph analysis, geospatial-temporal analysis, investigative case management, cross-source correlation, and, as the 2026 inflection, AI- and LLM-assisted investigation. The platform is source-agnostic by design: it is sold to a bring-your-own-source buyer who already has, or separately procures, the collection. The central product is the resolution-and-graph engine, not the connection to any one sensor.

What this front is NOT. Three boundaries matter.

First, it is not a collection silo with a built-in dashboard. A Monitoring Center that ships an analyst console (the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers front), a deep-packet-inspection appliance with a profiling UI (National Agencies), an IMSI-catcher with a mapping view (Tactical Intelligence), or an open-source collector with a results graph (Open-Source Intelligence) is graded in its collection front and only referenced here. The test is whether the vendor sells the fusion layer standalone to buyers who bring their own sources. Palantir, i2, Siren, DataWalk, Nuix, and Cognyte’s NEXYTE-as-platform pass that test; a collection box’s analytics module does not. This single discipline kills the largest double-counting risk in the report, since almost every collection vendor also markets “analytics,” and counting those modules as fusion contenders would charge the same revenue and the same product to two chapters.

Second, it is not the collection itself. Fusion does not tap a channel, deploy a device, or scrape the web; it consumes the output of the collection fronts. Where a vendor (Cognyte, Cellebrite, BAE) operates in both a collection front and the fusion layer, its fusion grade rests only on its standalone analytics product, re-sourced to a page that markets that product as a platform.

Third, it is not general-purpose business intelligence. Tableau-class dashboards and horizontal commercial “decision intelligence” platforms are decision-support software. The Fusion contender set is the investigative, intelligence-grade subset: entity-centric, relationship-first, provenance-aware, and deployable into accredited government environments. The arrival of an inaugural Gartner “Decision Intelligence Platforms” Magic Quadrant313 validates the category name commercially, but the government-intelligence fusion vendors graded here are a distinct, accreditation-gated cohort. The label overlaps; the buyer and the deployment do not.

Three buyer misconceptions

“Fusion is just a nicer dashboard on top of our collection.” The hard problem is not visualization. It is entity resolution at scale — deciding that “J. Smith,” “Smith, John,” and a bare phone number are the same person across millions of records — and relationship inference across heterogeneous sources. Palantir frames the differentiator not as the screen but as the ontology: software that “takes an organization’s vast, disparate data and formats it into a common and relatable picture,” a “semantic layer that integrates the data, logic, and actions of an institution.”314 The dashboard is the cheap part. The resolution-and-ontology engine is where the switching cost lives, which, as the barriers below show, is exactly why incumbency in this layer is so sticky.

“Whoever collects the data should own the analysis.” The market has decisively separated the two. A buyer can run multiple collection vendors — a signals box from one, OSINT from another, lawful interception from a third — into a single fusion platform. It increasingly wants to, precisely to avoid being locked into one vendor’s full stack. I read the standalone-fusion vendors as structurally betting against the vertically integrated collection-plus-analytics vendors on exactly this point. Source-agnosticism is their wedge, and it is also the grading line that defines who belongs in this chapter.

“Centralizing everything into one data lake is the only way to fuse it.” This is the live architectural debate of the front. A growing cohort markets federation — analyzing data where it lives, without bulk-copying it into a central store — as the answer for sovereignty-, classification-, and governance-constrained buyers. Siren’s federation capability, for instance, “enables seamless correlation across multiple distributed data sources… without centralizing them.”315 The “you must build the lake first” assumption is precisely what the federated camp contests.

The data and technology stack

The stack reads in three strata. An ingestion-and-integration layer pulls from the collection fronts and normalizes their wildly different outputs. A resolution-and-graph core turns normalized records into entities and relationships. An exploitation-and-workflow layer adds geospatial-temporal analysis, case management, governed collaboration, and AI-assisted investigation. The differentiation lives in how well a vendor does the core at scale and how openly it does the ingestion.

On ingestion, fusion is downstream of everything. Its inputs are the heterogeneous outputs of the four collection fronts: high-volume signals metadata from the National Agencies, evidentiary warrant-scoped intercept product and chain-of-custody from the Monitoring Centers, time-and-place-stamped field fixes from Tactical Intelligence, and variable-reliability open-web and dark-web extractions from Open-Source Intelligence. To those it adds the buyer’s own case files, watchlists, and identity databases. Vendors consume this through connectors and standard interfaces. Siren ingests “using a variety of tools including JDBC and web services,” combining “digital forensic data, metadata from audio and video, and call data records… with internal databases to provide a more complete picture.”315 Cognyte’s NEXYTE markets that it “Preloads OSINT, BIZINT and commercial data into one intelligence view,” fusing “text, image, audio & video files.”316 I read the connector inventory — how many of the collection fronts’ formats a fusion vendor ingests out of the box — as a plausible but hard-to-verify moat. I also read “fuses any source” claims as directional positioning rather than a disclosed integration surface, unless a vendor ties the claim to a published connector list.

The resolution-and-graph core is the genuinely hard part. Entity resolution — deciding that records across sources refer to the same real-world entity — is the central capability, with DataWalk describing a “powerful entity resolution facility to ensure an accurate view of connected, consolidated data” feeding “a single knowledge graph,”311 and Cognyte marketing “advanced entity resolution” to “resolve identities and uncover relations.”316 Link and graph analysis maps and traverses the relationships between resolved entities; “finding the shortest and most significant path across connected records (phone calls, messages, social links)” is described as “a typical example of a widely used investigative graph algorithm.”315 Geospatial-temporal analysis places entities and events in space and time for pattern-of-life and movement reconstruction.

The exploitation-and-workflow layer is where the analyst actually lives. Investigative case management is the system of record for an investigation; Nuix Neo markets “Intelligence, Collaboration & Analytics for Investigations.”317 Governed cross-agency collaboration shares resolved intelligence “across organizational boundaries while maintaining strict governance and permissions.”316 That is not a nicety but a deployment prerequisite, because a fusion platform aggregates data of mixed classification and must enforce need-to-know inside one workspace. AI-assisted investigation, the 2026 inflection, is framed throughout as positioning rather than verified architecture.

The axes buyers discriminate on

Five dimensions separate the serious fusion vendors, each mapping to a real, publicly observable cost-and-capability structure.

  1. Entity-resolution accuracy at scale. The accuracy of the resolution core under real-world volume and ambiguity — the difference between a graph that looks connected and one whose merges an analyst can defend in court. This is the least externally verifiable axis: no vendor publishes false-merge rates. I read a vendor’s willingness to tie resolution to an auditable provenance trail per edge as the stronger public signal, and the absence of one as a flag.

  2. Federated versus central-data-lake architecture — the central wedge. Whether a vendor requires data to be centralized into its own store or can federate: analyze data in place across distributed sources without bulk-copying it. Siren positions explicitly on federation, and the general technical case is that “data federation should be used when data must remain at source due to governance, compliance, sovereignty, or contractual requirements.”315318 I read federation as a genuine architectural wedge specifically for classification- and sovereignty-constrained government buyers. For them, bulk-copying mixed-classification data into one vendor’s lake is itself a security and policy problem, not merely a cost question. If, through H2 2026, federated-architecture vendors publish named government reference wins that explicitly cite data-residency or no-bulk-copy as the selection rationale, the federation wedge hardens from positioning into a procurement-grade discriminator. If those wins do not surface publicly, it stays a marketed architectural preference.

  3. Native-source breadth. How many of the collection fronts’ formats, plus the buyer’s internal systems, a vendor ingests out of the box, and how much custom integration each new source costs. The public proxy is enumerated data-type support (NEXYTE’s “text, image, audio & video” plus “OSINT, BIZINT and commercial”316) versus unquantified “all data” claims, which are positioning, not facts, unless tied to a published connector list.

  4. AI- and LLM-assisted investigation — as positioning, not verified architecture. An outside party cannot verify a vendor’s true internal architecture, so this axis must be read as how a vendor markets itself, with a falsifiable test on public proxies. The 2026 market is visibly attaching natural-language and agentic layers over the resolved graph. NEXYTE markets that it “Reveals hidden connections with AI and natural language search,”316 Palantir centers AIP, and the broader framing is Gartner’s prediction that “by 2027, 50% of business decisions will be augmented or automated by AI agents for decision intelligence.”310 I read “AI-assisted investigation” as the current category-defining positioning move in fusion — parallel to the OSINT front’s “agentic” race — not yet a verified architectural moat. If, by H2 2026, the AI-forward fusion vendors publish named government reference wins or independent (not vendor-asserted) time-to-resolution benchmarks, the claim graduates from positioning to a defensible differentiator. If not, it stays a watchlist item.

  5. Openness and integration versus walled garden. Whether a vendor is source-agnostic and integration-friendly — ingests rival vendors’ collection, exposes APIs, lets the buyer keep multiple collection vendors — or steers the buyer into a single-vendor full stack. The public proxy is explicit “bring your own source” and open-connector positioning (Siren, DataWalk, i2) versus a collection vendor’s fusion module that is most valuable atop that vendor’s own collection. I read this as the axis most correlated with the grading line itself. The more open a fusion product, the more clearly it is a true standalone; the more it presumes the vendor’s own collection, the closer it sits to being a collection-front dashboard that should be graded elsewhere.

The public barriers

Fusion’s defining barrier is not technology — it is incumbency and switching cost, with no clean analog in the collection fronts. Two structural barriers sit on top of that.

Accreditation as the deployment gate. A fusion platform aggregates mixed-classification data inside accredited environments, so cloud and deployment accreditation is a hard gate for U.S.-federal and allied work. Palantir’s posture is the clearest public evidence of the bar. It received “FedRAMP High Authorization” for its Federal Cloud Service covering “Palantir’s entire product suite including Gotham” (announced December 2024), and holds Department of Defense “Impact Level 5 and 6” authorizations, later extended via “PFCS Forward” to on-premises and edge deployments.319 With an IL6 authorization, “government agencies can fast track use… in place of having to run lengthy and bespoke audit and accreditation processes.”319 That means an un-accredited fusion vendor faces a multi-quarter accreditation slog before it can even be deployed, a structural barrier that favors incumbents who already cleared it. One discipline binds throughout: any accreditation or certification claim about a named vendor must cite the certifying body or the vendor’s own public statement, never an analyst assertion. A wrong accreditation claim on a named company is a credibility and a defamation hit.

Clearance and FOCI. For classified U.S. programs the vendor and its personnel must clear, and foreign ownership is a structural barrier independent of product quality. Contracts requiring access to classified information “will not be awarded to companies operating under foreign ownership, control or influence unless adequate safeguards are in place,” administered through the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency’s SF 328 process, with mitigation instruments such as “independent directors, visitation and access controls, [and] restrictions on communications with the foreign owner.”320 In May 2024 the Department of Defense expanded FOCI review “from solely US government contractors that access classified information to all US government contractors performing on certain unclassified contracts with a value exceeding US$5 million.”321 For non-U.S. fusion vendors — Israeli, UK, or EU-headquartered — selling into U.S. classified programs, FOCI is the gate an excellent product cannot route around without a mitigation structure. That is itself a reason cross-border vendors in this market stand up or acquire cleared U.S. delivery entities. The specific magnitude and timeline of any individual vendor’s FOCI posture is an inference from the regime’s general applicability here, not a quoted fact — a thin spot worth naming as one.

Build-versus-buy and Palantir’s incumbent gravity. This is the structural dynamic most specific to fusion, and it has two faces.

The first is in-house build at the top tier. The largest national agencies have historically built their own analytics, and the public record on Palantir’s early history notes that “the NSA in particular had been resistant because it had plenty of its own talent,” reflecting “the agency’s historical preference for developing solutions internally.”322 In-house build is the structural “Tier 0” non-vendor competitor in fusion. At the very top end, the buyer’s alternative to a commercial platform is its own engineering org, which caps commercial penetration of the most sensitive programs.

The second face is switching cost once a platform is the system of record. Palantir’s expansion is the public exemplar: from “a single NSA contract” to “the data integration architecture for the Department of Defense, the Department of Homeland Security, the Internal Revenue Service” and beyond. Public reporting puts “$970.5 million” in U.S. federal contracts in 2025 — “nearly double the prior year,” much of it via “a sequence of no-bid contracts.”323 The switching cost is the ontology: the “framework that connects disparate data systems into a coherent operational model is what creates switching costs and defensibility.”324 I read Palantir’s incumbency gravity as the dominant market-structure fact of this front. Challengers (Siren, DataWalk, i2, Nuix) compete substantially on cost and openness against lock-in rather than on raw capability parity. If, through H2 2026, a federated or cost-positioned challenger publicly displaces an incumbent fusion deployment at a named agency — a named filing, procurement notice, or named-outlet report — the “incumbency is unassailable” read weakens. If challengers keep winning only greenfield and cost-sensitive deployments while incumbents hold the top-tier programs, the gravity read holds.

4.2 The Terrain

Market size: three named markets, walled, never averaged

There is no clean public dollar figure for the government data-fusion software slice. The honest way to present the sizing is to set the public estimates of the adjacent markets next to each other and let the spread between definitions speak. The defining problem of this front is structural: no research publisher sells a methodology-disclosed “government data-fusion / decision-intelligence” figure, because publishers size fusion by the buyer’s vertical — commercial enterprise, law enforcement, defense — not by the fusion function. What exists publicly are three distinct, overlapping markets, each scoped differently. The right discipline is to keep them walled rather than conflate or sum them. All figures are research-publisher numbers and are directional.

The first market is decision intelligence, the broadest and most commercial-weighted definition — and the one closest to Cognyte’s own public product category. Treat it as the outer bound and the most scope-bled of the three, because the published DI total-addressable-market is dominated by commercial-enterprise decision-support rather than government intelligence.

Publisher Definition used Figure (as stated) CAGR / period
Grand View Research DI as integrating technology, structured processes, and human expertise; connecting decision support, management, and complex-systems applications USD 15.22B (2024) → USD 36.34B (2030)325 15.4% (2025–2030)
Research and Markets / TBRC DI software, data feeds, and services for augmented and automated decision-making USD 17.41B (2025) → USD 20.73B (2026)326 19.1% (2025→2026)
Precedence Research DI across decision support, management, and augmentation USD 16.34B (2025) → USD 18.91B (2026) → USD 68.20B (2035)327 15.7% (to 2032)

The three publishers bracket the 2025 DI market at roughly USD 15.2B–17.4B and the 2026 market at roughly USD 18.9B–20.7B, with CAGRs clustering tightly in the mid-teens to 19% range. I read this as a relatively converged number — unusual for this report — precisely because decision intelligence as published is a broad commercial category, the same one in which Gartner ranks enterprise-analytics houses, not intelligence primes. If a fourth methodology-disclosed publisher lands outside USD 14–18B for 2025, the convergence is weaker than I have assumed. The binding caveat: this is the outer commercial bound. The government and national-security fusion slice is a small, opaque sub-fraction of it that no publisher isolates.

The second market is investigative and crime analytics, the tightest fit to the front’s law-enforcement buyer — link analysis, cross-case correlation, pattern detection — narrower than DI and explicitly law-enforcement-scoped.

Publisher Definition used Figure (as stated) CAGR / period
Market.us software platforms for data integration, visualization, and predictive modeling enabling LEA and security orgs to analyze crime data with AI/ML USD 8.1B (2024) → USD 9.3B (2025) → USD 30.7B (2034)328 14.2% (2025–2034)
The Business Research Company crime analytics including predictive-policing solutions USD 8.25B (2025) → USD 9.4B (2026)329 13.9%

The two crime-analytics publishers bracket 2025 at roughly USD 8.25B–9.3B with ~14% CAGRs — a much tighter clustering than DI, and a smaller base consistent with the narrower scope. I read crime analytics as the single best public proxy for the law-enforcement fusion slice specifically, while noting that it still folds in records-management and predictive-policing adjacencies that are not pure fusion. If a publisher with a disclosed methodology ever isolates “link-analysis / investigative-fusion software” below USD 8B for 2025, this proxy over-states the front.

The third market is defense and big-data analytics, the relevant anchor for the military-intelligence buyer at the command-and-ISR end.

Publisher Definition used Figure (as stated) CAGR / period
The Business Research Company big-data analytics in defense and aerospace incl. integrated data management, multi-source acquisition, real-time operational intelligence USD 9.77B (2025) → USD 11.07B (2026) → USD 18.14B (2030)330 13.3% (to 2026)
Global Market Insights AI and analytics in military and defense USD 10.42B (2024) → USD 11.53B (2025) → USD 35.78B (2034)331 13.4% (2025–2034)

The two defense-analytics publishers bracket 2025 at roughly USD 9.8B–11.5B at ~13% CAGR. A wider public budget figure fixes the demand envelope without being mistaken for a software market: U.S. command-control-communications-computers-cyber-ISR (C5ISR) funding is reported at roughly USD 42.69B for FY2026, an ~11.4% increase.332 I carry the C5ISR figure strictly as a demand-envelope ceiling, never as a market size; it is total program funding, far broader than the fusion-analytics software slice.

These three markets overlap heavily: a Palantir or a Cognyte appears in all three publishers’ vendor lists, which is exactly why they must stay walled and must not be summed. Summing would triple-count the same vendors and the same revenue. Set side by side, decision intelligence (~USD 15–17B, 2025) is the commercial outer bound, crime analytics (~USD 8–9B) is the law-enforcement proxy, and defense analytics (~USD 10–11B) is the military-intelligence proxy. The spread between them — not within any one — is the finding.

The government slice: a labeled proxy, not a segment size

No clean public dollar figure isolates the government and national-security data-fusion software slice. Given the opacity of B2G intelligence budgets, that is an expected, honest result, not a gap to be filled by invention. The three definitions above bracket adjacent markets. The government-fusion segment is the accreditation-gated subset that sits somewhere inside the crime-plus-defense-analytics envelope and well below the commercial DI total, but no publisher sells that number, and I do not manufacture one. The harder public currency for this front is not any market derivative at all. It is the single named public issuer in it.

That issuer is Palantir, the only pure-play public company in the front. That makes its disclosed Government-segment revenue the one hard, filing-grade datapoint here, carried strictly as the disclosed segment, never as a market size and never as total company revenue. For the three months ended 31 March 2026 (Q1 FY2026), Palantir reported Government-segment revenue of USD 858M, which it stated grew 76% year-over-year, with U.S. Government revenue at USD 687M (+84%) and International Government at USD 172M (+51%). Total company revenue was USD 1.63B (+85%), carried here only as disclosed company context, not as a fusion-front market figure.333 A single vendor’s disclosed government revenue runs at roughly a USD 3.4B annualized rate (four times the disclosed ~USD 858M quarter, stated as arithmetic on the published figure, not a publisher number) and grows 76% year-over-year. I read that as the cleanest public evidence that government fusion and operational-analytics demand is real and accelerating, even though no publisher isolates the segment. If Palantir’s Government-segment year-over-year growth decelerates below ~20% across two consecutive quarters through 2026, the “accelerating government fusion demand” read weakens.

Demand drivers

Three forcing functions carry the analytical weight the market numbers cannot.

The data has outrun the analyst. The same gap the collection fronts name from the supply side reappears here from the demand side. The volume and heterogeneity of available data — signals, OSINT, records, geospatial, biometric, financial — has outrun any analyst team’s ability to correlate it manually. The defense-analytics publishers frame the driver as “multi-source data acquisition,” “integrated data-management platforms,” and “real-time operational intelligence.”330 The crime-analytics publishers frame it as the need to link and resolve patterns across “diverse data sources.”328 Fusion is the layer that monetizes that gap directly, and Cognyte states the need in its own public terms: NEXYTE “Preloads OSINT, BIZINT and commercial data into one intelligence view” and is built to “Fuse and analyze data across sources to resolve identities and uncover relations across datasets.”334 The structural point: every new collection source — a new OSINT feed, a new intercept modality, a new biometric database — increases the value of the fusion layer that correlates it. The analytical layer’s market is a derivative of the collection fronts’ growth.

Cross-agency fusion centers are institutionalizing shared analytics. The fusion-center model — a dedicated hub where multi-source data is collected, integrated, analyzed, and disseminated across agencies — is a named, standing institutional buyer of fusion software, distinct from any single agency’s own stack. The U.S. operates a network of state, local, and federal fusion centers, and the demand is framed explicitly around eliminating data silos for cross-agency collaboration, with one fusion-center platform vendor publicly claiming adoption by “over 30% of U.S. fusion centers.”335336 I read the fusion-center channel as the structural reason this front has a cross-agency, not just per-agency, buyer: the analytical layer is bought specifically to span organizational silos. If 2026–2027 fusion-center procurements consolidate onto in-house or single-prime stacks rather than commercial platforms, the cross-agency commercial-fusion read weakens.

Build-versus-buy is contested at the top tier. The sharpest 2025 public signal on demand structure is the build-versus-buy fight at top-tier agencies, crystallized in Palantir’s GAO protest against the Defense Intelligence Agency. On 30 June 2025 Palantir filed a protest challenging the DIA’s plan to award a sole-source contract for custom in-house software development. The target was the “Prometheus” program, which began as a small-business research project. Palantir argued the approach “violates the Competition in Contracting Act and Federal Acquisition Streamlining Act,” which prefer commercial products. The DIA countered that “it does not have the software rights or documentation that the agency can share with a group of competitors.”337 I read the Prometheus protest as the clearest public expression of the front’s demand fault line — commercial-off-the-shelf fusion platforms versus agency-built custom systems — and as confirmation that the boundary is contestable and recompeting rather than settled. That is exactly what creates the opening commercial vendors press into. If GAO or the courts side with the DIA’s sole-source custom-build rationale, or the pattern repeats at other agencies through 2026, the “commercial COTS displaces in-house build” thesis weakens. If Palantir’s protest succeeds — echoing its 2016 Army DCGS win at the Court of Federal Claims — it strengthens.

The AI and LLM shift

The clearest 2025–2026 public tech signal in fusion is that agentic AI on operational data has become the category benchmark, and Palantir’s AIP is the most-cited public reference point. I frame this strictly as what vendors publicly claim, because true architecture cannot be verified from outside.

Palantir’s own public positioning leads: AIP “connects AI with your data and operations” and is “designed to drive automation across operational processes.” It lets organizations “embed large language models (LLMs) and AI agents directly into the systems your teams use every day, enabling them to automate decisions, analyze enormous datasets, and execute tasks,” with builder tools that “enable the development of production-ready AI-powered workflows, agents, and functions.”338 Palantir also states publicly that AIP “provides tools for generating detailed audit trails, explanations, and evaluations of model decisions”338 — the governance framing that matters most for a defense and B2G buyer. The benchmark effect ripples across the rest of the front. Cognyte markets NEXYTE’s “agentic AI-based decision flows” and integrated NEXYTE with Microsoft Azure to enhance its AI data-analytics solution,334339 and i2 Group brought “i2 Insights for assisted data importing and analysis” to market in its FY2025.340

The shared public claim across these vendors is that large-language-model and agentic AI compress the analyst workflow from raw multi-source data to decision-ready output. You cannot verify the true architecture from outside, so the discipline is to treat this as “markets itself as agentic,” not “is agentic.” The observable proxies are public product-page repositioning toward “agentic,” named government accreditations covering the AI product (Palantir’s AIP falls under its FedRAMP High authorization, as the barriers section noted), and named government reference wins. If a fusion vendor’s AI positioning fails to convert into a named, dated government reference win or accreditation through 2026–2027, this trend demotes from a central convergence pillar to a watchlist item. For now, several of these claimants can be named from public pages, which is what keeps it a live candidate.

Procurement and accreditation structure

Fusion procurement is bimodal. At the very top tier it tracks the sovereign, sole-source pattern of the collection fronts — custom build versus prime award. The broader law-enforcement and defense-analytics layer is bought through the same accreditation-gated federal vehicles as the rest of government software. Both modes are public-anchorable.

The gating barrier is federal cloud accreditation, and Palantir’s public history is the cleanest table-stakes anchor. It holds DoD IL5 and IL6 accreditation for its Federal Cloud Service, with the IL6 Provisional Authorization announced 10 October 2022, and was granted FedRAMP High Baseline Authorization on 3 December 2024, stated to cover “the entirety of Palantir’s product offerings — including AIP, Apollo, Foundry, Gotham, FedStart, and Mission Manager.”341342 Palantir even markets the accreditation itself as a product through “FedStart,” which lets third-party software run inside its “already-accredited environment.”343 I read the accreditation stack — IL5/IL6 plus FedRAMP High covering the AI product — as the real barrier to entry in the U.S. government fusion market: a software-quality-agnostic gate that favors incumbents who have already paid the accreditation cost. If a new fusion entrant wins a named U.S. classified-workload contract in 2026 without IL5-or-higher accreditation, the accreditation-as-moat read is over-stated.

Above that floor sits the sole-source-versus-recompete fault line. At the top tier, fusion procurement splits between multi-year sole-source or custom-build awards and recompeted commercial-product buys, and the line between them is litigated on the public record. The clearest case is the Palantir-versus-DIA “Prometheus” protest, where Palantir invoked the Competition in Contracting Act and the Federal Acquisition Streamlining Act preference for commercial products as the lever to force a sole-source custom award into a recompete.337 I read the recurring protest pattern — the DIA in 2025, echoing the Army DCGS fight Palantir won at the Court of Federal Claims in 2016 — as evidence that the build-versus-buy boundary in government fusion is contested in public, in sharp contrast to the opaque sovereign-system awards of the collection fronts. Below the pure-plays, fusion analytics reaches government through defense primes and integrators (Leidos, GDIT, RTX and peers) and through established federal vehicles such as the GSA Schedule and Carahsoft-class resellers, with the fusion-center channel as a further named buying surface. The primes’ fusion-specific dollar exposure is not publicly isolable and is carried here as channel structure, never as a sized figure.

One ownership note bears on the contenders and war-chest analysis that follow. i2 Group — the Analyst’s Notebook lineage and the historical link-analysis standard — was divested by IBM to Harris Computer Corporation (announced 4 January 2022). It is now part of Constellation Software, not IBM. The “IBM i2” branding is legacy, and i2 reported a “40% year-on-year increase in bookings” for its FY2025.340344 Siren’s funding status could not be cleanly confirmed in this terrain pass and is flagged for re-verification when the war chests are graded.

4.3 The Contenders

Decision intelligence is the front where the candidate list looks deep and grades shallow. Pull a raw vendor universe for “government fusion” and you can name a dozen contenders without effort, but most of them dissolve once the front-local gates are applied. The layer test grades the multi-source analytical layer — entity resolution, link analysis, geospatial and temporal correlation, case management, cross-source fusion — only where it is sold to a buyer who brings their own sources. Disclosed-segment sizing governs diversified parents: a product line may be referenced on its own dated public page, but the report never uses total-parent economics as if they sized that fusion line. A vendor whose analytics are inseparable from its own collection is graded in its collection front and merely referenced here; a prime whose fusion line cannot be bounded publicly is retained as a market reference, not promoted with parent-wide scale. Together, these disciplines keep the front from becoming either a double-counting catch-all or a megacap-size comparison.

Six vendors are graded, not eight — and the gap is the point. The cap for this report is eight contenders per front. This front comes in under the cap by design, and not because the public material is thin. Each of the six graded here carries a rich, dated public footprint. The candidates that fell out did so under the front-local layer test or disclosed-segment sizing discipline, not through a missing-count convenience. This is the exact inverse of the monitoring-centre and tactical fronts, where the constraint is finding enough gradeable vendors to fill the buckets. Here the honest count of vendors that sell the investigative fusion layer to government bring-your-own-source buyers is smaller than the candidate list; manufacturing two more grades by relaxing the test would erase the finding. The six are placed across three tiers — 2 Gravity (the structural anchors a buyer cannot map the front without naming), 3 Attention (the vendors shaping 2026 demand, M&A, and the AI-native narrative), and 1 Challenger (the architecture bet against the incumbents). The candidates that did not make the cut, and why, are documented at the end of this section so the boundary can be defended.

A word on who is not graded, because in this front the exclusions are as central as the inclusions. The same three candidate categories recur at the detailed cut line: adjacent software layers and missions; a divested former contender; and diversified primes or integrators whose line cannot be sized from parent-wide economics. Microsoft, Scale AI, Anduril, and Air (formerly Govini) are retained as adjacent-layer or adjacent-mission references under the buyer-and-layer test. BAE Systems is retained for the divested NetReveal history.345 Airbus, Thales, Leonardo, Indra, Saab, Leidos, GDIT, RTX, and Oracle are retained as diversified-prime or integration-channel references under the front-local disclosed-segment discipline. All three exclusion categories are commentary, not grades. The same layer test that admitted the six below and the same sizing discipline that prevents parent-wide inflation govern the detailed findings.

Author’s read of public material, June 2026. Vendor positions are conceptual, not data-derived. Tier color-coding: Gravity (burnt orange), Attention (amber), Challenger (pale amber). Not investment advice.

Gravity tier

Palantir — the primary

“A commercially-available, AI-ready operating system that improves and accelerates decisions for operators across roles and all domains.” — Palantir, Gotham product description, accessed 2026-06-14 346

Palantir is the category-defining decision-intelligence platform — the de facto standard against which every other vendor in this front is positioned, and the one a buyer cannot map the terrain without naming first. Its Gotham platform is marketed as the government, defense, and intelligence product, with Foundry as the commercial equivalent. The stated wedge is the full stack: data integration through Gotham and Foundry, then an AI operationalization layer. That layer, AIP, launched in 2023, is one Palantir publicly describes as using “generative and agentic AI models, including large language models (LLMs)” directly inside both platforms.347 The public commercial-acquisition engine is the AIP Bootcamp, which converts evaluation into deployment on a customer’s own operational data.347 The target buyer is the archetype the layer test is written around: defense, national-intelligence, and military operators who bring their own data sources and pay Palantir for the fusion-and-decision layer on top. On pricing, the public record is sparse: no clean per-seat figure, only large multi-year government programs of record and enterprise Bootcamp-led commercial deals, with pricing largely dark beyond disclosed contract values. Architecturally, Palantir markets a central-platform-plus-ontology model with AIP positioned as a native generative-and-agentic layer over the ontology rather than a bolt-on. I carry that as positioning, not verified architecture, because true internals cannot be read from outside.

The most consequential public event in this front sits with Palantir. In a 9 March 2026 letter, Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg directed that the Maven Smart System be designated a Pentagon “program of record” across all military branches. Oversight moves from the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency to the DoD Chief Digital and AI Office, with the U.S. Army taking future contracting.348 A program-of-record designation is the difference between contestable pilots and locked-in, multi-year core infrastructure at the largest defense buyer in the world. I read this as Palantir hardening from “vendor” to “infrastructure” inside the U.S. defense estate. That raises the switching cost against every rival in this front, and the build-versus-buy play later in this chapter tracks it against public proxies. Sourcing here is the richest in the front: vendor-controlled self-positioning, heavy named-outlet coverage, and SEC-filer disclosure, since Palantir (NYSE: PLTR) is a public issuer and the trading-position disclaimer applies.

i2 Group

“The global industry standard for creating and sharing intelligence … The knowledge graph solution at the forefront of intelligence analysis.” — i2 Group homepage, accessed 2026-06-14 349

i2 Group is the legacy link-analysis standard — the incumbent the AI-native disruptors are positioned to displace, and the second name no map of this front can omit. Its Analyst’s Notebook, marketed under the “Intelligence Amplified” line, has been the entity-link-property analyst workbench for decades. It is the tool a vast installed base of NATO, intelligence, and law-enforcement analysts trained on. The method became a de facto standard in its own right. i2 positions Analyst’s Notebook as the knowledge-graph solution that helps analysts “discover the mission critical connections between events, locations, and people.”349 It extends the single-analyst workbench to an enterprise-fusion environment through its Enterprise Insight Analysis (EIA) platform, publicly described as providing “advanced fusion and multi-dimensional analytics to create actionable intelligence to detect, disrupt, and defeat sophisticated threats” by accelerating teams “through the process of acquiring, fusing, and analyzing data” across “internal, external, and open source data.”350 The stated moat is incumbency plus the entity-link-property method as an industry standard. The target buyer is defense, law enforcement, national security, and government. That base spans “thousands of organizations” across “more than 140 countries,” including most members of NATO.351 On pricing, i2 markets explicitly as “commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) solutions,”351 the accessible-procurement contrast to bespoke sovereign builds, though no clean per-seat figure is public. Architecturally it is graph-native — knowledge-graph at the core, analyst-workbench plus enterprise fusion — and it is adding “AI-enabled analytics”351 as a modernization layer over the established graph rather than rebuilding around a large-language-model core. The positioning is “modernize the incumbent standard,” not “replace it.”

The ownership fact matters and is frequently misstated: i2 is owned by N. Harris Computer Corporation, a division of Constellation Software — not IBM. Harris acquired the i2 product portfolio from IBM in a deal announced 4 January 2022 (effective 1 January 2022),352 and i2 has operated under Constellation since. The public momentum is real and recent: on 7 October 2025 i2 disclosed “a 40% year-on-year increase in bookings and continued double-digit organic growth across all business segments.”351 That followed an August-2024 disclosure of NATO-driven double-digit growth.353 The reason i2 grades as Gravity rather than as a fading incumbent is exactly this tension. It is the decades-old standard the AI-native platforms must displace, and the public scorecard shows it still growing double digits while they grow too. The displacement question, framed as a falsifiable conditional in the plays below, turns entirely on i2’s installed base.

Attention tier

Nuix

“Finding Truth in the Digital World … Leading AI-powered solutions, helping organizations protect, govern and unlock value from their data.” — Nuix homepage, accessed 2026-06-14 354

Nuix is the processing-first contender — the engine that makes vast, messy, multi-format evidence corpora investigable, sitting at the boundary where eDiscovery meets investigation meets intelligence. Where Palantir is ontology-first and i2 is graph-first, Nuix’s wedge is unstructured-data processing at investigative scale. It markets the ability to ingest “over 1000 file types” of “messy unstructured data” and turn it into “structured, searchable assets,”354 then apply “investigative analytics and intelligence software” on top, with Nuix Neo Investigations pitched to “uncover the truth with insights on a massive scale.”355 The target buyer is “law enforcement, legal firms, government departments and large corporations globally,” with public-record claims of “over 1800 organizations” and “90+ regulators worldwide.”354 Nuix is unusual in this front for the transparency its listing forces: it is ASX-listed (NXL), so contract economics are partly disclosed at the annual-contract-value level — a rarity here. Architecturally it markets a processing-engine core (its own “bespoke language models,” the 1000-plus file-type span) with the Neo platform as the modern analytics-and-AI layer over the top. It is adding graph and link-analysis through acquisition rather than a native rebuild.

The 2026 surface is the most active in the Attention tier. Nuix’s first-half-FY26 results, reported 23 February 2026, showed revenue of AUD 121.2 million (up 15% year-on-year) and a return to net profit. The Neo platform surged 148% year-on-year to roughly 20% of total annual contract value (total ACV AUD 234.4 million).356 Most relevant to its grading here, Nuix signed to acquire Linkurious SAS for €20 million on 3 December 2025 (approximately €7 million in ACV, positive EBITDA). That folds graph and link-analysis directly into its unstructured-data processing engine.357 I read this as the inorganic route to a complete fusion stack: a processing-first vendor buying the graph-analytics layer to move up-stack into full fusion, against i2’s organic incumbency and Palantir’s built ontology. It is a clean buy-the-layer move that materially strengthens Nuix’s claim to be graded as a fusion platform rather than a processing tool.

Cognyte (NEXYTE)

Disclosure: the author, Yohay Etsion, served as VP Product at Cognyte. This is independent ProductBeacon research based solely on publicly available material; it reflects the author’s personal analysis, not Cognyte’s position, and is not investment advice.

“Accelerate data-driven decision-making with data fusion and advanced analytics … Fuse and analyze data across sources to resolve identities and uncover relations … Apply agentic AI-based decision flows.” — Cognyte, NEXYTE Decision Intelligence Platform page, accessed 2026-06-14 358

Cognyte is graded in this front strictly on its publicly-marketed NEXYTE decision-intelligence platform plus its corporate positioning, sourced entirely to dated public pages with no internal knowledge. This front is the cleanest of the five for grading it, because NEXYTE is publicly buildable as a standalone fusion platform on its own product page. NEXYTE is marketed under the line “EVERY DECISION COUNTS” as a platform that fuses and analyzes “data across sources to resolve identities and uncover relations” and applies “agentic AI-based decision flows.”358 The corporate frame describes Cognyte as “a global leader in investigative analytics software that empowers a variety of government and other organizations with Actionable Intelligence for a Safer World™.”359 The publicly-readable USP is that NEXYTE passes the layer test directly. It markets data fusion, identity resolution, and relation analytics to bring-your-own-source buyers as a standalone decision-intelligence workspace, leaning on “preloaded OSINT, BIZINT and commercial data into one intelligence view”358 — a fusion-of-pre-integrated-sources pitch rather than a bring-nothing analytics shell. The target buyer, per the public pages, is law enforcement, national security, defense, and financial-crime and anti-money-laundering investigators. That sits within a base of “hundreds of customers in approximately 100 countries.”359 Architecturally, NEXYTE markets “domain-specific, pre-trained AI models,” “co-pilots,” and “agentic decision flows”358 — a positioning move toward AI-native decision intelligence. Whether the underlying architecture is large-language-model-native or a bolt-on cannot be verified from outside, so this is read as positioning only, the same standing caveat that governs every contender in this front.

A scope note matters here. Cognyte is graded as one contender among many on its public NEXYTE surface alone. Its broader portfolio breadth — the fact that its public capability pages span multiple of this report’s five fronts — is carried by the Convergence chapter rather than force-graded into each front. Here the question is simply whether NEXYTE is a standalone fusion platform on the public record, and it is. Cognyte (NASDAQ: CGNT) is a public issuer, so the trading-position disclaimer applies, and the author-independence banner above governs the grading.

DataWalk

“DataWalk is a unified graph and AI platform for data management, analysis, and investigative intelligence.” — DataWalk, Entity Resolution solution page, accessed 2026-08-22 360

DataWalk is the sixth graded contender and sits in Attention. It passes the layer test directly: its current public pages market a source-agnostic investigative platform that integrates internal and external data, resolves duplicate or ambiguous records into connected entities, carries provenance and lineage into a knowledge graph, and supports link, geospatial, time-series, and investigative workflows.360 The intelligence page extends that positioning to HUMINT, SOCMINT, SIGINT, GEOINT, sensor, and drone inputs, with on-premises, cloud, classified, and air-gapped deployment described by the vendor.361 Those are vendor claims and are treated as positioning, not independently verified performance.

The target buyer is explicit on those pages: intelligence, law-enforcement, national-security, and other government investigative teams bringing multiple internal and external sources to one analytical layer.360361 That buyer and product center are the reason DataWalk is not merely a name swap. Its core is entity resolution plus the governed graph an analyst must inspect and defend, rather than a collection box’s own dashboard or a general-purpose AI workbench. Architecturally, DataWalk positions an ontology-driven knowledge graph with connectors and APIs, deployable in sovereign or disconnected environments. Its “European alternative to Palantir” language is vendor positioning, not a parity finding.361

Attention is the evidence-based tier. DataWalk has a complete, current investigative-fusion product surface and a public issuer record, so Challenger would understate the product and commercial evidence. Gravity would overstate the record: the public sources do not show Palantir-scale program-of-record entrenchment or i2-scale installed-base ubiquity. DataWalk’s 2025 issuer report records consolidated sales revenue of PLN 37.783 million, up 53% year on year, cash and cash equivalents of PLN 39.623 million, and cash plus deposits over three months of PLN 57.740 million at year-end.362 That is a real public war-chest anchor, but far below the front’s Gravity-scale incumbents and not a claim about current valuation.

Challenger tier

Siren

“Accelerate the Intelligence Lifecycle with Siren … dashboard analytics, search and unstructured content processing, alerting, link analysis, entity resolution, integrated natural language processing (NLP), and artificial intelligence (AI).” — Siren, Law Enforcement and Intelligence page, accessed 2026-06-14 363

Siren is the Challenger because it bets against the one architectural assumption every Gravity-tier vendor is built on — the central data lake. Rather than ingesting everything into a single platform store, Siren federates over data where it lives. Its differentiating technology, Siren Federate, “enhances Elasticsearch with complex join operations and powerful data-linking capabilities, allowing seamless data correlation across multiple indices,”364 and the platform markets “investigative intelligence” as search-plus-graph-plus-correlation across distributed sources to enable “intelligence-led policing investigations.”363 That is the stated USP and the architecture-disruption story of the front in one move: if federated fusion can match central-lake performance at investigative scale, it undercuts the heavy-integration model the incumbents sell. The target buyer is law enforcement and intelligence agencies across national security, public safety, fraud and compliance, and cyber-threat operations.363 Pricing is private and not publicly disclosed; an aggregator funding lineage circulates but is carried here as undisclosed rather than as a fact. Architecturally Siren is explicit that it is not central-lake: a federated knowledge-graph over Elasticsearch doing “real-time big data correlations (joins) within Elasticsearch clusters.”364 Entity resolution is added through a Senzing partnership announced 15 October 2024,365 and U.S. public-sector distribution runs via an Elastic OEM partnership and Carahsoft.364

Consistent with the Challenger discipline, the read stays descriptive and hedged. Siren is private (headquartered in Galway, Ireland), and its 2024–2026 momentum is partnership-led — the Senzing entity-resolution partnership and the Elastic public-sector OEM, not a disclosed funding milestone or a named program win. The interesting bet is whether federated fusion pulls budget away from the central-lake incumbents, or stays a specialist architecture for agencies that cannot or will not centralize their data. I do not assert which way it breaks. The plays below frame it as a falsifiable conditional grounded on whether a named government agency publicly adopts a federated-fusion architecture for a mission previously run on a central lake.

The cut line — why three candidate categories are not graded here

The front’s apparent depth forces a defensible cut, and here the cut uses two named, front-local grounds rather than the cap: the buyer-and-layer test and disclosed-segment sizing for diversified parents. The first asks whether the product’s buyer is an investigative analyst resolving contested identities and relationships across brought-in sources. The second prevents a product line from borrowing total-parent scale where its own economics are not disclosed. These are Fusion-front rules, not a report-level scope statement.

  • Adjacent software layers and missions — Microsoft, Scale AI, Anduril, Air (formerly Govini). Microsoft remains the Azure Government and large-language-model substrate underneath Palantir under the dated August-2024 classified-cloud partnership.366 Scale AI gets its own current record: its May 2026 Pentagon agreement describes Scale Data Engine, the Scale GenAI Platform, and Donovan as data operations, model-building/deployment, and generative-AI decision support on classified networks.367 That is material government AI work, but the published center is AI infrastructure, agents, and unstructured-data decision support rather than this front’s relationship-first entity-resolution, graph, and investigative-case layer. Anduril leads with a different buyer and layer: Lattice fuses sensor tracks for command and control and battle management; the graded front resolves identities for investigative analysts. Its own pages call Lattice an open and extensible platform, and that openness is real.368 The June 2026 NGC2 stack boundary still places Lattice as the tactical data layer and Palantir Foundry as the cloud data layer. Anduril therefore fits C2 / battle management, a front this report does not cover. It is not F3 either: that front grades proximity RF collection against a present target, not a C2 platform consuming sensor tracks. Air (formerly Govini) now positions its Enterprise Readiness platform around defense acquisition and production, supply-chain and sustainment, logistics, and readiness, not the investigative identity-resolution subset graded here.369
  • Divested former contender — BAE Systems. BAE’s fusion-relevant NetReveal asset was divested to SymphonyAI in 2022 (announced July, closed October).345 The divestiture, rather than parent-company scale, is the market-structure datapoint; BAE is referenced, not force-graded in this front.
  • Diversified European primes and integration channels — Airbus, Thales, Leonardo, Indra, Saab, Leidos, GDIT, RTX, Oracle. Airbus proves that product absence is not the cut: it markets Fortion Massive Intelligence for “the unified exploitation of all available data” and to “uncover links between objects and information,” plus Fortion Multi-INT Centres for managing “the full intelligence cycle.”370 Airbus is therefore a real Fusion market reference. Airbus’s FY2025 results disclose Airbus Defence and Space at segment level but do not isolate Fortion; the report therefore has no separately disclosed Fortion economics for sizing and does not substitute total-company economics.370 For Thales, Leonardo, Indra, and Saab, a comparable dated, front-fit product-line page was not surfaced in the public search run for this report; that is a bounded search result, never a claim that a product is verified absent. Leidos, GDIT, RTX, and Oracle remain integration and delivery channels for fusion programs. Every parent in this category is sized only at a relevant disclosed line or segment where available, never at total-parent revenue.

A note on what is deliberately not a problem here: there is no surveillance-cohort exclusion to make in this front. None of the locked never-graded vendors (NSO, Candiru, Intellexa, Ability, Voyager Labs) competes in standalone government fusion, so none appears in the candidate set. Cellebrite is graded in the tactical front on its device-extraction collection — the product the buyer pays for — and is only adjacent to this front via its analytics layer. Per the cross-front ledger it is referenced here rather than re-graded, to avoid double-counting a vendor whose collection, not its analytics, is what the buyer pays for. The discipline that holds the graded set at six is the same discipline that keeps every one of these placements honest: grade the investigative layer, size a diversified parent only at its disclosed line or segment, and reference the rest.

4.4 Their Plays

Five strategic moves are in motion across the Fusion / Decision Intelligence front in 2026. Each is anchored to a dated public event, names its participants, and carries a falsifiable read grounded on a publicly observable proxy. Those proxies are a Pentagon designation memo, an earnings or bookings disclosure, a named M&A close, a strategic-investment announcement, or a public procurement record. Two of the five are consolidation plays (one M&A at the graph layer, one strategic-investment-led federation bet). One is the front’s central build-vs-buy displacement contest, one is the government program-of-record lock-in, and one is the structural “pick-a-lane” pattern that keeps the hyperscalers and primes out of the standalone fusion layer. Collection vendors that “wear a fusion hat” — DPI/monitoring-center boxes with a built-in dashboard — appear in this section only as commentary on the front’s boundary, never as graded fusion contenders, per the analytics-layer-not-silo test.

The five routes to a complete fusion stack, mapped to the plays in this chapter. Author’s read of public material, June 2026. Conceptual, not data-derived. Not investment advice.

Play 1: The Category Leader Converts Pilots Into Permanent Infrastructure

  • Observation. Palantir’s Maven Smart System was directed for designation as a Pentagon “program of record” across all military branches, per a 9 March 2026 letter from Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg. Oversight transfers from the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency to the DoD Chief Digital and AI Office, with the U.S. Army taking future contracting .371372 The designation moves Maven from contestable, renewable pilots toward locked-in, multi-year “core digital infrastructure,” securing stable funding at the largest defense buyer in the front. It runs alongside the U.S. Army’s TITAN multi-sensor data-fusion award to Palantir, reported at roughly $178M 373.
  • Participants. DoD / CDAO, U.S. Army, NGA, Palantir (NYSE: PLTR).
  • My read. I read this as the category leader hardening from “vendor” to “infrastructure” inside the U.S. defense estate — the single most consequential government event on the front, because program-of-record status raises the switching cost against every rival and converts a recompeted line item into a standing one.
  • Falsifiable read. If H2 2026 brings a second allied government designating a Palantir platform as a standing program of record (not a renewable pilot), the infrastructure thesis strengthens into a pattern. If instead public procurement records show a named agency dual-sourcing fusion — running i2 or a federated alternative alongside Palantir on the same mission — the lock-in is less complete than the program-of-record framing implies.
  • Evidence. DepSecDef Maven program-of-record memo, 9 Mar 2026, widely reported across defense-trade and national press 371372; U.S. Army TITAN award reported at roughly $178M per defense reporting 373.

Play 2: The Build-vs-Buy Displacement — AI-Native Platforms Pressure the Legacy Link-Analysis Standard

  • Observation. The front’s central tension is whether AI-native ontology/operationalization platforms displace the decades-old entity-link-property (ELP) analyst workbench, or whether the incumbent standard modernizes and holds its base. On one side: Palantir’s AIP-led operationalization positioning 374 and the Maven program-of-record scale above .371 On the other: i2 Group’s countervailing public disclosure of “a 40% year-on-year increase in bookings and continued double-digit organic growth across all business segments” (7 Oct 2025) 375, and Nuix’s Neo platform ACV surging 148% YoY in 1H FY2026 .376 The public scorecard is mixed — both the AI-native disruptor and the incumbent standard are growing double digits at the same time.
  • Participants. Palantir, i2 Group / Constellation Software, Nuix, and the NATO / law-enforcement ELP installed base.
  • My read. I read this as displacement-at-the-margin, not wholesale replacement — yet. The honest reading is that the disruptor and the incumbent are both winning, which is why this play scores MIXED. The incumbent’s installed base across “more than 140 countries” 375 is a real moat, and the AI-native platforms have not published the named “rip-and-replace” reference wins a clean displacement thesis would require. A parallel datapoint shows that government fusion procurement is genuinely contested: the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency’s “Prometheus” open-source data-analytics acquisition drew a GAO bid protest, the public marker that even AI-native-era fusion awards are litigated and recompeted, not simply handed to the category leader 377.
  • Falsifiable read. If through H2 2026 i2’s public bookings growth decelerates while Palantir or Nuix publish named government reference wins that explicitly replace a legacy link-analysis deployment, the displacement thesis hardens. If instead i2 keeps posting double-digit bookings growth and publishes its own AI-native modernization with named retention wins — and contested awards like Prometheus continue to be recompeted rather than sole-sourced to an AI-native incumbent — the “incumbent standard modernizes and holds” read wins.
  • Evidence. Palantir AIP positioning 374; i2 40% bookings growth, 7 Oct 2025 375; Nuix Neo +148% ACV, 1H FY26 376; DIA “Prometheus” GAO protest 377.

Play 3: Buy the Graph Layer — Fusion Vendors Acquire Link-Analysis to Complete the Stack

  • Observation. Nuix completed its acquisition of Paris-based graph-intelligence platform Linkurious SAS for up to €20M, the transaction having closed in April 2026 following French foreign-direct-investment approval. The deal folds graph/link-analysis (~€7M ACV) into its unstructured-data processing engine .378379 The disclosed structure was €12.5M upfront cash plus €2.5M escrow shares plus a €5M ACV-linked earnout, an A$~35M headline .379 The signed-to-acquire announcement dated to 3 December 2025 378.
  • Participants. Nuix (ASX: NXL), Linkurious, and government / law-enforcement / enterprise investigation buyers.
  • My read. I read this as the M&A route to a complete fusion stack for vendors that lead on one layer and lack another — a processing-first vendor buying the graph-analytics layer to move up-stack into full fusion, against i2’s organic incumbency and Palantir’s built ontology. It is the inorganic path to the collect-process-link-decide workflow, and the corrected €20M close price marks it as a bolt-on-scale tuck-in rather than a transformational deal.
  • Falsifiable read. If H2 2026 brings a second comparable acquisition of a graph/link-analysis or entity-resolution specialist by a fusion-adjacent vendor, the buy-the-layer pattern is the front’s consolidation mode. If instead these acquired graph capabilities surface only as bolt-on features without named government wins, the build (Palantir) and incumbency (i2) routes are out-competing the buy route.
  • Evidence. Nuix–Linkurious signed 3 Dec 2025 378; close (up to €20M), Apr 2026 379.

Play 4: Federated Fusion Emerges as the Alternative to the Central Data Lake

  • Observation. A standalone strategic-investment signal arrived for the federated-architecture bet: Elastic (NYSE: ESTC) announced a strategic investment in Siren on 2 December 2025, deepening a decade-long partnership and explicitly framed around AI-driven investigations for national security. The round size was not disclosed .380 Siren’s Federate technology enhances Elasticsearch with join operations and data-linking to correlate across distributed sources rather than ingesting everything into one central store 381. Entity resolution is added via a Senzing partnership (announced 15 October 2024) 382, and US public-sector distribution runs through the Elastic OEM relationship and Carahsoft 381.
  • Participants. Siren, Elastic, Senzing, and agencies constrained — by data sovereignty, scale, or governance — from centralizing their data.
  • My read. I read this as a genuine architectural counter-bet with a narrow-but-real beachhead, not yet a mainstream displacement. The federated model is the most direct public challenge to the central-platform model the Gravity tier (Palantir, i2) is built on. Consistent with Challenger discipline, the read stays descriptive. The open question is whether federated fusion pulls budget from the central-lake incumbents or stays a specialist architecture for agencies that cannot or will not centralize.
  • Falsifiable read. If through H2 2026 a named government agency publicly adopts a federated-fusion architecture for a mission previously run on a central-lake platform, the federated thesis graduates from specialist to contender-architecture. If federated deployments stay confined to data-residency-constrained niches without a named central-lake displacement, it remains a Challenger architecture rather than a category shift.
  • Evidence. Elastic strategic investment in Siren, 2 Dec 2025 380; Siren Federate / Elasticsearch-join architecture 381; Siren–Senzing partnership, 15 Oct 2024 382.

Play 5: Hyperscalers and Primes Pick a Lane — Cloud-and-Channel, Not Standalone Fusion

  • Observation. The largest adjacent players are positioning around the fusion layer rather than competing in it head-on. The August-2024 Palantir–Microsoft partnership deploys Foundry/Gotham/Apollo/AIP inside Azure Government and classified clouds (IL6 and Top Secret). Microsoft is the cloud-and-LLM layer beneath Palantir, not a standalone fusion product sold to bring-your-own-source buyers .383 In parallel, the systems-integrator and prime channel (Leidos, GDIT, RTX, Oracle) integrates fusion software — frequently Palantir or i2 — into programs rather than fielding its own standalone fusion platform.
  • Participants. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), Palantir, the prime integrators (Leidos / GDIT / RTX / Oracle), and government buyers.
  • My read. I read this as the hyperscalers and primes ceding the fusion-platform layer to specialists while monetizing the layers above and below it — the base layer (cloud + LLM) for Microsoft, the integration channel for the primes. The fusion-platform layer itself stays a structurally distinct specialist software market, even as the base layer and the channel concentrate. This is the structural reason Fusion’s gradeable contender set is honestly smaller than the raw candidate list: the megacaps that look like fusion players on a vendor map fail the standalone-to-BYO-source test and sit in this commentary instead.
  • Falsifiable read. If H2 2026 brings a hyperscaler launching a named standalone government fusion/decision-intelligence product (not a partner-hosting deal), the “ceding the layer” read weakens and the front faces a megacap entrant. If the partnership-and-integration pattern holds — base layer plus channel, no standalone product — the specialist fusion-software market stays structurally distinct from its cloud and integrator neighbors.
  • Evidence. Palantir–Microsoft classified-cloud partnership, 8 Aug 2024 383; systems-integrator channel (Leidos / GDIT / RTX / Oracle), referenced as the build/integration channel, disclosed-segment level only, never graded.

Market-force commentary: the divested and the collection-vendors-wearing-a-fusion-hat (not graded)

Two non-graded structures shape the front’s boundary. First, BAE Systems is named only as market-structure context. Its fusion-relevant analytics asset, NetReveal, was divested to SymphonyAI (announced 12 July 2022, closed 31 October 2022) 384, so BAE no longer fields a standalone government fusion software product on the public record that fits this front. The divestiture is itself the datapoint, no grade and no pattern claim. Second, the collection vendors that market a “fusion” dashboard on top of their own DPI or monitoring-center collection are referenced here, not graded. Per the layer test, a vendor whose analytics are inseparable from its own collection grades in its collection front (National Agencies, Monitoring Centers, or Tactical Intelligence) and is only referenced here. Cognyte’s portfolio-breadth across all five fronts is carried by the Convergence chapter, and in Fusion it is graded cleanly and only on its publicly-marketed NEXYTE decision-intelligence platform, not by importing its collection products into the fusion grade.

Commentary on the capital pattern (≤150 words)

Fusion splits cleanly into a public-company core and a thin private tail. The graded contenders are overwhelmingly public or public-owned: Palantir (PLTR), Nuix (NXL), DataWalk, and Cognyte (CGNT) trade on exchanges; i2 sits inside Constellation Software (CSU).390394 BAE is a public market reference, not a graded contender in this front. Palantir is the scale outlier. Government revenue of $858M/qtr growing 76% 385 dwarfs the specialists’ disclosed figures (Cognyte $400M FY 401; Nuix A$121.2M 1H 392; DataWalk PLN 37.783M FY 394; i2 undisclosed), and its >$4B cash, zero-debt balance sheet 387 gives it build-vs-buy optionality the specialists lack. The 2025–2026 capital signal is consolidation at the analytics layer, not greenfield funding: Nuix bought graph-intelligence firm Linkurious (up to €20M, closed Apr 2026) 393. The lone notable private event — Siren — was a strategic investment from Elastic (Dec 2025) 395 rather than a priced venture mega-round. Standalone private fusion bets are scarce.

4.6 Winning & Losing

Three patterns govern who is gaining ground and who is ceding it on the fusion / decision-intelligence front in 2026. Each is anchored to a specific public event, framed explicitly as opinion, and stated as a falsifiable prediction the next two quarters will confirm or refute. Read them in sequence. The first is the gravitational fact of the front: one vendor is hardening from supplier into infrastructure, and there is a public test of whether that grip holds. The second is the consolidation move every challenger is making in response: buying or federating the graph layer to assemble a complete stack. The third is the unresolved contest underneath both: whether the decades-old link-analysis standard gets displaced by the AI-native platforms, or modernizes and keeps its base. The scorecard on that last one is genuinely mixed, and the chapter says so.

Pattern Claim 1 — The Palantir-Gravity Thesis

Observation. In March 2026 the U.S. Deputy Secretary of Defense directed that Palantir’s Maven Smart System be designated a Pentagon “program of record” across all military branches, moving oversight to the DoD Chief Digital and AI Office and the U.S. Army for future contracting. That converts a sequence of pilots into stable, multi-year core infrastructure.404 The scale underneath the designation is filing-grade: Palantir reported Government-segment revenue of $858M for the quarter ended 31 March 2026, up 76% year-over-year (U.S. Government $687M, +84%), against a >$4B-cash, zero-debt balance sheet.405 406 The deployment moat is publicly observable. Palantir holds FedRAMP High authorization stated to cover “the entirety of Palantir’s product offerings — including AIP, Apollo, Foundry, Gotham, FedStart, and Mission Manager,” plus DoD Impact Level 5 and Impact Level 6 authorizations.407 408 Independent analysis of the platform frames the switching cost as the ontology — the “framework that connects disparate data systems into a coherent operational model is what creates switching costs and defensibility.”409

My read. I read this as one vendor hardening from “vendor” into “infrastructure” inside the U.S. defense estate, on three reinforcing public legs. The first is a program-of-record designation that locks in multi-year funding. The second is a Government-segment revenue line that dwarfs every specialist in the front. The third is an accreditation ledger (FedRAMP High + IL5/IL6 covering the AI product) that is itself a software-quality-agnostic barrier to entry. The challengers in this front — i2, Nuix, Siren — compete substantially on cost and openness-against-lock-in rather than on raw capability parity, because the gravity is structural, not merely competitive. The single most important public test of whether that grip is total runs through the build-vs-buy fault line: the Palantir–DIA “Prometheus” GAO protest (filed 30 June 2025). In that protest, Palantir challenged the Defense Intelligence Agency’s plan to award a sole-source contract for custom in-house software development, arguing the approach “violates the Competition in Contracting Act and Federal Acquisition Streamlining Act.” DIA countered that “it does not have the software rights or documentation that the agency can share with a group of competitors.”410 The in-house build remains the genuine Tier-0 competitor at the very top tier, and the boundary is contestable, not settled.

Conditional prediction. If H2 2026 brings a second allied government designating a Palantir platform as a standing program of record (not a pilot), or the DIA “Prometheus” custom-build path is forced back into a commercial recompete on the public record, the gravity thesis hardens into the defining structure of the front. The inverse runs two ways: public procurement records show a named agency dual-sourcing fusion — running i2 or a federated alternative alongside Palantir on the same mission — or GAO/courts sustain DIA’s sole-source custom-build rationale and the in-house-build pattern repeats at other top-tier agencies. On either path the lock-in is less complete than the program-of-record framing implies, and the build option is reasserting itself at the ceiling Palantir cannot price into.

Sources. 404 405 406 407 408 409 410

Author’s read of public material, June 2026. Conceptual, not data-derived. Not investment advice.

Pattern Claim 2 — The Layer-Consolidation Thesis

Observation. Across 2025–2026 the fusion front’s challengers moved to complete the stack by acquiring or federating the graph / entity-resolution layer rather than building it organically. Nuix — a processing-first vendor whose engine ingests “over 1000 file types” of unstructured data — signed to acquire Paris-based graph-intelligence specialist Linkurious for up to €20M (signed 3 December 2025, completion April 2026 following French FDI approval), folding link-analysis directly into its platform.411 412 On the architectural flank, Siren markets the federated alternative: its Federate technology “enhances Elasticsearch with complex join operations and powerful data-linking capabilities, allowing seamless data correlation across multiple indices” without centralizing the data.413 Siren assembled its entity-resolution capability through a Senzing partnership (announced 15 October 2024) and a strategic investment from Elastic (announced 2 December 2025), the latter “to advance AI-driven investigations for national security.”414 415

My read. I read this as two routes to the same destination — a complete collect-process-link-decide workflow — chosen by vendors that lead on one layer and lack another. Nuix takes the inorganic route: buy the graph layer outright and bolt it onto a best-in-class processing engine. Siren takes the architectural route: federate over data where it lives and partner in entity resolution, betting specifically on the classification- and sovereignty-constrained government buyer.
