For that buyer, bulk-copying mixed-classification data into one vendor’s lake is itself a security and policy problem, not merely a cost question. Both are competing against Palantir’s built ontology and i2’s organic incumbency by assembling the missing layer rather than out-engineering the whole stack. The capital signal of 2025–2026 confirms the pattern: the fusion front’s money is going into consolidation at the analytics layer — Nuix folding in Linkurious, Siren taking a strategic check from Elastic — not into greenfield standalone bets, which are scarce.

Conditional prediction. Two triggers would confirm the thesis: a second comparable acquisition of a graph / link-analysis or entity-resolution specialist by a fusion-adjacent vendor in H2 2026, or a named government agency publicly adopting a federated-fusion architecture for a mission previously run on a central-lake platform — explicitly citing data-residency / no-bulk-copy as the selection rationale. Either one confirms layer-consolidation as the front’s defining consolidation mode and graduates the federated wedge from positioning into a procurement-grade discriminator. The inverse holds if the acquired graph capabilities show up only as bolt-on features without named government reference wins, and federated deployments stay confined to data-residency-constrained niches without a named central-lake displacement. On that path the build (Palantir) and incumbency (i2) routes are out-competing the assemble-the-layer route, and consolidation is a financing story rather than a competitive realignment.

Sources. 411 412 413 414 415

Author’s read of public material, June 2026. Conceptual, not data-derived. Not investment advice.

Pattern Claim 3 — The Incumbent-Standard Stress Test

Observation. The front’s central tension is whether the AI-native operationalization platforms displace the decades-old link-analysis standard, or whether the incumbent standard modernizes and retains its base. The public scorecard is mixed, with both the disruptor and the incumbent growing double digits. On the disruptor side, Palantir positions AIP as the layer that lets organizations “embed large language models (LLMs) and AI agents directly into the systems your teams use every day,”416 and Nuix Neo’s ACV surged 148% year-over-year in its first half of FY2026 as the platform reached roughly 20% of total ACV.417 On the incumbent side, i2 Group — whose installed base spans “more than 140 countries,” including most members of NATO — disclosed “a 40% year-on-year increase in bookings and continued double-digit organic growth across all business segments” (7 October 2025).418 It brought “i2 Insights for assisted data importing and analysis” to market as its AI-enabled modernization layer over the established graph.419 i2 sits inside Constellation Software via N. Harris Computer (acquired from IBM in 2022), which does not break out the i2 line, so its segment financials are recorded as undisclosed.420

My read. I read this as displacement-at-the-margin, not wholesale replacement — yet — and that hedge is the finding, not a failure to commit. Both halves of the contest are posting double-digit growth from public disclosures: Palantir/Nuix on the AI-native operationalization story, i2 on incumbency plus an AI-enabled modernization of the same graph core it has shipped for decades. The legacy moat here is real and quantifiable. A NATO-wide installed base trained on one methodology is a switching cost no homepage repositioning erases in a quarter, which is why I score this MIXED rather than calling a winner. The genuine question is not who markets AI on the graph (they all do) but whether the AI-native platforms can produce named government deployments that explicitly replace a legacy link-analysis system, as opposed to winning greenfield missions alongside the incumbent’s retained base.

Conditional prediction. If through H2 2026 i2’s public bookings growth decelerates while Palantir or Nuix publish named government reference wins that explicitly replace a legacy link-analysis deployment, the displacement thesis hardens and the incumbent standard is being eroded at the core, not just the margin. If i2 keeps posting double-digit bookings growth and publishes its own AI-native modernization with named retention wins — or the parent begins disclosing the line as a growth segment — then the “incumbent standard modernizes and holds” read wins, and the AI-native platforms are taking the greenfield while the installed base stays put.

Sources. 416 417 418 419 420

Author’s read of public material, June 2026. Conceptual, not data-derived. Not investment advice.

Winners, Watch, Losers

Winners.

  • Palantir. The scale and momentum outlier of the front, on filing-grade evidence: $858M of Government-segment revenue in the quarter ended 31 March 2026, up 76% year-over-year.405 The momentum is reinforced by the Maven program-of-record designation (March 2026)404 and a U.S. Army TITAN multi-sensor data-fusion award reported at roughly $178M.421 The Winners label is opinion-labeled and scoped to the public momentum and accreditation position, not to the resolution of the build-vs-buy contest that the Palantir-gravity conditional flags as the open test.

  • Nuix. Returned to statutory profit and growing the modern layer fast: revenue of A$121.2M in the half to 31 December 2025 (+15% YoY), statutory net profit of A$11.1M, and a Nuix Neo ACV up 148% YoY. That growth is paired with an accretive, named acquisition (Linkurious) that buys the graph layer it lacked.417 411 I read Nuix as winning the “assemble the complete stack inorganically” position, with its ASX-disclosed financials a rare fusion-front transparency that lets the label rest on numbers rather than positioning.

Watch.

  • Cognyte. Graded public-only: its NEXYTE platform markets “data fusion and advanced analytics” with “agentic AI-based decision flows” to bring-your-own-source buyers.422 Its FY2026 results (year ended 31 January 2026) show revenue of $400.0M (+14.1%) and a return to GAAP operating income of $13.3M from a prior-year operating loss.423 424 On 3 June 2026 Cognyte reported Q1 FYE27 revenue of $105.5M (+10.4%) with adjusted EBITDA of $13.6M (+31.5%), and reaffirmed FY2027 revenue guidance of roughly $448M (±3%).425 On public evidence Cognyte has cleanly turned to GAAP profitability and is guiding to growth, which is a constructive public posture. It is placed on Watch rather than labeled a winner because the author served as VP Product at Cognyte. The public-only discipline of this report keeps the assessment to what filings and product pages disclose, no further. Watch signal: a named government reference win for NEXYTE-as-fusion-platform, or the next disclosed quarter (Q2 FYE27) testing the reaffirmed FY2027 growth guide.

  • DataWalk. The public product record now supports a full Attention-tier grade: a unified graph-and-AI investigative platform centered on entity resolution, knowledge graphs, link analysis, and government/intelligence workflows.426 The 2025 issuer record gives the tier a measurable base — consolidated sales revenue of PLN 37.783M (+53%) and PLN 57.740M in cash plus deposits over three months at year-end — while also showing a loss-making scale that remains far below Gravity.427 Watch signal: a named government production reference that identifies DataWalk as the investigative-fusion layer, paired with the next issuer report testing whether revenue growth converts into operating leverage.

  • Siren. The federated-architecture bet, the Challenger precisely because it contests the central-data-lake assumption the Gravity tier is built on. Its 2025–2026 momentum is partnership-led (Senzing for entity resolution, Elastic for capital and US public-sector OEM distribution, Carahsoft for federal availability).414 415 It rests on a privately held base whose funding is recorded as undisclosed for the 2025 round.428 Watch signal: a named government agency adopting federated fusion for a mission previously run on a central-lake platform — the threshold that would graduate the architecture from specialist to contender — or, conversely, federated deployments staying confined to data-residency niches.

Losers.

No graded Fusion contender earns a Losers label in this section. A vendor reaches this line only when a cited public event anchors a vendor-specific decline, per the casualty-evidence discipline: a layoff specific to the fusion business, a missed quarter, a down-round, a named executive departure framed as distress, or a customer-churn disclosure. The public events on this front are momentum and consolidation, not failure. Palantir, Nuix, Cognyte, and DataWalk are growing on disclosed revenue; i2’s parent publicly frames it as a growth unit; Siren took a strategic investment rather than a distress raise. DataWalk’s operating loss is carried as a Watch signal, not converted into an uncited casualty label.427 One market-structure datapoint sits near this line but does not earn a label: BAE Systems divested its fusion-relevant analytics asset, NetReveal, to SymphonyAI (announced 12 July 2022, closed 31 October 2022).429 That is a portfolio exit from standalone government fusion software, which is why BAE is referenced as market structure and not graded as a contender, not a casualty event. Quarterly refreshes will populate this line if a fusion-specific distress signal emerges on the public record.

4.7 The Campaign Ahead

Five watchlist items for H2 2026. Each names a public, observable threshold that would trigger re-assessment of a claim above.

  1. A second program-of-record designation, or a forced “Prometheus” recompete. Signal to monitor: an allied government designating a Palantir fusion platform as a standing program of record (not a pilot), or the GAO/court outcome of the Palantir–DIA “Prometheus” sole-source custom-build protest. Threshold for re-assessment: a second program-of-record designation, or DIA’s custom-build path forced back into a commercial recompete → Pattern Claim 1’s gravity thesis hardens. Inverse threshold: a named agency dual-sourcing fusion against Palantir on the same mission, or GAO/courts sustaining DIA’s sole-source custom build with the pattern repeating elsewhere → the in-house-build ceiling is reasserting. Primary source: DoD/CDAO and Army procurement records, GAO decision postings, named-outlet defense coverage (DefenseScoop, Washington Technology).

  2. A second graph / entity-resolution acquisition by a fusion-adjacent vendor. Signal: M&A announcements naming a fusion or fusion-adjacent acquirer of a graph, link-analysis, or entity-resolution specialist, following the Nuix–Linkurious template. Threshold: one such deal announced in H2 2026 → Pattern Claim 2’s layer-consolidation thesis is confirmed as the front’s consolidation mode. Inverse: acquired graph capabilities surfacing only as un-referenced bolt-on features → the buy-the-layer route is being out-competed by build and incumbency. Primary source: vendor press releases, ASX/SEC filings, named-outlet M&A coverage.

  3. A named federated-fusion displacement win. Signal: a named government agency publicly adopting a federated architecture (Siren-class) for a mission previously run on a central-data-lake platform, explicitly citing data-residency or no-bulk-copy as the selection rationale. Threshold: one such named win in H2 2026 → the federation wedge graduates from positioning into a procurement-grade discriminator (Pattern Claim 2’s first branch). Inverse: federated deployments staying confined to data-residency-constrained niches with no named central-lake displacement → federation remains a specialist architecture. Primary source: agency procurement notices, vendor reference-win press, Carahsoft/Elastic public-sector coverage.

  4. The legacy-standard scorecard — i2 bookings versus a named displacement. Signal: i2’s next public bookings/growth disclosure set against any named government reference win in which an AI-native platform explicitly replaces a legacy link-analysis deployment. Threshold: i2 bookings growth decelerating while Palantir or Nuix publish a named legacy-replacement win → Pattern Claim 3’s displacement branch hardens. Inverse: i2 sustaining double-digit bookings growth, publishing AI-native modernization with named retention wins, or Constellation beginning to disclose the i2 line as a growth segment → the incumbent-modernizes-and-holds branch wins. Primary source: i2 Group / Constellation Software disclosures, named government reference-win coverage.

  5. An AI-positioning claim converting to a named, accredited government win. Signal: whether the front’s agentic-AI positioning (Palantir AIP, Cognyte NEXYTE “agentic AI-based decision flows,” i2 Insights) converts into a named, dated government reference win or an accreditation explicitly covering the AI product, as distinct from homepage repositioning. Threshold: one vendor publishes such a named reference or AI-product accreditation through H2 2026 → the AI-native claim graduates from positioning to a defensible differentiator. Inverse: “agentic” remaining uniform marketing language across the front with no named-outcome win → the AI-native pillar demotes to a watchlist label rather than a central claim. Primary source: vendor newsrooms (Palantir, Cognyte, i2), FedRAMP/DoD authorization postings, federal procurement records.

Chapter 5 — The Open-Source Intelligence Market

Glossary.

  • OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence) — intelligence produced from publicly accessible, openly-available sources (web, social, public records, breach corpora, geospatial, technical data), collected and exploited without privileged network access, a warrant, or field hardware.430
  • WEBINT (Web Intelligence) — the web-resident subset of OSINT: data collected from the internet (surface, deep, and dark web) and processed toward an investigative objective; in vendor usage, often the umbrella term for an integrated web-collection-plus-exploitation platform.431
  • SOCMINT (Social Media Intelligence) — a subset of OSINT restricted to social-platform data: the collection and analysis of posts, networks, and metadata (timestamps, geolocation) to reveal information about individuals, groups, or trends.432

5.1 The Playing Ground

Open-source intelligence is the discipline of gathering and exploiting information that is already in the open. The sources are the web, social platforms, public records, breach corpora, satellite imagery, and the technical exhaust of the internet itself. The work is turning that raw material into something an analyst can act on. One vendor glossary in this exact market defines OSINT as “the process of gathering, analyzing, and utilizing information from publicly accessible sources.” It enumerates those sources as “social media platforms, websites and blogs, public government data, satellite imagery, public databases, academic publications and gray literature, technical data (WHOIS, DNS, Certificate Transparency), news and media outlets, public forums and online communities, leaked data, geospatial data, publicly available corporate documents, [and the] dark web.”433 The buyer is a national-intelligence or national-security agency, a law-enforcement investigations unit, a defense or military-intelligence cell, a corporate-security or threat-intelligence function, or a financial-crime and due-diligence team.

The defining property of this front — the line that keeps the chapter coherent — is the source being open and web-resident. Access is unprivileged: a vendor or its customer can reach the source without a court order, a carrier tap, or a deployed device. That single property separates OSINT from every other front in this report, and it is worth stating the boundary precisely, because “open-source intelligence” is the front most prone to category sprawl. The word “open” gets stretched to cover anything that touches the internet, and the result is double-counting.

What this front IS. Collection and exploitation of openly-available, web-resident, social, and dark-web data, where the access is unprivileged. The core product is the open-source collection-and-exploitation engine: the scrapers, the dark-web crawlers, the social harvesters, the multilingual entity extraction over web text. The collector is graded here, in Open-Source Intelligence.

What this front is NOT. Three boundaries matter.

First, it is not intercepted content. Three other fronts depend on privileged access to a communications channel: the mass network collection of the National Agencies front, the warrant-scoped lawful interception of the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers front, and the field radio-frequency collection of the Tactical Intelligence front. OSINT touches only what is openly broadcast or published. The bright line is the privilege of access, not the subject matter. A vendor can detect a threat actor’s chatter on a public Telegram channel and stay firmly inside Open-Source Intelligence; intercepting that same actor’s private call requires the machinery of the intercept fronts. Same target, different front, because the access right differs.

Second, it is not the fusion layer that ingests OSINT. An OSINT collector belongs to Open-Source Intelligence; a fusion platform that ingests OSINT belongs to the Fusion / Decision Intelligence front, with an Open-Source Intelligence reference. The test that keeps these apart is whether the collection or the analytics-over-supplied-data is the primary product. A vendor whose primary value is the open-source collection engine is graded here. A vendor whose primary value is multi-source analytics on top of feeds the customer supplies — link analysis, case management, cross-source correlation — is graded in the fusion front and merely referenced here. This is the single most important grading discipline for this front. Every serious OSINT vendor also markets analytics, so the only question that resolves the ambiguity is which half of the product the buyer is actually paying for.

Third, it is not generic cyber threat-intelligence that is not open-source-derived. Malware telemetry, honeypot data, proprietary sensor networks, and vendor-internal sinkhole data are threat intelligence but not OSINT — they are proprietary collection. Where a vendor blends OSINT with proprietary feeds, only the open-source-derived portion is the Open-Source Intelligence capability; the rest is adjacent. The heavy overlap between “OSINT platform” and “cyber threat-intelligence platform” is exactly why this front’s vendor universe overflows. The front’s problem is not finding enough contenders to grade. It is cutting the field down to the ones whose open-source collection is genuinely the product.

Three buyer misconceptions

“OSINT is free — it’s all on Google.” The public-source raw material is free; the differentiated product is everything that sits on top of it. Collection at scale, dark-web access, multilingual coverage, de-duplication and entity-resolution, and a provenance trail are what a buyer actually pays for. Babel Street, for example, markets searching “across thousands of sources… in over 200 languages with citations and data provenance.”434 The citations and the provenance are the product, not the raw posts. There is a real free floor here: community-edition tools and open-source toolkits, and increasingly general-purpose large language models running ad-hoc collection.435 But that floor only compresses the low end of basic open-web collection. It pushes commercial vendors up-stack, toward the capabilities the free tools cannot match.

“OSINT and SOCMINT are the same thing.” Social-media intelligence is a subset of OSINT, restricted to social platforms. OSINT spans the entire open web, public records, technical data, breach corpora, and geospatial sources.431 432 A vendor strong in social collection is not automatically strong in dark-web or breach-data collection; they are different disciplines with different access problems.

“If it’s public, collecting it is legal.” Public visibility does not equal lawful collection. Platform terms-of-service, anti-circumvention rules, and data-protection law all constrain how public data may be gathered — and the constraint has teeth, as the scraping litigation below shows.

The data and collection stack

The front has two strata: a collection-and-source layer, and an exploitation-and-analytics layer that turns raw open data into structured intelligence. Almost all the differentiation lives in which sources a vendor can reach and how well it exploits them.

On the collection side, the source classes line up roughly by how hard they are to reach.

The surface web — indexed news, blogs, corporate sites, forums, public-records portals — is the cheapest and most contested layer. Everyone collects it, and this is where scraping legality bites. Technical data (WHOIS, DNS, Certificate Transparency) sits here too, as a distinct “technical OSINT” discipline.

The deep web — content behind forms, logins, paywalls, or simply not indexed — is reachable without special privilege, but it requires per-source connectors and query automation. Deep-web breadth — the number of gated-but-public databases a vendor has built connectors for — is a quiet moat that is hard to verify from outside. I’d hypothesize that vendors’ “thousands of sources” claims gesture at this connector inventory, though, as the collection-breadth axis below notes, the figure is not independently verifiable.

The dark web — Tor and I2P forums, ransomware leak sites, illicit marketplaces, closed channels — is a specialist discipline requiring persona management, access maintenance, and operational tradecraft. Vendors anchor here explicitly, with Cybersixgill describing automated collection “from dark web forums, marketplaces, and social media platforms,”436 Flashpoint marketing intelligence across “Dark Web, Malware, Vulnerability, OSINT, Financial, Domain, Identity” classes,437 and Fivecast publishing a dedicated dark-web collection methodology.438

The social layer (SOCMINT) — posts, networks, metadata, sentiment — is the most legally exposed modality, for reasons the scraping case below makes plain.

Breach and leaked data — credential dumps and leaked databases circulating in cybercrime channels — is a recognized OSINT source class433 used for identity-resolution and exposure monitoring. It carries the heaviest data-protection and provenance risk of any source here.

Multilingual content — coverage of non-Latin scripts and low-resource languages — is a hard collection-and-exploitation problem that vendors market as a primary discriminator. Babel Street positions on processing “any publicly available input in hundreds of languages.”434 For a national-security buyer whose targets operate in Arabic, Farsi, Russian, Mandarin, and regional dialects, language coverage is not a feature line. It is a gating capability.

On the exploitation side, the analytics that stays inside an Open-Source Intelligence product — as distinct from a standalone fusion platform — runs to a handful of functions. They are collection orchestration and de-duplication, multilingual entity extraction and resolution, identity-graph construction across selectors, anomaly and network analysis over social data, and alerting on standing queries. The 2026 inflection adds large-language-model-assisted summarization and natural-language investigation. The grading test holds: this analytics stays inside Open-Source Intelligence when it operates over the vendor’s own open-source collection, and tips into the fusion front only when it is sold standalone over customer-supplied feeds.

The six axes buyers discriminate on

Six dimensions separate the serious vendors from the rest, and each maps to a real, publicly observable cost-and-capability structure.

  1. Language and translation coverage. The breadth of languages a vendor can collect, translate, and entity-resolve — not merely keyword-match. The public proxy is the vendor’s own stated language count tied to provenance (Babel Street’s “over 200 languages”434). This is the hardest-to-fake axis: keyword translation is cheap, but cross-script entity-resolution at investigative grade is not. I read a vendor’s willingness to publish a specific language count tied to provenance as a stronger signal than a generic “multilingual” claim.

  2. Dark and deep-web depth. Reach into Tor and I2P forums, ransomware leak sites, and gated-but-public databases — plus the tradecraft to maintain access. The public proxy is a published collection methodology and explicit source-class enumeration437 438 versus generic “we monitor the dark web” marketing. This is where the cyber-threat-intel cohort out-differentiates the social-first WEBINT cohort.

  3. Collection breadth. The raw count and diversity of connected sources across surface, deep, social, dark, breach, and records. The public proxy is the “thousands of sources” claim — directionally informative but not independently verifiable, so they read as positioning claims, not facts, unless tied to a published source inventory.

  4. LLM-native versus bolt-on AI — as positioning, not verified architecture. An outside party cannot verify a vendor’s true internal architecture. So this axis must be read as how a vendor markets itself, with a falsifiable test on public proxies. The 2026 market is visibly bifurcating between vendors retrofitting generative AI onto an existing collection stack and vendors positioning AI as the native interface. Babel Street markets “agentic AI” explicitly: “Insights Investigator is agentic AI that gives analysts a single natural language interface to run threat investigations, monitor emerging risks, and surface connections” and “plans and executes multi-step workflows.”439 I read “agentic AI” and “natural language interface” as the current category-defining positioning move in this front — not yet a verified architectural moat. The test runs through the second half of 2026. If the agentic-OSINT entrants publish named government reference wins or independent (not vendor-asserted) time-to-insight benchmarks, the LLM-native claim graduates from positioning to a defensible differentiator. If they do not, it stays a watchlist item rather than a claim the analysis can lean on.

  5. Identity-graph and correlation depth. How deeply a vendor resolves selectors — an email, a phone, a handle, an image — into unified entities, and maps relationships across sources. This is the difference between “here are forty hits for this handle” and “here is the resolved person, their aliases, their network, with provenance on each edge.” The public proxy is published case studies and the presence of cross-source correlation in product descriptions, versus single-source search.

  6. Data provenance and defensibility. Whether collected intelligence carries an auditable chain — source, timestamp, citation — that survives legal and evidentiary scrutiny, and whether the collection method itself is defensible (terms-of-service-compliant, not fake-account scraping). The public proxy is explicit “citations and data provenance” positioning434 and, inversely, litigation exposure. I read provenance and defensibility as having flipped from a compliance checkbox to a competitive axis. A buyer that adopts a vendor whose collection method is legally contestable inherits that vendor’s litigation risk. So defensible collection is now a sales differentiator, not just a hygiene item.

The public barriers

Two structural barriers are most specific to this front, and one — scraping legality — has no analog anywhere else in this report.

Export controls on surveillance technology. Open-source tooling sold for surveillance use sits inside the dual-use export-control net. That net gates who a vendor may sell to across borders. The multilateral baseline is the 42-state Wassenaar Arrangement, which added commercial surveillance technologies to its dual-use control list beginning in 2013. The precise placement matters and is often mis-stated. In the implementing regimes, intrusion-software controls fall under Category 4 (Computers), while IP-network communications surveillance systems fall under Category 5 Part 1 (Telecommunications) — not both under “Category 5,” as the shorthand sometimes has it.440

The U.S. implementation came via a Bureau of Industry and Security interim final rule published on 2021-10-21. It controls two categories. The first is software “specially designed… for the generation, command and control, or delivery of ‘intrusion software’” under ECCN 4D004. The second is “IP network communications surveillance systems or equipment” under ECCN 5A001.j. Both are controlled for national-security and anti-terrorism reasons, and a new License Exception ACE (Authorized Cybersecurity Exports) carves out certain destinations.441

The European Union’s Dual-Use Regulation 2021/821 adds an Article 5 catch-all on cyber-surveillance items. It requires an export authorization where the items “are or may be intended for use in connection with internal repression and/or the commission of serious violations of human rights.” Covered technologies named in the guidance include “telecommunications interception systems, internet surveillance systems, intrusion software and forensic tools.”442 One honest qualifier: a public analysis from SIPRI finds that “use of the new catch-all control has been limited to date”442 — the control exists on paper, but enforcement practice is still maturing.

Pure open-source collection over public data sits at the lighter-touch end of this net relative to intrusion and implant tooling. But the export-control frame supplies the front’s legitimacy boundary, and it is the natural place to seat the surveillance-vendor discussion. One discipline binds throughout. Any certification or clearance claim about a named vendor must cite the certifying body or the vendor’s own public statement, never an analyst assertion — a wrong certification claim on a named company is a credibility and a defamation hit.

Platform terms-of-service and scraping legality. This barrier has no analog in the intercept fronts, because this front collects from third-party platforms whose terms bind the collector. The clearest public case is Meta v. Voyager Labs. Meta sued Voyager in January 2023 in the Northern District of California, alleging that Voyager “created 38,000 Facebook accounts” and used them “to scrape data from more than 600,000 social media users,” including “posts, likes, friend lists, photos, and comments.”443 In May 2024, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin allowed the suit to proceed, rejecting Voyager’s motion to dismiss and finding that Meta’s allegations could support claims that Voyager violated Facebook’s and Instagram’s terms of service.444 The case ultimately settled, with Voyager agreeing “to refrain from scraping Facebook and Instagram and to permanently delete any data collected from Meta.”445

Voyager is in this report’s never-graded set, so this is descriptive market structure only, not a pattern claim about the company. But the structure it reveals is real: a major platform pursued, and a court allowed to proceed, terms-based claims against an OSINT vendor for collecting publicly visible data through fake accounts, and the matter ended in a settlement that barred the collection. I read the case as the public market’s clearest signal that collection method — not just what data is public — is now a structural constraint on this front, and that platform enforcement is a live competitive variable. The test runs through the second half of 2026. If additional platform-versus-vendor enforcement actions surface in the public record as named filings or settlements, the “defensible collection” axis hardens into a table-stakes procurement question. If enforcement stays a one-off, it remains an elevated-risk axis rather than a gate.

Behind the single case sits a genuinely unsettled legal backdrop across jurisdictions — U.S. terms-breach theories, EU lawful-basis and purpose-limitation constraints on reusing personal data, platform anti-circumvention rules. The absence of a settled rule is itself the barrier: each vendor must make a defensibility bet, and that bet is now visible in both its positioning and its litigation exposure.

Clearance and accreditation. For U.S.-federal and allied national-security buyers, the software-side gates that recur across this report apply here too: facility and personnel security clearances, and cloud accreditation (FedRAMP authorization, DoD Impact Levels) for hosted delivery. I did not extract a verbatim accreditation-requirement line from a live OSINT-specific U.S. solicitation in this pass. So the specific magnitude and timeline of the gate is an inference from the regime’s general applicability rather than a quoted fact — a thin spot worth naming as one. The war-chest analysis later in this chapter is better placed to answer it, through the pattern of specialists acquiring cleared U.S. delivery organizations.

One freshness correction for the contenders that follow. As of a 2026-06-14 web check, Cobwebs Technologies operates under PenLink, both held by the private-equity firm Spire Capital, with PenLink’s July 2023 acquisition announcement recording undisclosed terms. Estimate: approximately USD 200M, as reported by CTech. PenLink is integrating Cobwebs’ web-intelligence capability into its digital-investigation platform for “law enforcement, public safety, and national security customers.”446 Babel Street does not own PenLink or Cobwebs — those sit under Spire Capital, and Babel Street is a separate vendor.446 Named-outlet and co-investor reporting identify Babel Street as Veritas-backed at the time of its January 2024 Vertical Knowledge acquisition. The live Veritas portfolio page does not list Babel Street as of 2026-08-22, so current ownership is left unresolved and no reason is inferred from the non-listing.447

5.2 The Terrain

Market size: three estimates, side by side, never averaged

There is no single number for the size of the OSINT market, and the honest way to present the sizing is to put the public estimates next to each other and let the spread speak. Three named research publishers size the broad OSINT market, and their definitions diverge widely enough that the disagreement is the finding, not a measurement error to be smoothed away.

Publisher Definition used Figure (as stated) CAGR / period
Mordor Intelligence software platforms, data feeds, and managed services that gather, enrich, and analyze information in publicly available domains (excludes classified intel, standalone threat-hunting, hardware-only sensors) USD 18.20B (2025) → USD 21.06B (2026) → USD 43.49B (2031)448 15.62% (2026–2031)
The Business Research Company OSINT revenues from “human intelligence and dark web analysis”; factory-gate values USD 18.07B (2025) → USD 22.95B (2026) → USD 60.02B (2030)449 27.2% (to 2030)
GlobalData / Global Market Insights OSINT “gathered from publicly available sources” across government and commercial sectors USD 12.7B (2025) → USD 15.9B (2026) → USD 133.6B (2035)450 26.7% (2026–2035)

The three publishers bracket the 2025 OSINT market at roughly USD 12.7B–18.2B, and the 2026 market at roughly USD 15.9B–22.95B. The growth rates split into two camps: Mordor’s mid-teens against the two high-twenties figures. I read this as a genuinely unsettled category boundary rather than a counting error. Mordor’s definition explicitly excludes standalone threat-hunting and hardware sensors. That is why its base and growth rate sit below the wider-scoped figures that fold dark-web analysis and broader cyber-intelligence into “OSINT.” If a fourth named publisher with a disclosed methodology lands inside USD 13–19B for 2025, the bracket holds; a figure outside it would mean the definitional drift is wider than I have assumed.

It is worth marking the overlap boundary with an adjacent, separately-tracked market. Mordor sizes the broader threat intelligence market at USD 9.21B (2025) rising to USD 18.85B (2031) at a 12.7% CAGR, with the strategic-intelligence segment at a 33.60% revenue share.451 Grand View Research separately projects the threat-intelligence platforms market to USD 36.53B by 2030.452 I include these only to fix the seam. Cyber-threat-intel and OSINT share vendors — Recorded Future, Flashpoint, Cybersixgill all appear in both — but are tracked as distinct markets, and double-counting across the two is the principal sizing hazard in this front.

The government slice: a labeled proxy, not a segment size

No clean public dollar figure isolates the government and national-security OSINT software slice. Given the opacity of government intelligence budgets, that is an expected, honest result, not a gap to be filled by invention. What is publicly stated is the government share of the OSINT market by named publishers, which I carry strictly as a proxy — a share-of-market, not a standalone segment size. Mordor puts government intelligence agencies at 38.40% of 2025 OSINT revenue, the single largest end-user segment, with military and defense as a further distinct category.448 Global Market Insights puts national security at 32% of 2025 market value, the dominant application segment, covering “counterterrorism, counter-intelligence, strategic warning and foreign capability assessment.”450

Applying those published shares to the publishers’ own market totals is bracketing arithmetic, and I label it as exactly that, not as a publisher figure. Mordor’s 38.40% government share of its USD 18.20B total implies an order-of-magnitude proxy near USD 7B for the government-intelligence OSINT slice in 2025. GMI’s 32% national-security share of its USD 12.7B total implies near USD 4B. The proxy range — roughly USD 4–7B for 2025 — is arithmetic on published application-share splits, not a methodology-disclosed segment sizing, and no publisher sells the latter. The harder currency for this front is not any market-derivative at all; it is the named, dated procurement evidence below.

Demand drivers

Three forcing functions carry the analytical weight that the market numbers cannot.

The open-data exhaust has outrun manual analysis. The publishers converge on a single root driver: the volume of openly-available data has grown faster than any analyst team can read it. Global Market Insights frames demand around the “rapid increase in publicly available online data” across “blogs, social media sites, news sites, web forums, internet of things (IoT) devices.”450 Multilingual scale is a named buyer requirement rather than a feature. Babel Street states publicly that it analyzes content across “over 200 languages,” finding connections in multilingual data “from social media, the deep web, and public records.”453 (Dataminr’s own filing-grade description cites “trillions of daily computations across billions of public data inputs from over 100,000 unique public data sources.” It spans “global and regional social media platforms, blogs, web forums… the deep and dark web, cyber signals, and public IoT sensors” — a vivid statement of the source span. But it dates to a 2021-03-23 press release, so I carry it as a description of breadth, not as a current metric.454) Dark and deep-web depth is a distinct vector the publishers single out, with The Business Research Company defining part of its OSINT market as “dark web analysis” revenue.449 Every expansion of the open-data exhaust — more platforms, more languages, more dark-web venues — widens the gap between what is publicly knowable and what a human can manually process. That gap is precisely what commercial platforms monetize.

Government buyers are institutionalizing OSINT as a named discipline. The U.S. intelligence community has publicly committed to OSINT as a standing mission rather than an ad-hoc capability. The CIA has publicly released an OSINT strategy that calls for building data-science and AI talent and explicitly enlists large language models in its OSINT mission.455 The buyer set the publishers name is broad and government-weighted — government intelligence agencies, military and defense, federal, state, and local law enforcement, plus financial-services and corporate-security threat-intel teams.448 450 Recorded Future’s own public client claim — “more than 1,900 clients across 75 countries, including the governments of 45 countries” — is a public datapoint on the government density of the buyer base.456

A commercial base sits below the government buyers. The same publishers that put government at 32–38% of revenue also show financial services, cybersecurity providers, and corporate-risk firms as material end-user segments.448 450 I read this as the structurally important feature of this front relative to the classified-collection fronts. OSINT has a large commercial recurring-revenue base — the part that needs no warrant and no clearance — which several specialists use as the platform from which they attack government tenders. If the named OSINT specialists’ public disclosures show government revenue growing materially faster than commercial through 2027, the “commercial base funds the government push” read weakens.

The AI and LLM shift

The clearest 2025–2026 public signal in this front is that the incumbents are re-positioning around generative and agentic AI to compress the analyst workflow. The discipline here is the same one the differentiation axis above demands: this is framed strictly as what vendors publicly claim, because true architecture cannot be verified from outside — “positions itself as,” not “is.”

The capital is explicitly chasing it. Dataminr raised USD 100M from Fortress Investment Group in April 2025 “to accelerate its development of generative and agentic AI products,” following USD 85M (March 2025) from NightDragon and HSBC.457 I flag the “$4.1B valuation” figure that circulates with Dataminr as the 2021 Series F mark, not a current valuation;454 the 2025 raises are convertible or credit, not a fresh primary equity mark.457 Babel Street publicly markets “agentic AI for accelerated insights into global security,” with “multilingual data summarization, pattern identification, and social connection analysis” as its AI workflow claim.458 Palantir positions its AIP — using “generative and agentic AI models, including large language models (LLMs)” inside Gotham and Foundry, deployed to government from 2023 — as the operationalization layer over intelligence data.459 Palantir’s relevance to this front, though, is as the fusion layer that ingests OSINT, not as a pure collector. And Fivecast, the Australian specialist, raised an AUD 30M Series A for an “AI and machine-learning-powered” platform scanning “social media and the dark web.”460

The shared public claim across these vendors is that large-language-model and agentic AI compress the time from raw public-data ingestion to analyst-ready insight. The observable proxies are funding explicitly earmarked for generative or agentic AI (Dataminr’s April-2025 round states this purpose verbatim), public product-page repositioning toward “agentic,” and named government reference wins. If the AI-native entrants cannot be named from public pages with a public capability claim, this trend demotes from a central convergence pillar to a watchlist item. For now, several of them can be named, which is what keeps it a live candidate.

Regulatory and procurement structure

How U.S. federal OSINT is bought. Government OSINT in the United States is bought predominantly through commercial-off-the-shelf software subscriptions on established federal vehicles, not through bespoke sovereign systems. That is the accessible-procurement pattern, and a sharp contrast to the classified-collection fronts. The GSA Schedule, via reseller Carahsoft, is the dominant vehicle: Babel Street’s “AI-powered solutions,” OSINT included, were added to “Carahsoft’s GSA Schedule contract,” making them available to “Federal, State and Local Government agencies.”461 The named, dated award evidence on the public record makes the contestability concrete:

Buyer Vendor Value What it bought
FBI Babel Street up to USD 27M (2022) 5,000 software licenses462
DoD (PADELS) Dataminr USD 24,923,076.93 enterprise OSINT alerting subscription, 36-week + 15-week option463

I read the Babel Street–versus–Dataminr GAO bid protest over the DoD PADELS award463 as the cleanest public signal that this is a recompeted, contestable procurement lane. Vendors litigate the awards on the public record — in contrast to the incumbent-locked sovereign systems elsewhere in this report.

The In-Q-Tel signal. In-Q-Tel, the intelligence community’s non-profit strategic investor, “funded primarily by the Central Intelligence Agency,” is the public signal of which commercial data and AI capabilities the community is steering toward. It has invested in roughly 490 companies over 25 years, with 37 investments in 2025.464 I carry it as a directional procurement-intent signal — where IC capital flows is where IC demand is forming — not as an OSINT-specific dollar figure. Its portfolio spans data and AI infrastructure broadly, and pinning a specific OSINT thesis on it from public sources would over-claim.

Consolidation as a market-structure force. The 2024–2025 deal flow shows OSINT and intelligence assets being absorbed into larger platforms. Mastercard acquired Recorded Future for USD 2.65B from Insight Partners (announced September 2024), framing it as “the world’s largest threat intelligence company.”456 465 Cobwebs Technologies, the Israeli WEBINT vendor, joined PenLink after PenLink announced the acquisition through Spire Capital. Spire Capital owns both companies. Estimate: approximately USD 200M as reported by CTech; transaction terms were undisclosed. This is the deal that defines the current PenLink/Cobwebs entity referenced in this report.466 That single-entity status is confirmed. Named-outlet and co-investor reporting identify Babel Street as Veritas-backed at the time of the January 2024 Vertical Knowledge acquisition; current ownership remains unresolved.447

The scraping and privacy vector — asymmetric, and the front’s defining medium-term risk. OSINT’s raw material is openly-available data, which puts it squarely inside the 2024–2026 tightening of data-broker and scraping law. That is a real force, but an asymmetric one, because national-security and law-enforcement use is frequently carved out.

On the commercial edge, scraping of public personal data is under sustained legal pressure. Clearview AI’s facial-image scraping drew more than EUR 91M in fines across 15 jurisdictions by 2025, including a EUR 20M Italian order and a EUR 30.5M Dutch order. It also drew a roughly USD 51M class-action settlement that received final approval on 2025-03-20. The regulatory backdrop is one in which EU authorities have held that “public availability is not a sufficient lawful basis under GDPR.”467 U.S. enforcement tightened and then partly reversed, with a carve-out running through both moves. The FTC finalized orders in January 2025 against Mobilewalla, Gravy Analytics, and X-Mode/Outlogic barring the sale of sensitive location data — orders that exempt national-security and law-enforcement purposes.468 Meanwhile the CFPB’s broader data-broker rule, which would have classed some brokers as FCRA consumer-reporting agencies, was withdrawn on 2025-05-15.469

I read the net regulatory vector as ambiguous-but-tightening on the commercial edge and carved-out on the government edge. Consumer-facing data-broker selling is constrained, while law-enforcement and national-security access is repeatedly exempted, and the most sweeping U.S. broker rule was withdrawn. If a major OSINT or WEBINT vendor loses a government contract or faces a regulator order specifically tied to public-data scraping during 2026–2027, the “government edge is carved out” read weakens. The carve-outs are publicly contested. Citizen Lab’s analysis of PenLink’s ad-based geolocation and Amnesty International’s reporting on Palantir and Babel Street surveillance concerns are the named-outlet evidence of that468, and I surface those only as descriptive public market-force commentary, not as a pattern claim. This legal vector is, to my read, the most likely source of a 2026–2027 discontinuity in this front.

5.3 The Contenders

Open-source intelligence is the front where the candidate list overflows the cap rather than struggling to fill it. The structural map surfaces sixteen-plus public OSINT/WEBINT vendors with quotable self-positioning, so the discipline here is cutting. The job is to choose the eight that define the front’s center of gravity, shape its 2026 demand, and carry the architecture-disruption story — not to backfill thin rows. Eight vendors are graded across three tiers: 3 Gravity (the structural anchors a buyer cannot map the front without naming), 4 Attention (the vendors shaping demand, M&A, and the AI-native narrative), and 1 Challenger (the funded specialist whose trajectory is the interesting bet). The remaining candidates are placed deliberately — as cross-references, as Plays, or cut — and the cut line is documented at the end of this section so the selection can be defended.

Author’s read of public material, June 2026. Vendor positions are conceptual, not data-derived. Tier color-coding: Gravity (burnt orange), Attention (amber), Challenger (pale amber). Not investment advice.

Gravity tier

Recorded Future

“Threat Intelligence cuts through the noise with a clear and comprehensive view of the threats that matter to your organization.” — Recorded Future, Threat Intelligence product page, accessed 2026-06-14 470

Recorded Future is the category’s structural anchor, publicly described as “the world’s largest threat intelligence company, with more than 1,900 clients across 75 countries, including the governments of 45 countries and over 50% of the Fortune 100.”471 Its stated USP is breadth of collection: indexing surface web, dark web, and technical feeds into a single Intelligence Graph that produces risk scores, with customers citing “the huge amount of sources from which they are gathering intelligence.”470 Target buyer is the threat-intelligence team, threat analyst, and SOC team across enterprise and government. Pricing signal: named-outlet aggregation puts entry pricing for small organizations at “$50,000–$100,000 annually,”472 a rare public anchor in a front where most pricing is dark. Architecturally — and this is positioning, not a verified internal read — it presents as a graph-native data platform with bolt-on generative-AI assistance, marketing AI as an analyst accelerant layered on the Intelligence Graph rather than an LLM-native core. Sourcing here is rich: vendor-controlled self-positioning plus heavy named-outlet coverage.

The single most consequential ownership fact in the front sits here: Mastercard acquired Recorded Future for $2.65B, announced 12 September 2024 and closed 20 December 2024. The category’s largest pure-play is now a payments-giant subsidiary inside Mastercard’s cyber and identity portfolio.473 I read this as the central tension of the Gravity tier. The structural anchor is no longer independent, which is both a distribution windfall (Mastercard’s reach) and an open question about how a government-sector franchise fares inside a commercial payments parent.

Dataminr

“AI-Powered Real-Time Event, Threat & Risk Intelligence … Dataminr’s AI platform delivers the earliest warnings on high impact events.” — Dataminr homepage, accessed 2026-06-14 474

Dataminr is the speed archetype of the front. It positions as “The Leading AI Platform for Real-Time Event, Threat & Risk Intelligence,”474 and its defining claim is earliest signal, first-alert latency rather than depth of after-the-fact analysis. The stated differentiation is real-time scale across “1M public data sources,” built on “50+ proprietary LLMs.” That stack adds multi-modal fusion, generative, and agentic AI.474 Target buyer spans corporate security, the public sector (“100+ U.S. government agencies, 20+ international governments”), and newsrooms (“1,500+ newsrooms”).474 On architecture, Dataminr markets itself among the most AI-native vendors in the front. The multi-modal-fusion / generative / agentic stack is presented as the product’s core, not a bolt-on, and in March 2026 it launched “Dataminr for Cyber Defense,” a suite “built with agentic and predictive AI at its core.”475 That this is positioning rather than externally verifiable architecture is the standing caveat across the whole front. Ownership: private; the 2026 story is the cyber-defense expansion, which I read as Dataminr extending from real-time alerting toward the fusion/analytics layer — a move up the stack toward where Recorded Future and the Fusion / Decision Intelligence platforms already sit.

Babel Street

“Babel Street Data Dominance™ helps you turn chaotic and multilingual digital exhaust into verified, contextual intelligence — at scale.” — Babel Street homepage, accessed 2026-06-14 476

Babel Street is the multilingual-and-licensed-data anchor of the Gravity tier. Its 2026 framing leads with “Agentic Risk Intelligence” and “Governed AI agents on rights-cleared, mission-grade data to produce decision-ready intelligence in minutes, not days,” under the buyer line “Trusted by those who can’t afford to be wrong.”476 The stated USP pairs multilingual breadth (a “200+ languages” lineage) with a “rights-cleared, mission-grade data” governance pitch — positioning data-licensing and provenance as the differentiator against scrape-only rivals. Target buyer is national defense, law enforcement, global enterprise, and FinTech. Architecturally it markets a 2026 repositioning toward “governed AI agents” over a proprietary licensed-data foundation (positioning, not verified). Ownership and freshness: private. Named-outlet and co-investor reporting identify Babel Street as Veritas-backed at the time of the January 2024 Vertical Knowledge acquisition. The live Veritas portfolio page does not list Babel Street as of 2026-08-22, so current ownership remains unresolved and no reason is inferred from the non-listing.447

The 2025–26 surface is an aggressive build-and-hire cycle. John Larson (ex-Booz Allen) appointed President and Chief AI Officer in December 2025, alongside Maura Burns, former CIA COO, joining the Board of Advisors in November 2025 and a new CRO — a leadership stack I read as signalling a deeper federal-and-AI push.477 (The IP M&A that built the analytics base spans the Dunami link-analysis IP assets that Babel Street announced it had acquired on 8 June 2020, Rosette announced 28 November 2022 and recorded closed 31 December 2022, and Vertical Knowledge announced and recorded closed 22 January 2024. That is a sustained multi-year build-and-buy programme, not a single 2020 event, and is named here to place the lineage rather than as 2026 momentum.478)

Attention tier

Flashpoint

“The Best Data for The Best Intelligence … Stay ahead with intelligence sourced from where threats begin, guided by experts and AI.” — Flashpoint homepage, accessed 2026-06-14 479

Flashpoint is the primary-source-depth contender — its third pillar is “Industry’s Deepest Primary Source Intelligence … Access data from real adversary spaces that others can’t reach.”479 Where Recorded Future and Dataminr lead on open-web breadth, Flashpoint leads on direct access to closed adversary spaces (illicit forums, marketplaces), with human-analyst enrichment as an explicit pillar (“Enriched by Expert Analyst Insight”).479 Target buyer spans CTI/SOC, fraud, corporate and physical security, vulnerability management, national security, and insider-threat teams, with named clients including the US DoD and Microsoft.479 On architecture it positions human-plus-AI. In 2025 it added “AI Summarization … for Search and Investigations within Flashpoint Ignite,”480 framing AI as an analyst force-multiplier over a primary-source data lake (the Echosec acquisition supplied its social/OSINT collection layer). Ownership: private; the 2026 surface is the Ignite platform plus AI summarization and the annual Global Threat Intelligence Report as a demand-gen anchor.481 My read: Flashpoint’s wedge is depth-over-breadth, and the durable question is whether primary-source access stays defensible as the generalists’ AI layers get better at synthesizing the open web.

Cognyte (LUMINAR / external threat intelligence)

Disclosure: the author, Yohay Etsion, served as VP Product at Cognyte. This is independent ProductBeacon research based solely on publicly available material; it reflects the author’s personal analysis, not Cognyte’s position, and is not investment advice.

“Cognyte is a global leader in investigative analytics software that empowers a variety of government and other organizations with Actionable Intelligence for a Safer World™.” — Cognyte corporate homepage, accessed 2026-06-14 482

Cognyte is graded in this front strictly on its publicly-marketed external/web intelligence product, LUMINAR, plus its corporate positioning — sourced entirely to dated public pages, with no internal knowledge. LUMINAR is positioned as an “AI-powered external threat intelligence solution that empowers security and risk management leaders with comprehensive visibility into their threat landscape,” spanning “brand protection, fraud monitoring, executive protection and deep/dark web monitoring.”483 The publicly-readable USP is the web and deep/dark-web collection layer, marketed alongside the NEXYTE decision-intelligence platform — breadth-of-source into a single investigative workspace rather than a standalone OSINT-collector pitch. (Cognyte’s public pages present LUMINAR and NEXYTE as a pairing; I do not assert a verified data pipeline between them from public material.) Target buyer, per the public pages, is “national SOCs, as well as the critical infrastructure, telecom, financial services, transportation and healthcare sectors,”483 within a government, law enforcement, and national-security base of “hundreds of customers in approximately 100 countries.”482

Architecturally, NEXYTE markets “domain-specific, pre-trained AI models,” “co-pilots,” and “agentic decision flows.”484 That is a positioning move toward AI-native decision intelligence. Whether the underlying architecture is LLM-native or bolt-on cannot be verified from outside, so this is read as positioning only. A scope note matters here. Cognyte’s broader WEBINT family beyond LUMINAR is not forced into a grade here, because no clean public quotable pillar for it exists; its portfolio breadth across the five fronts is carried by the Convergence chapter rather than manufactured into a grade in this section. My read: the public LUMINAR + NEXYTE framing places Cognyte squarely on the boundary between Open-Source Intelligence and Fusion, where LUMINAR is an external-collection product marketed next to a decision-intelligence platform, which is exactly the collector-or-fusion ambiguity this front turns on.

Maltego

“OSINT & Cyber Investigations Platform for High-Stakes Cases … From data to intelligence - in minutes.” — Maltego homepage, accessed 2026-06-14 485

Maltego is the analyst-workbench archetype — graded not as a data feed but as the link-analysis surface other data providers plug into. It positions “the all-in-one investigation platform that accelerates complex cyber investigations from hours to minutes.”485 Its stated USP is graph-first link analysis: “the most widely used graph analysis platform for OSINT in the world,”486 drawing “relationships between people, domains, infrastructure, social networks and leaks from open sources and commercial APIs, all on a single interactive graph.”486 The connector/transform ecosystem is the moat — Maltego is the de facto standard analyst workbench that third-party data providers (including Social Links) integrate into. Target buyer, per its own page, is “Government organizations (2K+)” and “Private companies (4K+)” across law enforcement, defense and national security, CTI, banking, and insurance.485 Architecture: graph-native, connector-driven, usage-based, adding “AI-powered sentiment analysis”485 as a bolt-on rather than an LLM-native rebuild. Ownership: Maltego Technologies GmbH (Munich); the 2026 positioning is incremental AI features on the graph workbench. The reason it earns a grade is architectural distinctness — it is the investigator-workbench / link-analysis archetype sitting at the boundary between Open-Source Intelligence and Fusion, structurally different from the data-feed archetype of the Gravity three.

Fivecast

“Fivecast delivers an open-source intelligence platform that cuts through complex digital noise to surface the signals that matter.” — Fivecast homepage, accessed 2026-06-14 487

Fivecast is the clearest mission-built-for-government OSINT collector in the cut. Its pillars run under the brand line “ENGINEERED FOR INTELLIGENCE”487: “transforms digital noise into clarity, data into insight, and insight into decisive action” and “AI-powered technology that enables intelligence teams to uncover critical insights from masses of online data - before risk becomes reality.” They frame a platform “born from collaboration between governments and research institutions,” with “deep, targeted, and continuous data collection in near-real time.”487 That is its stated USP. It is purpose-built for the national-security, defense, and law-enforcement mission, distinct from the cyber-CTI lean of Recorded Future and Flashpoint. Target buyer, per its page, is “Government agencies (40+),” “Law enforcement (30+ police departments),” plus national security, defense intelligence, financial crime, and border security.487 Architecturally it markets AI-powered collection-and-analysis as the core and positions on continuous “living intelligence” collection. Ownership: private, Australia-headquartered with a global footprint. The 2026 momentum is partnership-led — the Tranquility AI partnership announced in March 2026 (covered in the Plays section) — alongside a heavy government-event presence at the OSINT Tech Expo and SOF Week 2026.488489 My read: Fivecast is the test case for whether a government-mission specialist can reach a full collect-to-evidence workflow through partnership stacks rather than M&A.

Challenger tier

Strider Technologies

“The Frontier of Strategic Intelligence … One Platform, Powered by Agentic Intelligence.” — Strider Technologies homepage, accessed 2026-06-14 490

Strider is the Challenger because it reframes what OSINT is for. The rest of the front serves cyber-threat and LEA-investigation centers; Strider instead markets a vertical the generalists don’t own — nation-state and economic-espionage risk derived from public data. Its pillars promise to “make faster, more confident decisions with unparalleled insights into state-sponsored threats” and to “continuously discover, connect, and analyze global data to illuminate nation-state risk.”490 Its stated USP is a “Zero-touch architecture requiring no internal client data” with a claimed reach across “90K+ Hard-to-access sources,”490 repositioning OSINT toward strategic counterintelligence — supply-chain, talent, IP, and PRC/Russia/Iran linkage. Target buyer, per its page, is “Fortune 100 companies and world leaders,” critical infrastructure, financial services, high-tech/AI, academia, and government.490 Architecturally it markets an “agentic intelligence” platform and positions as AI-native, though, as with every contender in this front, true architecture is unverifiable from outside. Ownership and freshness: private; it raised a $55M Series C led by Pelion in September 2024, reaching roughly $117M total.491 Consistent with the Challenger discipline, the read stays descriptive and hedged. The interesting bet is whether “strategic intelligence” hardens into a category that pulls net-new budget away from the cyber-CTI incumbents, or stays a well-funded vertical — a question the wedge Play in the next section tracks against public proxies rather than asserts.

The cut line — why nine more public candidates are not graded here

The front’s overflow forces a defensible cut. Each vendor below is real and publicly sourced; the cap simply requires a choice, and each is placed where it fits best — closer to a neighbouring front, duplicative of a graded archetype, or better carried as a Play.

  • Cybersixgill — a strong dark-web CTI specialist (its public material cites collection of “7 million intelligence items from over 1,000 underground forums … daily”492). Cut because its positioning overlaps Flashpoint’s primary-source-depth pillar without a distinct wedge in this front, and carried as a Flashpoint cross-reference and War Chest color.

  • ZeroFox — external cybersecurity / digital-risk protection. Cut because it skews DRP/brand-protection (nearer a cyber-security front than government OSINT) and its 2026 story is an ownership event, not a positioning one (taken private by Haveli for $350M in May 2024493), making it a War Chests / consolidation data point.

  • PenLink (Tangles / WebLoc, ex-Cobwebs) — a major LEA web-intelligence and location product. Cut from the graded set because its center of gravity is law-enforcement investigative tooling at the boundary between Open-Source Intelligence and the Monitoring Centers, and it is litigation-sensitive on location-data sourcing — carried as a consolidation Play and a Monitoring-Centers-adjacent cross-reference.

  • Primer — defense/IC NLP-on-OSINT; cut because it positions as an AI analysis layer over unstructured data (adjacent to Fusion / Decision Intelligence) more than as an OSINT collector — placed as Convergence AI-native color and a Fusion / Decision Intelligence reference.

  • Social Links — markets “industry-leading OSINT solutions” with “law enforcement agencies from 80+ countries.”494 Cut because much of its reach is as a data provider inside Maltego — the graded Maltego entry absorbs the archetype, and Social Links is named as ecosystem color.

  • ShadowDragon — an LEA / financial-crime OSINT toolset; cut because it duplicates the Maltego / Social Links investigator-tooling archetype at smaller scale — named-reference only.

  • Skopenow — an end-to-end OSINT platform with a sanctions / restricted-parties workflow lean; cut as sub-scale against the graded eight and overlapping the investigator-platform archetype — named as reference and as Play color on the compliance-OSINT trend.

  • HENSOLDT Analytics (formerly SAIL LABS Technology) — a real OSINT business inside a diversified defense-sensor parent. HENSOLDT’s public record says it acquired SAIL LABS in 2021 as a provider of AI-based OSINT, processing public text, image, video, and audio sources across 30 languages.495 It is therefore placed on this front’s cut line, not Fusion’s. The parent is referenced at the disclosed business-line or segment level only; no total-parent economics are used to imply the size of HENSOLDT Analytics.

A note on what is deliberately not graded: Voyager Labs is adjacent to this front but sits in the locked never-graded set and appears only as descriptive market-force commentary in the Plays section — no grade, no pattern claim, no distress label. The same discipline governs any NSO/Candiru/Intellexa/Ability-class mention: never graded here, descriptive only, and any negative anchored to a named outlet or dropped.

5.4 Their Plays

Five strategic moves are in motion across the OSINT / WEBINT front in 2026. Each is anchored to a dated public event, names its participants, and carries a falsifiable read grounded on a publicly observable proxy — an acquisition close, an earnings or funding disclosure, a public procurement record, or a named product-line launch. Two of the five are consolidation plays, one is a front-wide positioning convergence, and two are growth bets on new buying centers. The surveillance-vendor cohort appears in this section only as descriptive market-force commentary; it is never graded.

Play 1: The Category Leader Is Absorbed Into a Payments Network

  • Observation. Mastercard agreed to acquire Recorded Future for $2.65B, with Insight Partners as the selling owner 496497. The deal release described Recorded Future as a company serving “the governments of 45 countries and over 50% of the Fortune 100” 498, and the transaction was announced 12 September 2024 and finalized 20 December 2024. This is the largest single ownership event on the front: the OSINT/threat-intelligence category’s biggest pure-play is now a subsidiary of a payments network, folded toward identity, fraud, and real-time decisioning.

  • Participants. Mastercard (NYSE: MA), Recorded Future, Insight Partners (seller).

  • My read. I read this as the leading edge of OSINT being absorbed into adjacent platform companies rather than persisting as a standalone software category. Threat intelligence has become strategic enough that a non-defense platform buys the category leader outright — and the buyer’s logic is data adjacency (fraud, identity, transaction risk), not the government-intelligence mission that built Recorded Future’s roster.

  • Falsifiable read. If H2 2026 brings a second large OSINT or cyber-threat-intelligence pure-play acquired by a non-defense platform — payments, cloud, or identity — the absorption thesis strengthens into a pattern. The read flips if instead Recorded Future’s named public-sector references visibly contract after the close, with government customers dropping from its published roster: the integration is straining the government franchise rather than extending it.

  • Evidence. Mastercard acquisition release, 12 Sep 2024 498; Mastercard close announcement, 20 Dec 2024 497.

Play 2: “Agentic AI” Repositioning Sweeps the Entire Front

  • Observation. Across the graded set, vendors are simultaneously reframing from “search and alert” to “agents that act.” Dataminr launched “Dataminr for Cyber Defense,” a suite it describes as “built with agentic and predictive AI at its core,” in March 2026 499. Babel Street’s 2026 homepage leads with “Agentic Risk Intelligence” and “Governed AI agents on rights-cleared, mission-grade data” 500. Strider markets “One Platform, Powered by Agentic Intelligence” 501. Cognyte’s NEXYTE platform page cites “agentic decision flows” 502. Maltego and Flashpoint, by contrast, add AI as bolt-on summarization rather than rearchitecting around it 503504.

  • Participants. Dataminr, Babel Street, Strider, Cognyte leading the reframe; Maltego and Flashpoint adding AI as an analyst force-multiplier.

  • My read. I read this as a positioning convergence, not yet a verified capability gap. Every contender is racing to attach the “agentic” label to its homepage. But whether the underlying architecture is genuinely LLM-native or a generative-AI layer over an existing graph or data foundation cannot be verified from outside. The claims are marketing surface, and treating them as architecture would be an error. This is the falsifiable form of the report’s cross-front “AI-native disruption” pillar: name the public claimants, frame each as “positions itself as,” and let a public proof point decide it.

  • Falsifiable read. The test through H2 2026 is whether any of these vendors publishes a named-reference customer attributing a decision or operational outcome to autonomous agentic action — as distinct from analyst-assisted workflow. If that proof point lands for one vendor and not the others, the AI-native claims begin to separate into a real differentiator. If “agentic” remains category-wide marketing language with no named-outcome reference behind it, it is a label the whole front shares, not a moat any single vendor holds — and the pillar demotes to a watchlist item.

  • Evidence. Dataminr “Cyber Defense” launch, Mar 2026 499; Babel Street homepage 500; Strider homepage 501; Cognyte NEXYTE page 502.

Play 3: Private Equity Rolls Up the LEA Web-Intelligence Suite

  • Observation. Private equity is assembling law-enforcement-facing investigative-OSINT suites out of fragmented point products. PenLink announced the Cobwebs acquisition in July 2023; Estimate: approximately USD 200M as reported by CTech, with transaction terms undisclosed, both held under Spire Capital 505506. PenLink’s Tangles product was subsequently signed by the Texas Department of Public Safety on a five-year contract worth approximately $5.3M in June 2025 507. In parallel, ZeroFox was taken private by Haveli Investments at an enterprise value near $350M, a deal that closed 13 May 2024 508.

  • Participants. Spire Capital, Haveli Investments, the rolled-up vendors (PenLink/Cobwebs, ZeroFox), and US state and federal law-enforcement buyers.

  • My read. I read this as PE betting on two things. First, that fragmented LEA-OSINT tooling consolidates into platform suites, combining web-intelligence collection with location and forensic analysis under one owner. Second, that public procurement keeps funding the category even as privacy scrutiny intensifies around location-data sourcing. The Texas DPS contract is the public proof that the demand curve is still live despite that scrutiny.

  • Falsifiable read. If H2 2026 brings another PE-backed acquisition combining a web-intelligence collector with a location or forensics product, the roll-up thesis holds. The thesis faces a public-policy headwind if instead new state-level procurement restrictions on location-data tools appear in the public record, following the documented Texas/PenLink scrutiny — a headwind the roll-up’s economics did not price in.

  • Evidence. PenLink/Cobwebs acquisition, 2023 505506; Texas DPS Tangles contract, Jun 2025 507; Haveli/ZeroFox close, May 2024 508.

Play 4: Government-Mission Pure-Plays Grow Through Partnership Stacks

  • Observation. The government-mission OSINT specialists are reaching a fuller collect-to-evidence workflow through partnership rather than acquisition. Tranquility AI and Fivecast announced a partnership “to Accelerate Open-Source Intelligence Analysis for Government and Law Enforcement” in March 2026, combining Fivecast’s large-scale collection with Tranquility’s evidence-analysis platforms 509. Fivecast’s 2026 posture is heavily event-led, with a documented presence at SOF Week 2026 and the OSINT Tech Expo 510.

  • Participants. Fivecast, Tranquility AI, and government / law-enforcement buyers.

  • My read. I read this as the specialists deliberately choosing partnership over M&A to assemble the full workflow. It is a lighter-weight path to a collect-to-evidence stack than the capital-intensive roll-ups of Play 3, and one that keeps the specialist independent rather than absorbed. It is the mirror image of the consolidation trade: build the workflow by alliance, not by balance sheet.

  • Falsifiable read. If H2 2026 brings a second comparable collection-plus-analysis partnership, or a named government reference win attributed to the Fivecast–Tranquility stack, the partnership-stack model is working as an independent growth path. If instead these stacks get acquired into a generalist’s portfolio, it confirms that the consolidation pull of Plays 1 and 3 is stronger than the case for independent specialist growth.

  • Evidence. Tranquility AI–Fivecast partnership, BusinessWire, 17 Mar 2026 509; Fivecast SOF Week / OSINT Tech Expo presence, 2026 510.

Play 5: A Nation-State / Strategic-Intelligence Wedge Draws Net-New Budget

  • Observation. A vertical the generalists do not own — corporate strategic and supply-chain counterintelligence against nation-state risk — is attracting its own capital. Strider Technologies raised a $55M Series C led by Pelion Venture Partners in September 2024, its largest round to date and roughly $117M in total funding 511. Its positioning is “unparalleled insights into state-sponsored threats” and a “Zero-touch architecture requiring no internal client data” 501. Babel Street, meanwhile, has built out a federal-and-threat leadership stack through 2025, including appointing John Larson (ex-Booz Allen) as President and Chief AI Officer in December 2025 512.

  • Participants. Strider, Babel Street, and Fortune-100 / critical-infrastructure buyers.

  • My read. I read this as a genuinely new buying center — corporate strategic, supply-chain, and IP-protection counterintelligence — splitting off from the established cyber-CTI and LEA-investigation centers, rather than a repackaging of generic threat intelligence. The funded specialist (Strider) and the incumbent building toward the same wedge (Babel Street) are both betting that “strategic intelligence” becomes a line item of its own.

  • Falsifiable read. If through H2 2026 a generalist — Recorded Future under Mastercard, or Dataminr — publicly launches a named “nation-state” or “supply-chain risk” product line, it validates the wedge as a category the incumbents must answer. If instead Strider’s next disclosed funding round stalls, or it pivots its public messaging back toward generic threat intelligence, the wedge was narrower than the raise implied.

  • Evidence. Strider Series C, Sep 2024 511; Strider homepage positioning 501; Babel Street leadership build, Dec 2025 512.

Market-force commentary: the surveillance-vendor shadow (not graded)

Voyager Labs sits adjacent to this front as a social-media-analysis and web-intelligence vendor that has been the subject of public litigation regarding social-media data collection. It is named here as descriptive market-force context only — no grade, no pattern claim, and no distress, decline, or sanctions characterization. Any such statement would require a named-outlet anchor that is out of scope for a non-graded vendor. Its relevance to the OSINT/WEBINT front is as a marker of the litigation-and-platform-policy risk surface that shadows the social-media-intelligence sub-segment as a whole — the same headwind that Play 3’s public-policy conditional turns on. The same discipline applies to any mention of the remote-mobile-exploitation cohort: never graded, descriptive only, and named-outlet-attributed-or-dropped on any negative.
