5.6 Winning & Losing

Three patterns govern who is gaining ground and who is ceding it on the OSINT/WEBINT front in 2026. Each is anchored to a specific public event, framed explicitly as opinion, and stated as a falsifiable prediction the next two quarters will confirm or refute. Read them in sequence. The first is the structural fact of the front: the independent brand is being absorbed. The second is the positioning move every survivor is making in response: the agentic pivot. The third is the demand-side dynamic that determines who keeps pricing power once the smoke clears — an accessible, contestable procurement lane with a free floor pressing up from below.

Pattern Claim 1 — The Strategic-Acquirer Absorption Thesis

Observation. In an eighteen-month window the OSINT/WEBINT front lost three of its most prominent independent brands to acquirers, and a fourth agreed to roll up a fifth. Mastercard bought Recorded Future — described in the deal release as “the world’s largest threat intelligence company, with more than 1,900 clients across 75 countries, including the governments of 45 countries”527 — for $2.65B, announced 12 Sep 2024 and finalized 20 Dec 2024528. Bitsight agreed to acquire dark-web specialist Cybersixgill for ~$115M (announced 14 Nov 2024)529. Haveli Investments took ZeroFox private for ~$350M enterprise value at $1.14/share, closed 13 May 2024530. PenLink, owned by PE firm Spire Capital, had earlier absorbed Israeli WEBINT vendor Cobwebs Technologies (Estimate: ~USD 200M, CTech; terms undisclosed, July 2023)531. And Dataminr — itself last priced at $4.1B in 2021 and recapitalized in 2025 via a $100M Fortress convertible rather than a fresh equity mark532 — announced intent to acquire ThreatConnect for $290M on 21 Oct 2025533.

My read. I read this as the closing of the independent-OSINT-brand path. The category has become strategic enough that the buyers are no longer other intelligence specialists — they are payments networks (Mastercard), security-ratings platforms (Bitsight), and PE control vehicles (Haveli, Spire) folding collection assets into larger portfolios. The standalone-public route has effectively shut: ZeroFox de-listed, Recorded Future was absorbed into a payments giant, and no fresh standalone primary mega-round on a pure-play collector surfaced in named-outlet reporting across the window. The evidenced surviving independents (Flashpoint, Fivecast, Strider) are now either acquisition candidates or vertical specialists narrow enough to be uninteresting to a generalist acquirer — which is its own kind of moat. Babel Street is excluded from that enumeration because named-outlet and co-investor reporting identify it as Veritas-backed at the time of the January 2024 Vertical Knowledge acquisition; current ownership remains unresolved.447

Conditional prediction. The absorption thesis hardens into the defining structure of the front under one of two triggers: H2 2026 brings a second large OSINT/CTI pure-play acquired by a non-defense platform company (payments, cloud, identity, or ratings), or a further roll-up is announced following the now-closed Dataminr/ThreatConnect deal. Remaining independents should then increasingly be read as acquisition candidates rather than durable standalones. The pull is weaker than the deal flow implied — and independent growth is still financeable — under two inverse signals. Either a pure-play collector raises a fresh, named-lead primary equity mega-round at an up valuation, or Recorded Future’s government-sector roster visibly contracts post-close, with a loss of named public-sector references signaling integration strain.

Sources. 527 528 529 530 531 532 533

Pattern Claim 2 — The Agentic Repositioning

Observation. Across 2025–2026 the front’s contenders converged on near-identical “agentic AI” homepage language. Dataminr launched “Dataminr for Cyber Defense,” a suite “built with agentic and predictive AI at its core” (Mar 2026)534, and took a $100M Fortress financing explicitly “to accelerate gen AI and agentic AI product innovation” (Apr 2025)532. Babel Street’s 2026 homepage leads with “Agentic Risk Intelligence” and “Governed AI agents on rights-cleared, mission-grade data to produce decision-ready intelligence in minutes, not days”535. Strider markets “One Platform, Powered by Agentic Intelligence”536. Cognyte’s NEXYTE platform markets “co-pilots” and “agentic decision flows”537. Maltego and Flashpoint, by contrast, add AI as bolt-on summarization on an existing engine538539.

My read. I read this strictly as a positioning convergence, not a verified capability gap — a distinction this report’s grounding discipline and its security-architecture caution both require, because true internal architecture cannot be verified from outside. What is observably real is the funding earmarked for it (Dataminr’s April-2025 round states the purpose verbatim532) and the simultaneity of the pivot. When every contender’s hero copy carries “agentic” in the same quarter, the word has stopped differentiating and started signaling table-stakes. The genuine question is not who markets agentic AI — they all do — but who can produce a customer willing to attribute an outcome to it.

Conditional prediction. Suppose by Q4 2026 one of these vendors publishes a named-reference customer attributing a specific decision or outcome to autonomous agentic action — as distinct from analyst-assisted search — and the others cannot. In that case the agentic claims begin to separate into a real differentiator, and that vendor earns a durable wedge. If “agentic” instead remains uniform marketing language across all of them with no named-outcome reference win through 2026 — no independent time-to-insight benchmark, no government reference framed around autonomous action — then it is a category-wide label rather than a moat. It then demotes from a central convergence pillar to a watchlist item.

Sources. 532 534 535 536 537 538 539

Pattern Claim 3 — The Contestable-Lane-and-Free-Floor Squeeze

Observation. Unlike the classified-collection fronts, U.S. government OSINT is bought predominantly through commercial-off-the-shelf subscriptions on established federal vehicles. Babel Street’s AI-powered solutions were added to “Carahsoft’s GSA Schedule contract,” making them available to “Federal, State and Local Government agencies”540. Those awards are openly recompeted and litigated: Babel Street and Dataminr fought a GAO bid protest over the DoD PADELS publicly-available-information alerting award (valued at $24,923,076.93)541, while the FBI bought 5,000 Babel Street licenses for “up to $27M” (2022)542. Underneath that accessible lane sits a compressing free floor — Maltego community editions, open-source OSINT toolkits, and general-purpose LLMs now performing ad-hoc collection543 — alongside the government-share data showing government intelligence agencies as the single largest end-user segment at “38.40%” of 2025 OSINT revenue per one named publisher544.

My read. I read these two facts as a vise on the middle of the market. Because the procurement lane is genuinely accessible — GSA/Carahsoft subscriptions, recompeted enterprise licenses, publicly-litigated protests — a software/data specialist can enter this front without owning sovereign infrastructure. That is exactly why the front overflows with contenders and why it consolidates so fast. But the same accessibility means the low end is being eaten from below by free tooling and commodity LLMs. The vendors who keep pricing power are the ones who climb up-stack to where the free floor cannot follow: multilingual exploitation at investigative grade, dark/deep-web depth with maintained access, defensible provenance, and accredited government deployment. The bifurcation is between vendors anchored to a government mission (Fivecast, Strider, the gov-share leaders) and vendors competing on commodity open-web collection — and the second group is structurally squeezed.

Conditional prediction. If H2 2026 public procurement records show continued recompeted, contested OSINT awards on GSA/Carahsoft-class vehicles (new named awards or bid protests), the accessible-lane structure holds and the government-anchored specialists keep their pricing premium. The “government edge is carved out” assumption weakens instead if a major OSINT/WEBINT vendor loses a government contract or draws a regulator order specifically tied to public-data scraping during 2026 — the scenario the front’s contested scraping-law backdrop makes plausible. The squeeze then migrates upward from the commodity tier into the mission tier.

Sources. 540 541 542 543 544

Winners, Watch, Losers

Winners.

  • Recorded Future. Sold at the top of the cycle. The $2.65B exit to Mastercard from PE owner Insight Partners528 is the largest disclosed transaction in the front. It is the cleanest “winning” outcome available to a pure-play: a strategic acquirer paid a payments-network premium for the category’s most-cited brand. The Winners label is opinion-labeled and scoped to the transaction, not to post-close execution, which the conditional in Pattern Claim 1 flags as the open risk.
  • Dataminr. The lone independent still acting as a consolidator rather than a target: a $100M Fortress financing (Apr 2025)532 funding the agentic build, plus its $290M ThreatConnect acquisition (announced Oct 2025, closed 2025-11-25)533 extending it from real-time alerting toward the fusion/analytics layer. I read Dataminr as winning the “independent that buys rather than gets bought” position in 2026. The caveat is that its last priced mark is the 2021 $4.1B Series F and the 2025 raise was a convertible, not a fresh equity up-round532.
  • Strider Technologies. Winning the net-new vertical, not the incumbent fight. A $55M Series C led by Pelion (Sep 2024, ~$117M total)545 funds a nation-state / economic-espionage wedge — “The Frontier of Strategic Intelligence”536 — that the cyber-CTI generalists do not own. It is winning a budget line, not a market-share war, which is the defensible thing to win when the generalists are consolidating.

Watch.

  • Babel Street. An active build-and-hire platform in 2026, with documented historical sponsor backing — “Agentic Risk Intelligence” repositioning535, a federal-and-AI leadership stack (John Larson, ex-Booz Allen, as President and Chief AI Officer, Dec 2025)546, and a Carahsoft/GSA federal channel540. Named-outlet and co-investor reporting identify Veritas backing at the time of the January 2024 Vertical Knowledge acquisition, while current ownership remains unresolved.547 Watch signal: a current-owner disclosure or a fresh named-lead primary round that establishes whether the ownership branch has changed; further add-on M&A would test whether the sponsor-backed roll-up continues.
  • Fivecast. The clearest government-mission OSINT pure-play in the cut — “Government agencies (40+),” “Law enforcement (30+ police departments)”548 — pursuing a partnership stack rather than M&A to reach a full collect-to-evidence workflow. That is the Tranquility AI collection-plus-evidence partnership, Mar 2026549, on a US$20M Series A base (2023)550. Watch signal: a named government reference win from the partnership, or the partnership stack itself getting acquired into a generalist’s portfolio.

Losers.

No graded contender in this front earns a Losers label in this section. A vendor reaches this line only when a cited public event anchors a vendor-specific decline, per the casualty-evidence discipline. The qualifying events are a layoff specific to the OSINT business, a missed quarter, a down-round, a named executive departure framed as distress, or a customer-churn disclosure. The public events on this front are consolidation and strategic exit, not failure. ZeroFox’s $1.14/share take-private530 sits well below its SPAC-era levels but is a PE de-listing, not a documented operational collapse; Dataminr’s reported 2023 staff reduction551 and Primer’s pre-turnaround leadership change552 are descriptive context, not casualty labels. Voyager Labs and the NSO/Candiru/Intellexa/Ability cohort are litigation-sensitive and never graded; they appear only as descriptive market-force commentary elsewhere in the chapter, with no decline label asserted here. Quarterly refreshes will populate this line if an OSINT-specific distress signal emerges on the public record.

5.7 The Campaign Ahead

Five watchlist items for H2 2026. Each names a public, observable threshold that would trigger re-assessment of a claim above.

  1. A second non-defense-platform acquisition of an OSINT pure-play. Signal to monitor: M&A announcements naming a payments, cloud, identity, or security-ratings acquirer of a standalone OSINT/CTI collector. Threshold for re-assessment: one such deal announced in H2 2026, or — with the Dataminr/ThreatConnect acquisition already closed (2025-11-25)533 — a further roll-up, or a Dataminr IPO pricing → Pattern Claim 1’s absorption thesis hardens into the front’s defining structure. Inverse threshold: a fresh named-lead primary equity mega-round at an up valuation on a pure-play collector → independent growth is still financeable. Primary source: named-outlet M&A coverage (Reuters, Bloomberg, Calcalist), vendor press releases.

  2. A named-outcome agentic reference win. Signal: public reference customers attributing a specific decision or outcome to autonomous agentic action, as distinct from analyst-assisted search, from any of Dataminr, Babel Street, Strider, or Cognyte. Threshold: one vendor publishes such a named reference (or an independent time-to-insight benchmark) and the others do not → the agentic claims begin separating into a real differentiator per Pattern Claim 2’s first branch. Inverse: “agentic” stays uniform marketing language across all of them through Q4 2026 with no named-outcome win → demote the AI-native convergence pillar to a watchlist label. Primary source: vendor press releases (Dataminr, Babel Street, Strider, Cognyte newsrooms), government reference-win coverage.

  3. A scraping-law action against a government-facing OSINT vendor. Signal: a regulator order or lost government contract specifically tied to public-data scraping affecting a named OSINT/WEBINT vendor. The backdrop is contested — GDPR’s “public availability is not a sufficient lawful basis” line and the FTC’s national-security-carved-out location-broker orders553. Threshold: one such named action in 2026 → the “government edge is carved out” read in Pattern Claim 3 weakens and the squeeze migrates from the commodity tier into the mission tier. Inverse: scraping-law enforcement stays confined to consumer-facing brokers (e.g., the Clearview-class fines553) → the carve-out holds. Primary source: regulator press (FTC, EU DPAs), named-outlet legal coverage, Citizen Lab / Amnesty public analysis.

  4. Recorded Future’s government franchise post-close. Signal: Recorded Future’s named public-sector reference roster and any government-contract activity following the Mastercard close (20 Dec 2024)528. Threshold: visible contraction of named public-sector references, or a public-sector contract loss attributable to the acquisition → integration is straining the government franchise (Pattern Claim 1’s inverse branch). Conversely, retained or expanded named government references → the strategic acquirer preserved the franchise. Primary source: Recorded Future / Mastercard newsroom, federal procurement records (USAspending), named-outlet coverage.

  5. A generalist answering the nation-state / supply-chain wedge. Signal: whether a generalist (Recorded Future/Mastercard, Dataminr) publicly launches a named “nation-state risk” or “supply-chain / vendor risk” product line answering Strider’s strategic-intelligence wedge536. A related signal is whether Babel Street’s standing-up of a dedicated threat-and-vendor-risk function546 expands into a named product. Threshold: a generalist ships a named competing line in H2 2026 → the vertical wedge is validated as a category the incumbents must answer (a winning signal for Strider’s position). Inverse: Strider’s next disclosed round stalls or its messaging reverts to generic threat intel → the wedge was narrower than the raise implied. Primary source: vendor product-launch pages and press releases, funding-round coverage.

The Convergence Synthesis — The Market as One Battlefield

Key terms used in this chapter.

  • The five fronts. National Agencies / SIGINT (mass-scale network collection); Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers (warrant-scoped lawful interception); Tactical Intelligence (field RF / device collection); Fusion / Decision Intelligence (the analytical layer); Open-Source Intelligence / WEBINT (open-source and web intelligence).
  • The collection–fusion stack — the structural relationship between the fronts: National Agencies, Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers, Tactical Intelligence, and Open-Source Intelligence produce intelligence material; Fusion / Decision Intelligence makes sense of it. Fusion sits on top of the other four by construction.
  • Portfolio breadth — here, a count of how many of the five practices a single vendor’s public product pages span, each span anchored to a dated page. It is a measure of public positioning, not of an internally verified product suite.
  • AI-native / agentic positioning — a vendor’s public marketing of large-language-model-driven, autonomous, or “agentic” capability. Whether the underlying architecture is genuinely AI-native cannot be verified from public material; the term is used throughout as “markets itself as,” not as an architectural finding.

C.1 Leading Briefing

Read the five fronts together and the government-intelligence software market resolves into a single battlefield with a clear shape. Four of the fronts are collection — strategic network collection (National Agencies), warrant-scoped interception (Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers), tactical field collection (Tactical Intelligence), and open-source / web collection (Open-Source Intelligence). The fifth, fusion (Fusion / Decision Intelligence), is not a collection silo at all; it is the analytical layer every other front feeds. That asymmetry is the master fact of the market: collection is fragmenting and commoditizing front by front, while the value migrates upward to the layer that resolves, links, and decides. The vendors winning the decade are the ones climbing toward that layer; the vendors being squeezed are the ones stuck in commoditizing collection beneath a free or sanctioned floor.

Across the fronts, four cross-market patterns recur with enough public evidence to name.

First, portfolio breadth concentrates unevenly — most vendors hold one practice, a cluster holds two, and exactly one of this report’s graded vendors spans the whole stack on public pages. A network-interception cluster — ClearTrail, Vehere, Trovicor — spans the two interception fronts (National Agencies mass collection plus Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers warrant-scoped lawful interception) on public pages. Palantir spans the analytical layer plus the feeds it ingests (graded in fusion, referenced wherever it ingests SIGINT or OSINT feeds). And one vendor — Cognyte — carries graded public-page pillars across all five practices: collection in National Agencies (network-intelligence glossary), Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers (the NEXYTE-LEA “lawful interception … data source” line), and Tactical Intelligence (border-protection “SIGINT, OSINT and VISINT”), fusion in Fusion / Decision Intelligence (NEXYTE), and OSINT in Open-Source Intelligence (LUMINAR).554555556557558 Among this report’s graded vendors, that is the only full collection-to-fusion span on this report’s own grading of public pages. But that widest span is breadth of public positioning, assembled across separate pages, a SEC filing, and a registered trademark. It is not evidence of an integrated, verified five-front product suite. It is a span across the public-marketing stack, not an owned, unified product across it.

Second, the AI-native repositioning is concentrated in the two analytical fronts. “Agentic” is now the lead homepage word in fusion and OSINT — Palantir’s AIP, Cognyte’s “agentic AI-based decision flows,” Dataminr’s “built with agentic and predictive AI at its core,” Babel Street’s “Governed AI agents… in minutes, not days,” Strider’s “One Platform, Powered by Agentic Intelligence.”559560561562563 In SIGINT, AI is defensive — encrypted-traffic intelligence to recover visibility lost to TLS 1.3 and QUIC564.565 In lawful interception and tactical, the front is not AI-led at all; it is led by standards and by encryption-and-hardware physics.

Third, consolidation is running on two distinct engines. One is strategic acquirers absorbing the OSINT layer into adjacent platforms, with Mastercard’s $2.65B purchase of Recorded Future the signature deal.566 The other is private equity rolling up the collection and interception layer (Thoma Bravo’s ~C$1.8B take-private of Magnet, followed by bringing Magnet and Grayshift together; Mill Point’s acquisition of SS8).567568

Fourth, the fronts are not equally in play — OSINT and fusion are the contested, fast-moving, AI-native battlegrounds; lawful interception is the most defended and least disrupted; SIGINT faces an existential technology shift in encryption; tactical is bifurcating as device forensics rises and classic RF interception declines.

The strategic reading is the same for any operator in this market, whether incumbent prime, specialist collector, OSINT pure-play, or new entrant: the floor is rising under collection and the ceiling is rising over fusion. The defensible positions in 2026 are three. The analytical layer, if you can pass accreditation and prove AI actually compresses time-to-decision. The standards-gated interception niche, if you can afford the 5G conformance bar. And government-anchored mission depth, if the free OSINT floor cannot follow you up-stack. The exposed positions are commodity open-web collection, content-interception value propositions that encryption is hollowing out, and any vendor whose breadth is asserted rather than visible on a public page.

C.2 The Market Reassembled — One Stack, Five Fronts

The five fronts are usually sold, bought, and analyzed separately, and the front chapters treat them that way for good reason: each has its own buyer, its own barrier, and its own competitive logic. But the convergence view requires seeing how they stack. Four of the five fronts collect; one fuses.

The collection fronts produce material along different axes. National Agencies collects at the network backbone, at mass scale, as standing infrastructure. Its defining property is volume and permanence, and its public anchors are vendor pages for “lawful interception,” “network intelligence,” and DPI engines.565569 Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers collects the same kind of traffic but under a fundamentally different trigger: a per-target warrant, mediated through standards-certified handover interfaces (ETSI TS 102 232; 3GPP TS 33.127/128; US CALEA / J-STD-025).570 Tactical Intelligence collects in the field, against a present target, with portable RF and device hardware — IMSI catchers, direction-finding, device extraction.571572 Open-Source Intelligence collects from openly available, web, social, and dark-web sources, with no privileged access, no warrant, and no field hardware.573 These four are technically distinct and, critically for this report, non-overlapping by buyer and trigger. The bright line between National Agencies and Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers is the legal trigger and scale, not the technology; the bright line around Tactical Intelligence is physical proximity; the bright line around Open-Source Intelligence is that the source is open.

Fusion sits on top of all four. Fusion / Decision Intelligence is the analytical layer that ingests already-collected data and resolves it into entities, maps relationships, places them in space and time, and turns the result into a decision — sold standalone to a bring-your-own-source buyer.574 This is why fusion is the front where breadth and AI-native positioning both concentrate: a fusion platform by construction touches every collection front’s output, so the vendors that want to span the market climb into fusion rather than try to own every collection silo.

Cognyte’s national-security NEXYTE page makes the stack explicit in a vendor’s own words. It describes intelligence generated “by unifying agencies’ data sources, including lawful interception, digital forensics, open sources and government databases” — lawful interception and forensics appearing on that page as input sources the fusion platform consumes, which is what anchors Cognyte’s fusion grade in Fusion / Decision Intelligence.575 Separately, on other dated public surfaces, Cognyte carries graded collection pillars in their own right — a network-intelligence/SIGINT glossary (National Agencies), a border-protection page citing “SIGINT, OSINT and VISINT” sources (Tactical Intelligence), and a registered VANTAGE trademark and SEC filing describing “interception, collection, monitoring” (corroborating National Agencies / Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers).554556 The two surfaces coexist: the fusion page frames collection as analytics input, while the glossary, border-protection page, filing, and mark carry the collection positioning directly. The public record does not show a current standalone monitoring-centre product page; the warrant-scoped LI grade rests on the NEXYTE-LEA “data source” line and the filing/trademark lineage, not on a marketed standalone collection product. Palantir’s platform is described in the same architectural register, as “a commercially-available, AI-ready operating system that improves and accelerates decisions for operators across roles and all domains.”576

The consequence of the stack is what I read as the single most important structural fact in the convergence: value is migrating up. Collection is doing three things at once. It is fragmenting (the National Agencies front’s seven-plus specialists, the Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers’ private long tail, Tactical Intelligence’s two-issuer-plus-tail, Open-Source Intelligence’s sixteen-plus contenders). It is commoditizing (the open-source free floor; encryption hollowing National Agencies’ and Tactical Intelligence’s content yield). And in places it is being sanctioned out of legitimacy (the surveillance cohort). Fusion, by contrast, is consolidating at the top, defended by accreditation, and is where the AI-native money is being raised and spent. Every cross-front pattern below is, at root, a consequence of that upward migration.

C.3 Portfolio Breadth — Who Actually Spans the Market

The most-asked question about this market is which vendor “does everything.” The clean-room-safe way to answer it is not to repeat any vendor’s marketing claim of a complete suite. Instead, count public spans across this report’s graded vendors: for each graded vendor, how many of the report’s practices does its own public product material actually cover, each span anchored to a dated page? Airbus and other market references remain references; they are not silently imported into the measured universe. Counted that way, breadth is real but uneven, and it concentrates in distinct shapes.

Within this report’s graded-vendor universe, Cognyte is graded across all five practices on distinct dated public pillars, a different quoted line per front, never one pillar reused across fronts. The pillars are National Agencies on its network-intelligence/SIGINT glossary,554 Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers on the NEXYTE-LEA “lawful interception … data source” line,555 Tactical Intelligence on the border-protection “SIGINT, OSINT and VISINT” line,556 Fusion / Decision Intelligence on NEXYTE,557 and Open-Source Intelligence on LUMINAR.558 The span is breadth of public positioning measured across pages, not evidence of a verified integrated five-front product suite (see Pattern Claim 1).

Two shapes fall out of the ledger. The first is the network-interception cluster. ClearTrail, Vehere, and Trovicor each carry public pillars in both interception fronts. ClearTrail, for example, markets solutions that “enable the LEAs to perform MASS, TARGETED & TACTICAL Monitoring and Analysis across a variety of communication networks” (National Agencies). It also markets a separate ETSI-compliant lawful-interception product that “interfaces with the mediation device to acquire, decode, and reconstruct ETSI-compliant Voice and IP traffic over HI2 and HI3 interfaces” (Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers).569577 These vendors span both interception fronts because the underlying technology (DPI, mediation) genuinely serves both the mass-collection and the warrant-scoped buyer. The span is real and public, and it is the closest thing in the study to a two-front collection suite.

The second shape is the full-stack public span, and it is where Cognyte sits. Cognyte is the only vendor among this report’s graded set whose public material carries graded pillars in all five practices, each anchored to a distinct dated surface. Collection appears in National Agencies (its network-intelligence/SIGINT glossary), Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers (the NEXYTE-LEA page positioning “lawful interception … digital forensics, open sources and government databases” as unified data sources), and Tactical Intelligence (its border-protection page “fusing together with SIGINT, OSINT and VISINT sources”). Fusion appears in Fusion / Decision Intelligence (NEXYTE — “Apply agentic AI-based decision flows”; “Fuse and analyze data across sources to resolve identities and uncover relations”). And OSINT appears in Open-Source Intelligence (LUMINAR — “AI-powered external threat intelligence solution … with comprehensive visibility into their threat landscape”).554555556557558 That is, on my reading of the public pages, the widest span among this report’s graded vendors — the only full-stack public span on this report’s own grading of public pages, the only one that runs the full distance from collection to fusion.

It is essential to state precisely what that span is and is not. It is breadth of public positioning measured across pages, filings, and a registered trademark. It is not evidence of an integrated, verified five-front product suite. On Cognyte’s own surfaces the breadth assembles from separate places. The national-security NEXYTE page frames lawful interception and forensics as analytics inputs the fusion platform consumes (graded in Fusion / Decision Intelligence). The collection pillars are carried separately on the glossary (National Agencies) and the border-protection page (Tactical Intelligence), and corroborated by a SEC filing and a registered mark (National Agencies / Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers). It does not assemble from one unified suite page marketing all five as a single product. Palantir occupies a narrower, fusion-anchored breadth from the other direction — graded in fusion, referenced wherever its platform ingests SIGINT or OSINT feeds. That is the structural signature of the upward migration: vendors are broad because they sit at or climb toward the fusion layer that touches everything, not because they publish one verified product spanning every collection silo.

The rest of the cross-front ledger anchors single practices on its public pages, and surfacing those pillars is what makes the full-stack span distinctive by contrast. i2 Group markets “The knowledge graph solution at the forefront of intelligence analysis” — fusion only.586 BAE Systems markets its IntelligenceReveal portfolio for “Communications Intelligence and Multi-Source Analysis” in SIGINT; it divested its NetReveal fusion line to SymphonyAI in 2022, so on public pages it now anchors SIGINT only.584585 Babel Street anchors OSINT, marketing “Governed AI agents on rights-cleared, mission-grade data to produce decision-ready intelligence in minutes, not days.”561 Septier spans the interception and tactical fronts with two genuinely distinct products: a lawful-interception mediation solution “for all telecom and data networks using any technology” (Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers) and an Identities Catcher “capturing up to 11 different identifiers for each cellular device” (Tactical Intelligence).582583 That is a real cross-front footprint, but two separate boxes rather than one platform. These are not breadth plays; they are the reminder that most of the market remains single-practice, which is exactly what makes Cognyte’s full-stack public span — and Palantir’s narrower fusion-anchored breadth — the exception worth naming.

Pattern Claim 1 — Breadth Is a Stack Position, Not a Verified Suite

One vendor among this report’s graded vendors — Cognyte — carries graded public-page pillars across all five practices: collection in National Agencies (network-intelligence/SIGINT glossary), Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers (the NEXYTE-LEA “lawful interception … data source” line), and Tactical Intelligence (the border-protection “SIGINT, OSINT and VISINT” line); fusion in Fusion / Decision Intelligence (NEXYTE); and OSINT in Open-Source Intelligence (LUMINAR). On my reading of the public pages that is the only full collection-to-fusion span among this report’s graded vendors on this report’s own grading of public pages. But the widest span is breadth of public positioning across pages, not evidence of an integrated, verified five-front product suite. On Cognyte’s own pages the interception and forensic capabilities surface via a SEC filing, a registered trademark, and deeper product/glossary pages rather than a single unified suite page. Palantir holds a narrower, fusion-anchored breadth from the analytics-prime side (graded in fusion, referenced wherever its platform ingests SIGINT or OSINT feeds). The only multi-collection-front breadth among the rest (ClearTrail, Vehere, Trovicor across National Agencies and Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers) is confined to the two interception fronts that share DPI/mediation technology. The pattern, on my reading: the broadest public span is a position spanning the marketing stack, not proof of an owned, verified product across it.

Falsifiable test. Suppose that through H2 2026 a single vendor publishes an integrated, named, single-platform reference unifying three or more collection-and-fusion practices as one verified product, not a span of separate product pages, public filings, and trademarks. Then the “public-span-not-a-verified-suite” reading weakens toward a real integrated suite. If instead the broadest footprint stays a span of distinct public surfaces (separate pages, filings, marks) rather than one verified integrated platform, the claim holds. Primary signal: vendors’ own dated product pages, single-platform reference architectures, and investor materials; analyst reclassification.

C.4 The AI-Native Repositioning — Concentrated, Not Universal

“AI-native” and “agentic” are the words of 2026 across this market, but they are not distributed evenly. Read across the fronts, the agentic repositioning concentrates almost entirely in the two analytical fronts, is defensive in SIGINT, and is essentially absent — as a leading positioning — in lawful interception and tactical.

In fusion and OSINT, agentic is the lead message. In fusion, Palantir markets AIP as embedding “large language models (LLMs) and AI agents directly into the systems your teams use every day, enabling them to automate decisions, analyze enormous datasets, and execute tasks,” and Cognyte’s NEXYTE markets “agentic AI-based decision flows.”559560 In OSINT, the agentic language is even denser: Dataminr describes its platform as “built with agentic and predictive AI at its core,” Babel Street markets “Governed AI agents on rights-cleared, mission-grade data to produce decision-ready intelligence in minutes, not days,” and Strider leads with “One Platform, Powered by Agentic Intelligence.”561562563 The money follows the message: Dataminr’s $100M Fortress financing in April 2025 was explicitly raised “to accelerate gen AI and agentic AI product innovation.”587 These are the named, public, AI-native entrants the convergence claim rests on. That nameability is exactly the test the report set for keeping AI-native as a central claim rather than demoting it to a watchlist item: the entrants can be named from their own public pages.

In SIGINT, AI is defensive, not offensive. The National Agencies vendors market AI/ML primarily to recover capability that encryption is taking away: ipoque’s encrypted-traffic intelligence “combines improved DPI with artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques to restore visibility into encrypted network traffic,” and ClearTrail and Vehere market AI-on-big-data and “AI-powered Network Intelligence.”565569578 The framing is telling. In fusion and OSINT, AI is sold as a new capability that compresses time-to-decision. In SIGINT, AI is sold as the mechanism of survival against the TLS 1.3 / ECH / QUIC erosion of classic passive content inspection564.

In lawful interception and tactical, the front is not AI-led. The Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers’ graded contenders’ warrant-scoped pages carry no “AI-native” or “agentic” framing. The front differentiates on standards conformance and on “immutable audit trails,” and adapts to 5G through 3GPP-defined functions, not through AI.570 Tactical Intelligence’s vendors market AI as acceleration — Cellebrite’s “AI-powered decoding,” MSAB’s GPU-accelerated brute-force moving extraction “to the field” — not as autonomous agentic systems.571572 The disruptive force in tactical is encryption and the lab-to-field collapse, with compute as the enabler, not AI as the disruptor.

Pattern Claim 2 — The Agentic Line Has Not Yet Been Drawn

Across fusion and OSINT, “agentic” has become uniform marketing language, but as of mid-2026 no vendor has published a named government or enterprise reference attributing a specific decision or outcome to autonomous agentic action, as distinct from analyst-assisted search. The repositioning is real as positioning; it is unproven as differentiated capability.

Falsifiable test. Suppose that by Q4 2026 one or more vendors in fusion or OSINT publish named-customer references — or independent time-to-insight benchmarks — that attribute a decision or outcome to autonomous agentic action, and competitors do not. In that case the agentic claims begin separating into a real differentiator, and AI-native becomes a genuine competitive axis. If “agentic” stays uniform across all of them through Q4 2026 with no named-outcome win, the layer is positioning, not capability, and should be read as table stakes rather than separation. Primary signal: vendor press releases and government reference-win coverage (Dataminr, Babel Street, Strider, Cognyte, Palantir newsrooms); the architecture itself remains unverifiable from outside.

C.5 Where the Pressure Is Highest — Multi-Market Pressure

Not all five fronts are equally in play. Read them by the intensity of competitive and structural pressure — growth, entry barrier, concentration, deal tempo, and exposure to the AI-native and encryption shifts — and the pattern is consistent. That pattern is itself a strategic finding: the pressure is highest exactly where the value is migrating (the analytical layer) and where the floor is rising fastest (open-source collection), and lowest where standards still hold the line (lawful interception).

Order Front Growth (public CAGRs) Entry barrier Concentration AI / tech-shift exposure Why it sits here

2 Fusion / Decision Intelligence High (15.4%–19.1%)591 High (FedRAMP High / DoD IL6 accreditation)576 Concentrated at top (Palantir gravity)576 High (agentic over resolved graphs) Highest-value layer and AI-native battleground, but accreditation-defended — value capture concentrates at the top

The pressure order is not a claim about which front is largest or most profitable — it is a claim about where the competitive ground is moving fastest. OSINT and fusion sit highest because that is where the AI-native repositioning, the M&A tempo, and (for OSINT) the commoditization squeeze all converge. SIGINT sits third on a technology-shift threat that is existential but slow-moving and export-control-gated. Tactical sits fourth as a bifurcating front. Lawful interception sits lowest on pressure precisely because it is first on defensibility: the standards-conformance barrier is the hardest in the study, and the front adapts to 5G inside the standards rather than being displaced from outside.570

C.6 The Consolidation Map — Two Engines, One Direction

Cross-front dealmaking is the loudest signal of 2026, and read across the fronts it runs on two distinct engines pulling in the same direction — value up, collection rolled up or absorbed — with a regulatory-restructuring strand and a fusion-accretion strand running alongside.

Engine one: strategic acquirers absorbing the OSINT / analytical layer. The signature deal is Mastercard’s $2.65B acquisition of Recorded Future, announced September 2024 and closed December 2024 — a payments network paying a premium for the category’s most-cited OSINT brand.566 It is not alone. Bitsight acquired Cybersixgill (~$115M, November 2024). And the front’s largest independent, Dataminr, is itself acting as an acquirer: its $290M acquisition of ThreatConnect, announced in October 2025, closed on 2025-11-25, extending Dataminr from real-time alerting into the fusion/analytics layer.589596 The logic is consistent: OSINT — the most accessible collection front — is being pulled up into adjacent platforms (payments, security ratings, alerting) that want its data and its analytical layer.

Engine two: private equity rolling up the collection and interception layer. Where strategic acquirers chase OSINT, PE chases the opaque, government-anchored collection assets. Thoma Bravo took Magnet Forensics private and then brought it together with Grayshift after the ~C$1.8B Magnet transaction (2023), rolling up the tactical device-forensics layer. Haveli Investments took ZeroFox private (~$350M, May 2024), and Spire Capital’s PenLink absorbed Cobwebs (Estimate: ~USD 200M, CTech; terms undisclosed, 2023). And in lawful interception, Mill Point Capital acquired SS8 Networks (2025), with Cy4Gate (the one public, Euronext-listed Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers issuer) having earlier absorbed the Aurora Group including RCS Lab (2022).567590597568598 PE is doing to the collection layer what strategic acquirers are doing to OSINT — but privately, taking surveillance-adjacent assets off the public market and rolling them up.

Two strands run alongside. First, a regulatory-restructuring strand. Four public events line up here: Sandvine’s 2024 Entity-List designation; its announced exit from 56 “non-democratic” countries (~45% of its 2023 revenue base, on its own disclosure); its removal from the list “following significant corporate reforms”; and its 2025 rebrand to AppLogic Networks. Together they make the clearest public case of regulation, not the market, restructuring a collection vendor.599600601602 Second, a fusion-accretion strand: the analytical layer buying graph and entity-resolution capability — Nuix’s up-to-€20M acquisition of Linkurious (signed December 2025, closed April 2026) and Elastic’s strategic investment in Siren (December 2025).603604 Both strands point the same way as the two main engines: capability and capital accreting at and above the fusion layer, collection rolled up or constrained beneath it.

Pattern Claim 3 — Up-and-Out: Collection Consolidates, Analytics Gets Absorbed

The M&A in this market is not random dealmaking; it is the upward migration made visible. Strategic acquirers are absorbing the OSINT/analytical layer into adjacent platforms (Mastercard/Recorded Future, Bitsight/Cybersixgill). Private equity is rolling up the collection and interception layer off the public market (Thoma Bravo/Magnet-Grayshift, Mill Point/SS8, Haveli/ZeroFox, PenLink/Cobwebs). And the fusion layer is accreting graph and entity-resolution capability (Nuix/Linkurious, Elastic/Siren). All three vectors move value toward the analytical layer and roll up or constrain collection beneath it.

Falsifiable test. Suppose H2 2026 brings either (a) a further strategic-acquirer purchase of an OSINT or analytics pure-play by a non-defense platform, or (b) a further PE roll-up in the collection/interception layer. Then the up-and-out pattern hardens into the market’s defining structure. The inverse would be the next major deals running the other way: a collection specialist acquiring an analytics platform as an independent, or a fresh named-lead primary equity round re-financing a standalone collector at an up valuation. That would weaken the pattern and show that independent collection is still financeable on its own. Primary signal: dated M&A announcements and funding rounds with named leads (vendor newsrooms, Reuters/Bloomberg/Calcalist, regulator press for export-control actions).

C.7 The Campaign Ahead — Cross-Front Watchlist for H2 2026

Five falsifiable signals, each spanning more than one front, will tell whether the convergence reading holds through the back half of 2026. Each grounds on a publicly observable event.

  1. A named agentic-outcome reference win (Fusion / Decision Intelligence + Open-Source Intelligence). Signal: any vendor in fusion or OSINT publishes a named government or enterprise reference — or an independent time-to-insight benchmark — attributing a specific decision or outcome to autonomous agentic action. Threshold: one such named win and competitors silent → AI-native begins to separate into a real differentiator (Pattern Claim 2’s first branch). Inverse: “agentic” stays uniform with no named-outcome win through Q4 2026 → demote to table stakes. Primary source: Dataminr, Babel Street, Strider, Cognyte, Palantir newsrooms; government reference-win coverage.

  2. A third strategic-acquirer absorption of an OSINT/analytics pure-play (Open-Source Intelligence → adjacent). Signal: a payments, cloud, identity, security-ratings, or alerting acquirer buys a standalone OSINT/analytics collector. Threshold: one such deal in H2 2026 — or, with the Dataminr/ThreatConnect acquisition now closed, a further roll-up (or a Dataminr IPO pricing) → Pattern Claim 3’s absorption engine hardens. Inverse: a fresh named-lead primary mega-round at an up valuation on a pure-play → independent collection is still financeable. Primary source: named-outlet M&A coverage; vendor press releases.

  3. A verified-suite move — a vendor publishing an integrated single-platform reference across collection and fusion (cross-front). Signal: any vendor publishes a dated, named, single-platform reference that unifies three or more collection-and-fusion practices as one verified product. It would be one product, not a span of separate product pages, public filings, and trademarks. Threshold: one vendor crosses that line → Pattern Claim 1’s “public-span-not-a-verified-suite” reading weakens toward a real integrated suite. Inverse: the broadest footprints stay spans of distinct public surfaces → the claim holds. Primary source: vendors’ own product pages, single-platform reference architectures, and investor materials; analyst reclassification.

  4. An encryption-erosion or 5G-SA inflection (National Agencies + Law Enforcement Monitoring Centers + Tactical Intelligence). Signal: a public demonstration of durable 5G-SA content interception at scale (which would relieve the National Agencies and Tactical Intelligence squeeze), or, conversely, accelerating 4G sunset and ECH/QUIC adoption reported as breaking deployed interception. Threshold: either event named publicly → re-rank the technology-shift pressure on the three interception-and-collection fronts. Primary source: 3GPP/ETSI standards activity, vendor ETI product-page changes, named-outlet telecom coverage.

  5. A further export-control or accountability action (National Agencies + Tactical Intelligence). Signal: a new Entity-List designation, EU Dual-Use enforcement, or sanctions action against a named collection or surveillance vendor — or a cured-and-restructured re-entry on the Sandvine model. Threshold: one named action → the regulatory-restructuring strand of Pattern Claim 3 extends and the legitimate gradeable set narrows further. Primary source: US BIS / Federal Register, EU DPA and dual-use enforcement press, Citizen Lab / Amnesty public analysis.

The throughline of all five signals is the same one the convergence opened on: value is migrating up the stack, the floor is rising under collection, and the contest in 2026 is for the analytical layer. Where a vendor sits relative to that migration — climbing toward fusion, defending a standards-gated niche, or stuck in commoditizing collection — is the single best public predictor of which side of this market’s consolidation it will be on.

All sources are public: vendors’ own dated product pages, public filings, and dated named-outlet reporting, carried over from the five front chapters this synthesis reconciles. Market-size figures are cited to their publishers and are never averaged. Capability is reported as public positioning (“markets itself as”), not as verified architecture.
